teile.einleitung: Vegetables are edible parts of plants, for example leaves, roots, tubers or stalks. Vegetables are healthy because they contain lots of vitamins, minerals and fibre and little fat.
wichtigste: Vegetables are edible parts of plants such as leaves, roots or tubers.
Broccoli, carrots, lettuce and leeks are vegetables.
Apples, pears and cherries are fruit.
Vegetables contain lots of vitamins and fibre.
Several portions of vegetables are recommended every day.
Many vegetables also grow in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Vegetables are parts of plants that are usually eaten cooked or raw as a side dish or main course. With **broccoli** you eat the flower buds, with **lettuce** the leaves. With **carrots** you eat the root, with the **potato** the tuber. With the **leek** it is the stalk.

**Fruit** is usually the sweet produce of trees and bushes, such as apples, pears or cherries. Vegetables often taste less sweet. Some plants are hard to sort: tomatoes and cucumbers are really the fruit of the plant, but in the kitchen they count as vegetables. A simple way to remember: broccoli is a vegetable, the apple is a fruit.

Vegetables provide **vitamins** and **minerals** that the body needs. They have lots of **fibre**, which is good for digestion and fills you up. And vegetables are low in fat. Nutrition experts recommend eating three portions of vegetables and two portions of fruit every day.

Many vegetables grow in Switzerland, for example carrots, potatoes, cabbage, leeks, lettuce and onions. A lot of vegetables come, for instance, from the **Seeland** in the canton of Bern. Vegetables that are in **season** are often especially fresh and do not have to be transported far. A seasonal calendar shows when each vegetable is harvested.

gewusst: Broccoli is closely related to cauliflower, Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi; they all come from wild cabbage.
The potato originally came to Europe from South America.

teile.einleitung: There are lots of invisible germs on our hands. Washing your hands thoroughly removes them and protects you and others from illness. It is very simple with water and soap.
wichtigste: You wash your hands with water and soap.
You rub them for at least 20 seconds.
You wash your hands before eating and before cooking.
You always wash your hands after going to the toilet.
Thumbs and the spaces between the fingers are often forgotten.
Afterwards you dry your hands well.

abschnitte.text: We touch lots of things with our hands, for example door handles, toys or animals. This puts **germs** on our hands. You cannot see them, but they can make you ill. If we then touch food or rub our eyes, the germs can get into the body. Washing your hands helps to prevent this.

You wash your hands before **eating** and before **cooking**, so that no germs get into the food. You always wash them after **going to the toilet**. It is also sensible to wash your hands after playing outside, after blowing your nose and after stroking animals.

First you wet your hands. Then you take **soap** and rub your hands for at least **20 seconds**. That is about as long as singing “Happy Birthday” twice. Do not forget your **thumbs**, your **fingertips** and the spaces **between your fingers**. Then you rinse off the soap with water.

Finally you dry your hands well with a **clean towel**. Germs can survive and spread more easily on wet hands. At school or in public toilets there are often paper towels or hand dryers. At home it is best for each person to have their own towel.

gewusst: Soap works because it loosens grease and dirt from the skin, so that the water can wash the germs away.
As long ago as the 19th century, the doctor Ignaz Semmelweis showed that handwashing in hospital saves lives.

teile.einleitung: **Seasonality** means that fruit and vegetables only ripen at certain times of year. If you shop seasonally, you choose products that are growing in your region at the time. This is often better for the climate and brings fresh flavour to your plate.
wichtigste: Shopping seasonally means buying what is ripe in your region at the time.
Swiss outdoor strawberries are available roughly from May to July.
Pumpkin is a typical autumn vegetable.
Stored vegetables such as carrots and cabbage are available from Switzerland even in winter.
Air-freighted goods and vegetables from heated greenhouses are very bad for the climate.
A seasonal calendar shows what is in season.

abschnitte.text: Seasonal products have grown in the **region** at the right **time of year** and been harvested ripe. They have short **transport routes** and usually do not need heated greenhouses. A **seasonal calendar** lists month by month which fruit and vegetables are available fresh from Switzerland. Such calendars come as posters, in brochures or as apps.

In **spring** people gather **wild garlic** in the woods, a wild herb that smells of garlic. You have to tell it apart carefully from poisonous plants such as lily of the valley and autumn crocus. In **early summer**, roughly from May to July, there are Swiss **outdoor strawberries**. In late summer and **autumn**, **pumpkins** are harvested, which can be stored for a long time. In winter people eat **stored vegetables** such as carrots, cabbage, celeriac and beetroot.

Some fruit comes by **aeroplane** from faraway countries. Aeroplanes use a great deal of fuel and give off a lot of **CO2**. That is why air-freighted goods are much worse for the climate than goods that come by ship or lorry. Tomatoes from a **heated greenhouse** in winter can also harm the climate. Heating takes a lot of energy, often from fossil fuels.

Seasonal vegetables grown **outdoors** need no extra heating energy. They are harvested ripe and so often taste better. Regional products also support **farms** nearby. And because a lot is harvested in season, it is often cheaper too.

gewusst: Air-freighted goods can cause many times more CO2 than the same goods transported by ship.
Well-stored carrots and cabbage from Switzerland are available until well into spring.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland a chimney sweep is called Kaminfeger rather than Schornsteinfeger. Chimney sweeps clean chimneys and check heating systems. In this way they make sure that no fires start and the air stays clean.
wichtigste: In Switzerland people say Kaminfeger instead of Schornsteinfeger.
Chimney sweeps clean chimneys and heating systems.
Soot builds up in the chimney and can catch fire.
Chimney sweeps also measure the exhaust gases from heating systems.
They have been seen as bringers of good luck for a long time.
You learn the job as a chimney sweep EFZ.

abschnitte.text: When wood, oil or gas burns, **smoke** is produced. It goes outside through the **chimney**. As it does so, **soot** sticks to the walls. If too much soot is not removed, it can catch fire, and a dangerous **chimney fire** breaks out. That is why chimney sweeps clean chimneys regularly.

Chimney sweeps work with round **brushes**, which they pull through the chimney on a long line or on rods. With scrapers they loosen stubborn soot. A **soot vacuum** makes sure that nothing in the flat gets dirty. Chimney sweeps often climb onto the **roof** for this. That is why they must not be afraid of heights and need good safety equipment.

Chimney sweeps do not only clean, they also **check**. With measuring instruments they test the **exhaust gases** from heating systems. This shows them whether a heating system burns well and does not pollute the air too much. They also advise house owners on **fire safety** and saving energy. A well-adjusted heating system uses less fuel.

In the past, a chimney fire was dangerous for whole villages. When people saw the chimney sweep, they knew they were safe. That is why the chimney sweep is still seen today as a **bringer of good luck**, especially at New Year. In Switzerland you learn the job as a **chimney sweep EFZ**. The black work clothes are typical, with a **top hat** on formal occasions.

gewusst: In the past, in some countries, even children climbed through narrow chimneys to clean them. This has long been forbidden.
Many people touch a chimney sweep because it is supposed to bring good luck.

teile.einleitung: The regional employment centre, RAV for short, helps people who are looking for a job. It advises jobseekers, passes on vacancies and checks whether they are applying enough. However, the money from unemployment insurance is not paid by the RAV, but by an unemployment fund.
wichtigste: The RAV advises jobseekers, finds them vacancies and checks their efforts.
The daily allowances are paid by an unemployment fund that you can choose freely.
In principle the daily allowance is 80 per cent, in certain cases 70 per cent, of the insured earnings.
Usually you need at least 12 months of contributions within two years.
Young insured people up to 25 with no maintenance obligations receive at most 200 daily allowances.
The general waiting period is in principle five days.
Jobseekers must prove their efforts to find work every month.

abschnitte.text: If you lose your job, you register with the **RAV**. A **personal adviser** discusses with the person which jobs might be suitable. The RAV passes on vacancies and can offer courses, for example on applications or languages. It also checks whether jobseekers are making enough effort to find new work. There are RAVs in all the cantons.

The money from **unemployment insurance** (ALV) is called a **daily allowance**. It is not paid by the RAV, but by an **unemployment fund**, which you can choose freely. In principle the daily allowance is **80 per cent** of the insured earnings. Anyone who does not have to support children and would get a daily allowance of more than 140 francs receives **70 per cent**. Before the first daily allowance there is in principle a **waiting period** of five days.

To receive unemployment benefit you usually need at least **12 months of contributions** within a **qualifying period** of two years. There are exceptions, for example after training or an illness. How many daily allowances you get depends on your age and the period of contributions. Young insured people up to 25 with no maintenance obligations receive at most **200 daily allowances**. This is meant to encourage a quick start in the world of work.

Jobseekers must prove their **efforts to find work** to the RAV every month, which means showing where they have applied. They must attend advice meetings and accept reasonable jobs. Anyone who makes too little effort can receive **suspension days**. On these days no daily allowance is paid. The aim is always to find work again as quickly as possible.

Since 2018 there has been an **obligation to report vacancies**. In occupations with high unemployment, employers must first report vacancies to the RAV. At the beginning the threshold was an unemployment rate of 8 per cent, and since **2020** it has been **5 per cent**. For **five working days**, only the RAV and registered jobseekers can see these vacancies. Only after that may they be advertised publicly.

gewusst: Unemployment insurance is financed through deductions from wages, which employers and employees each pay half of.
If you are registered with the RAV, you can see jobs that other people do not even know about yet.

teile.einleitung: The Marine Stewardship Council, MSC for short, is an organisation that promotes sustainable fishing. Its blue label appears on wild-caught fish products where the fish stocks are not overfished.
wichtigste: MSC stands for Marine Stewardship Council.
The MSC label stands for sustainably caught wild fish.
The MSC was founded in 1997 by WWF and Unilever.
Since 1999 the MSC has been independent.
For farmed fish there is the ASC label.

abschnitte.text: The **MSC label** marks fish and seafood that are **wild-caught**. The fishery must show that the **fish stocks** are not overfished and can recover. It should also harm the marine environment as little as possible. Independent inspectors check that the rules are kept. You can find the label in many Swiss shops.

The MSC was founded in **1997** by the environmental organisation **WWF** and the food company **Unilever**. The background was that many fish stocks around the world were being heavily fished. Since **1999** the MSC has been an **independent** non-profit organisation.

For fish from **aquaculture**, that is from fish farming, there is the **ASC label** (Aquaculture Stewardship Council). In short: MSC is for wild-caught fish, ASC for farmed fish. Other labels cover other areas: **FSC** stands for wood and paper, **IP-Suisse** for Swiss farm products.

gewusst: The English word “stewardship” means roughly responsible management or care.
The MSC label is blue and shows a stylised fish with a tick.

teile.einleitung: In a **shared flat**, called a WG in German, several people share one flat. This is cheap and sociable, but it also comes with rules: about the tenancy agreement, about money and in everyday life.
wichtigste: In a shared flat, several people share the kitchen, bathroom and often the living room.
If everyone signs the tenancy agreement, each member is liable for the whole rent.
If there is a main tenant, only she is liable to the landlord.
A joint tenancy agreement must be terminated by all the tenants together.
Only one radio and television licence fee is paid per household.
A shared kitty helps with joint expenses.

abschnitte.text: If all the members of a shared flat sign the tenancy agreement, they are **joint tenants**. Then **joint and several liability** applies: if the rent is not paid, the landlord may demand the whole rent from each individual person. Giving notice is also only possible **together**: all the tenants must sign the notice. So if someone moves out, an agreement with the landlord is needed.

Often there is a **main tenant** who signs the contract alone. The others live with her as **subtenants**. Then only the main tenant is liable to the landlord. She needs the landlord's consent for subletting. According to the Code of Obligations, he may only refuse for certain reasons, for example if the terms of the sublet are abusive, such as a room price that is far too high.

The costs are usually shared. An example: the flat costs 2400 francs rent plus 300 francs service charges, 2700 francs together. With three people sharing equally, each pays 900 francs. The **radio and television licence fee** is charged per household, so a shared flat only pays it once. Many shared flats keep a **shared kitty** for cleaning products, toilet paper or basic food.

To make life in a shared flat work well, clear agreements help. A **chore rota** sets out who cleans, takes out the rubbish or does the shopping when. Quiet times and visitors should also be discussed. If there are arguments, a regular flat meeting helps. Many young people in training or at university live in a shared flat.

gewusst: Older people also sometimes set up shared flats so that they do not live alone in old age.
If you move into a shared flat, you have to register with the municipality.

teile.einleitung: The Passerelle is a bridge from the vocational path to university. If you have a vocational Matura, you can study at a university or at the ETH after an additional examination. The word Passerelle comes from French and means footbridge.
wichtigste: The Passerelle is an additional examination after the vocational Matura.
It makes it possible to study at a university or the ETH.
Without the Passerelle, the vocational Matura leads to a university of applied sciences.
Preparation usually takes about a year.
Several general education subjects are examined.
The word Passerelle means footbridge.

abschnitte.text: The **Passerelle** is a supplementary examination for people with a vocational Matura or specialised Matura. Those who pass it have the same opportunities as with a gymnasial **Matura**. They may then study at all Swiss universities and at both ETHs. It was introduced to make the education system more flexible.

First you do an apprenticeship with a **vocational Matura**, either during the apprenticeship or afterwards. Then you attend a preparation course for the Passerelle. This usually lasts two semesters, so about a year. Some people also prepare on their own.

The subjects examined include German or another first language, a foreign language and maths. On top of that come **natural sciences** such as biology, chemistry and physics. Humanities and social sciences such as history and geography are also included. The examination is organised by the Swiss **Matura Commission**.

The Passerelle shows that in Switzerland many paths lead to the goal. You can first learn a trade and still later study medicine, law or physics. This way you combine practical **work experience** with university study. Many skilled workers value this second chance.

The Passerelle is demanding and requires a lot of hard work. It is worth finding out about it early from the careers advice service. If you know what you want to study, you can plan more precisely. For some courses, for example medicine, you also need an **aptitude test**.

begriffe.erklaerung: French for footbridge; here, a bridge to university.
A qualification alongside or after an apprenticeship that opens the way to a university of applied sciences.
The qualification from the Gymnasium that entitles you to study at university.
Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich or Lausanne.

gewusst: With the Passerelle, an apprentice can later become a doctor or a researcher.
You can also later get into a university via a university of applied sciences with a bachelor's degree, so the Passerelle is not the only way.

teile.einleitung: Clean clothes are part of everyday life. With a few simple rules, your washing stays nice for a long time, and you save electricity and water as well.
wichtigste: You sort washing by colour so that nothing runs.
The washing temperature and the type of fabric also matter.
Washing at a lower temperature saves the most energy.
Care symbols on the label show how to treat an item of clothing.
Drying washing in the air uses no electricity.

abschnitte.text: Before washing, the laundry is **sorted**. Light and dark clothes are washed separately so that dark colours do not **run** onto light ones. Otherwise a new red T-shirt can turn a white shirt pink. You also sort by fabric: delicate things such as wool need their own programme. Before washing, you empty all the pockets.

Almost every item of clothing has a label with **care symbols**. The **washing tub** shows the highest washing temperature; a hand in it means hand wash. The **triangle** stands for bleaching, the **square** for drying and the **iron** for ironing. A circle concerns dry cleaning. If a symbol is crossed out, you must not do it.

You save the most energy by washing at a **lower temperature**. For normally dirty washing, 30 or 40 degrees is often enough. The machine should be well filled, but not overfilled. You use the amount of washing powder given on the packet, because too much harms the environment and does not help. Drying washing on a clothes horse or a line uses no electricity, whereas a tumble dryer uses a lot.

gewusst: In many Swiss blocks of flats people share a washing machine in the laundry room, with a rota saying who may wash when.

teile.einleitung: **Tidiness** means that everything has its own fixed place. In a tidy room you can find things again quickly. With a few simple rules it stays tidy too.
wichtigste: Everything has a fixed place.
Dirty washing goes in the laundry basket.
After playing you put things away again.
In a tidy room you find everything more quickly.
Tidying up a little every day is easier than doing a lot at once.

abschnitte.text: Dirty socks, T-shirts and trousers belong in the **laundry basket**. That is where you collect clothes until they are washed. You put clean clothes in the **wardrobe** or in the drawer. This way no clothes are left lying on the floor. And you always know what is clean and what needs washing.

Being tidy is easy if everything has a **fixed place**. Toys go in a box, books on the shelf and pens in a tin. After playing you put everything back in its place. Boxes with pictures or names on them help with this. This way everyone in the family knows where things belong.

If you tidy up for **a few minutes** every day, you never have to spend hours clearing up chaos. A good time is in the evening before bed. It is also best to pack your **school bag** the evening before. Then everything is ready in the morning and you do not forget anything.

In a family everyone helps. You clear away your plate, hang up your jacket and put your shoes away neatly. This is fair, because otherwise one person has to do everything alone. Tidiness saves **time** and **trouble**, because you do not have to search for a long time.

gewusst: Many people spend several minutes every day looking for things such as keys or mobile phones.
If you always put things down in the same place, you hardly ever have to look for them.

teile.einleitung: How much nature does a person need for their life? The **ecological footprint** gives an answer to this. It shows whether we use more than the Earth can replace.
wichtigste: The ecological footprint measures the area you need for your lifestyle.
It is usually given in global hectares.
The Swiss Mathis Wackernagel helped to develop the concept in the 1990s.
According to the FOEN, if everyone lived as people do in Switzerland, almost three Earths would be needed.
On Earth Overshoot Day, nature's annual budget has been used up.
Biocapacity shows how much nature in a country can replace.

abschnitte.text: The **ecological footprint** measures how much fertile land is needed to produce everything a person uses. This includes fields for food, forests for wood, pastures, fishing grounds and land for houses and roads. The forest that would be needed to absorb the CO₂ given off is also included. The result is usually given in **global hectares**. This is an area of average fertility.

The concept was developed in the 1990s by **Mathis Wackernagel** and William Rees at a university in Canada. Wackernagel comes from Basel. He later founded the **Global Footprint Network**, which calculates the footprint of many countries. The idea is simple: you compare what we use with what nature can provide.

**Biocapacity** shows how much nature in a country can replace. Switzerland uses much more than its own nature provides. According to the Federal Office for the Environment, **almost three Earths** would be needed if everyone lived the way people do in Switzerland. Each year **Earth Overshoot Day** marks the day on which humanity has used up nature's annual budget. After that, it is living on credit, so to speak.

Everyone can make their own footprint smaller. Travelling **by train instead of by plane** makes a big difference. Eating less meat, choosing regional food, heating less and using things for a long time also help. On the internet there are calculators you can use to estimate your personal footprint.

gewusst: Besides the ecological footprint, there is also a water footprint and a carbon footprint.
Earth Overshoot Day now falls much earlier in the year than it did 50 years ago.

teile.einleitung: If you do not pay a bill in Switzerland, debt collection proceedings (Betreibung) can be started against you. This is a regulated procedure that a creditor can use to collect their money with the help of the state. It is governed by the Federal Debt Collection and Bankruptcy Act, SchKG for short.
wichtigste: The creditor submits a debt collection request to the debt collection office.
As a first step, the debtor receives a payment order.
Within 10 days the debtor can lodge an objection.
The debt collection office does not check whether the claim really exists.
In a wage seizure, the subsistence minimum always remains.
Debt collection proceedings appear in the debt collection register, which landlords often want to see.

abschnitte.text: Debt collection proceedings begin with the creditor's **debt collection request**. For private individuals, the responsible office is usually the **debt collection office where the debtor lives**. The office delivers a **payment order** to the debtor. It calls on the debtor to pay the debt within 20 days. Important: in Switzerland anyone can start debt collection proceedings without proving the claim.

If the debtor does not agree, he can lodge an **objection** (Rechtsvorschlag). He must do this within **10 days** of delivery. The objection stops the proceedings for the time being. Now the creditor must prove that the claim exists. If he has a signed **acknowledgement of debt**, he can ask the court for **provisional removal of the objection**. With a court judgment there is **definitive removal of the objection**.

If the debtor still does not pay, the office can **seize** assets or wages. Only the part of the income above the **subsistence minimum** may be seized. What is absolutely necessary to live on stays with the debtor. If the money is not enough, the creditor receives a **certificate of loss**. This claim only expires 20 years after it is issued.

All debt collection proceedings are entered in the **debt collection register**. Many landlords ask for an **extract** from it before they let a flat. Five years after proceedings have ended, third parties no longer receive information about them. Since 2019 you can defend yourself against unjustified proceedings: no earlier than three months after they began, you can submit a **request for non-disclosure**. If the creditor does not prove within 20 days that he has taken further steps, the proceedings are no longer disclosed to third parties.

gewusst: Because the office does not check the claim, in Switzerland proceedings can be started against you even without a real debt.
If you talk to the creditor early or go to a debt advice service, you can often avoid debt collection proceedings.

teile.einleitung: **Nutrients** are the substances in our food that the body needs to live. They provide energy, serve as building materials or control important processes in the body. A varied diet supplies us with all the nutrients.
wichtigste: Only carbohydrates, fats and protein provide energy.
Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients that the body needs in tiny amounts.
Protein is the most important building material for muscles and cells.
An adult's body consists of about 50 to 60 per cent water.
The nutrition table shows how many nutrients there are in a food.
On the list of ingredients, the ingredient with the largest share comes first.

abschnitte.text: The body needs **carbohydrates**, **fats** and **protein** in larger amounts. That is why they are called **macronutrients**. They contain energy that the body uses for moving, thinking and growing. Carbohydrates are found, for example, in bread, pasta and potatoes. Fat provides especially a lot of energy. **Protein** is also the most important **building material** for muscles, skin, hair and cells.

The body needs **vitamins** and **minerals** only in milligrams or micrograms. That is why they are called **micronutrients**. They provide no energy, but are essential. They regulate many processes, such as the **immune system** or metabolism. That is why they are also called **protective and regulating substances**. Fruit, vegetables and wholegrain foods are good sources.

**Water** also counts as a vital substance. An adult's body consists of about **50 to 60 per cent** water, and in children the proportion is a little higher. Water provides no energy, but it carries nutrients and regulates temperature. Plants also produce **secondary plant compounds** such as carotenoids or flavonoids. They give fruit and vegetables their colour and scent and are thought to be good for health.

On packaged food you will find the **nutrition table**. It shows how much energy, fat, carbohydrates, sugar, protein and salt it contains, usually per 100 grams or 100 millilitres. The **list of ingredients**, on the other hand, says what a product is made of. The ingredients are listed **by amount**, the largest first. If sugar is right at the front, it is a main ingredient.

gewusst: One gram of fat provides more than twice as much energy as one gram of carbohydrates or protein.
Babies are made up of an even larger proportion of water than adults.

teile.einleitung: **Milk** is a white drink that mammals produce for their young. The milk we buy in the shop usually comes from the **cow**. In Switzerland milk has been one of the most important foods for a long time.
wichtigste: Most milk in Switzerland comes from cows.
There is also milk from goats and sheep.
Butter, cheese, yoghurt and cream are made from milk.
Milk contains calcium, which makes bones and teeth strong.
Milk must be kept in the fridge.

abschnitte.text: A cow gives milk after she has had a calf. The farmer usually **milks** the cows twice a day, today often with a **milking machine**. The milk is cooled and then collected by a lorry. At the **dairy** it is tested, heated and bottled. Besides cow's milk there is also milk from **goats** and **sheep**.

Many foods are made from milk; they are called **dairy products**. From the fat of the milk, the **cream**, **butter** is churned. With the help of bacteria, milk becomes **yoghurt**. And from a great deal of milk, **cheese** is made. One kilo of hard cheese needs about twelve litres of milk. Switzerland is famous for cheeses such as Emmental, Gruyère or Appenzeller.

Milk contains **protein**, fat, milk sugar and vitamins. The mineral **calcium** is especially important. It helps **bones and teeth** to become strong. Some people cannot digest milk sugar well. They drink lactose-free milk or drinks made from oats or soya instead.

Fresh milk goes off quickly when it is warm. That is why it belongs in the **fridge**. An opened carton should be finished within a few days. If the milk smells sour, it is no longer good. **Long-life milk** has been heated strongly and, unopened, can stand outside the fridge for a long time.

gewusst: One kilo of hard cheese needs about twelve litres of milk.
A cow eats and drinks a great deal every day: she often needs more than 50 litres of water.

teile.einleitung: In a circular economy, materials should be used for as long as possible instead of ending up as rubbish. Products are shared, repaired, reused and finally recycled. This means fewer new raw materials are needed.
wichtigste: The linear economy follows the principle: take, make, throw away.
The circular economy keeps materials in circulation for as long as possible.
In the waste hierarchy, prevention comes first.
Cradle to Cradle means “from cradle to cradle”.
In upcycling, something more valuable is made from waste.
Planned obsolescence deliberately shortens the life of a product.
In Switzerland more than 90 per cent of glass is collected.

abschnitte.text: In the **linear economy**, raw materials are extracted, made into products and thrown away after use. In short: **take, make, throw away**. The **circular economy** wants to change this. Materials should stay in circulation for as long as possible. An important promoter of this idea is the **Ellen MacArthur Foundation** from Britain, which the sailor Ellen MacArthur founded in 2010.

The **waste hierarchy** shows what is best: first **prevent**, then **reuse**, then **recycle**, then recover energy, which means burning the waste and gaining energy. Only right at the end comes disposal. The best waste is waste that never arises at all. In Switzerland many materials are collected. More than 90 per cent of **glass** is collected, and PET and aluminium also have high collection rates.

The **Cradle to Cradle** concept comes from Michael Braungart and William McDonough. It means “from cradle to cradle”. After use, products should return completely to **biological** or **technical cycles**. In **upcycling**, a higher-value product is made from waste. A well-known Swiss example is bags made from used lorry tarpaulins.

With **planned obsolescence**, a product is deliberately made so that it breaks or becomes outdated early. This goes against the circular economy. One alternative model is **“product as a service”**: you do not buy a lamp, but pay for light. The manufacturer remains the owner and therefore has an interest in long-lasting, repairable products.

gewusst: Used glass can be melted down again and again without losing quality.
Since 1993 the Zurich company Freitag has been making bags from old lorry tarpaulins.

teile.einleitung: Not all work is paid with wages. Cooking, cleaning, looking after children or helping in a club is **unpaid work**. The Federal Statistical Office (FSO) measures how much of it is done in Switzerland and what it is worth.
wichtigste: According to the FSO, about 9.8 billion hours of unpaid work were done in Switzerland in 2020.
That is more than the number of paid working hours.
The value of this work in 2020 was about 434 billion francs.
In 2020 women did about 60 per cent of the unpaid work.
Housework makes up the largest part, followed by care work.
Unpaid work is missing from gross domestic product.

abschnitte.text: Unpaid work covers three areas. The largest part is **housework**: cooking, cleaning, washing and shopping. Next comes **care work**, for example looking after children or caring for a relative who is ill. The third area is **voluntary work**. **Formal** voluntary work is done in clubs or charities, **informal** voluntary work privately, for example helping neighbours.

For **2020**, the FSO recorded about **9.8 billion hours** of unpaid work. That is **more** than the number of paid working hours in the same year. **Women** did about **60 per cent** of the unpaid work, while men did the larger part of the paid work. The FSO estimated the money value of unpaid work for 2020 at about **434 billion francs**.

abschnitte.titel: Why it is missing from GDP
abschnitte.text: **Gross domestic product** (GDP) mainly records goods and services traded at **market prices**. If you cook at home yourself, value is created, but there is no turnover. That is why unpaid work does not appear in GDP. The FSO therefore adds the **household production satellite account** to the national accounts. It makes housework and family work visible in the statistics.

There are different methods for valuing unpaid work in francs. The **market cost method** uses the wage that an employed **specialist** would receive for the same task, for example a cook's wage for cooking. The **opportunity cost method**, on the other hand, uses the wage that the person could earn in their own job. Depending on the method, the total value comes out differently.

gewusst: In Switzerland more work is done unpaid than paid.
The value of unpaid work is comparable to a large part of gross domestic product.

teile.einleitung: Food does not stay fresh for ever. On the packaging there is a date that helps with the shelf life. If you understand the dates properly, you eat safely and throw away less food.
wichtigste: “Best before” is the manufacturer's guarantee of quality.
After this date a food is often still good.
You check it with your eyes, nose and tongue.
“Use by” appears on highly perishable foods such as mince.
After the use-by date you no longer eat the food.
Many things keep longer if they are stored cool and properly.

abschnitte.text: The **best-before date** says that until this day the manufacturer guarantees the food is good, if it is stored properly. After that it is often still fine to eat for a long time. So a yoghurt that is one day past the date does not have to be thrown away straight away. You **look** at it, **smell** it and **taste** it carefully.

Highly perishable foods such as mince, fresh fish or raw poultry say **“use by”**. This is the **use-by date**. After this day you should no longer eat the food, even if it still looks fine. That is because you often cannot see or smell germs that cause illness.

How long something keeps also depends on how it is **stored**. Dairy products, meat and fish belong in the fridge at no more than about 5 degrees. Bread, pasta and rice are stored dry. You close opened packets well. If **mould** appears, you no longer eat the food.

gewusst: Sugar, salt and honey keep almost indefinitely if stored dry.
A lot of food that would still be good ends up in the bin just because of the best-before date.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, choosing a career usually begins at lower secondary school. At about 13 to 15, many young people try out different jobs. This way they can find out which apprenticeship suits them.
wichtigste: Taster apprenticeships are usually done at lower secondary school.
Most young people are then about 13 to 15 years old.
At school, choosing a career is supported in the subject of vocational orientation.
Many apprenticeship places are given out about a year before the apprenticeship starts.
That is why it is worth starting taster days early.

abschnitte.titel: Choosing a career at lower secondary school
abschnitte.text: After primary school comes **lower secondary school**, which in some cantons is also called secondary level I. This is where **choosing a career** begins. At school, young people get to know different jobs and think about what suits them. Teachers, parents and the **careers advice service** help with this. An important part of this is the taster apprenticeships.

Many young people do their first taster days at about **13 or 14**. In their last school year they then apply for an **apprenticeship place**. Many companies give out their apprenticeship places about a year before the apprenticeship starts. If you start taster days early, you have more time to compare. That leaves enough time to try out several jobs.

Before your taster days, it is worth thinking about your own **strengths and interests**. Do you like working with your hands, with people or on the computer? The **careers advice service** has tests and information about many jobs. A visit to a **careers fair** can also help. This way you find out where you would like to try things out.

gewusst: In Switzerland about two thirds of young people do an apprenticeship after compulsory school.

teile.einleitung: Food waste means that edible food ends up in the bin or is lost along the way. This happens all the way from the field to the plate. Switzerland wants to halve these losses by 2030.
wichtigste: Food waste means that edible food is lost.
In Switzerland about 2.8 million tonnes of food are lost every year.
Most losses occur in processing, followed by households.
For 2017, about 330 kg of avoidable losses per person were calculated.
In 2022 the Federal Council adopted an action plan.
By 2030, avoidable losses are to be halved compared with 2017.
A shopping list helps against food waste.

abschnitte.text: **Food waste** means food that could actually be eaten but is thrown away or lost. According to the Federal Office for the Environment (**FOEN**), about **2.8 million tonnes** of food are lost every year because of Swiss consumption. For 2017, about **330 kg** of avoidable losses per person were calculated, across the whole chain from field to plate.

There are losses in the field, in **processing**, in shops, in restaurants and in **households**. According to a 2019 study by ETH Zurich for the FOEN, about a third of the losses occur in processing, for example as peelings and rejects. In second place come private households, with just over a quarter.

Growing, transporting, chilling and processing food needs **water**, **land** and **energy**. If the food is thrown away, all these resources were used for nothing. That is why in 2022 the **Federal Council** adopted an **action plan** against food waste. The aim: avoidable losses are to be halved by **2030** compared with 2017.

If you shop with a **shopping list** and according to a plan, you buy too much less often. You check foods with a best-before date with your eyes and nose before throwing them away. You let **leftovers** from lunch cool quickly and put them in the fridge, well covered. The next day you can eat them or make them into a new dish.

gewusst: You can make delicious dishes from old bread, for example French toast (Fotzelschnitten).
Crooked carrots or small apples are just as good, but are often sorted out because they do not meet the standard.

teile.einleitung: Before a loaf is in the shop, many businesses have worked on it. Each stage turns a product into something more valuable. This sequence is called the **value chain**.
wichtigste: A value chain shows all the stages from raw material to finished product.
Value added is the sales value minus the inputs.
All the value added along the chain together gives the value of the end product.
In 1985 Michael E. Porter described the value chain of a company.
If a company carries out several stages itself, this is called vertical integration.
The Covid-19 pandemic showed how vulnerable global chains are.

abschnitte.text: A farmer sells wheat for 100 francs to a mill. The mill sells the flour for 250 francs to a bakery, and the bakery sells the bread for 600 francs. The **value added** at one stage is its sales value minus the **inputs**, that is what it had to buy in itself. For the bakery that is 600 minus 250, which is 350 francs. If you add up all the stages (100, 150 and 350 francs), you get 600 francs: exactly the value of the bread.

In 1985 the American economist **Michael E. Porter** presented the model of the **value chain** in his book “Competitive Advantage”. It shows where value is created within a single company. **Primary activities** include purchasing, production, sales and customer service. **Support activities** such as human resources or technology development help with this. This way a company can see where it is particularly strong.

Stan Shih, the founder of the computer company Acer, described the so-called **smiling curve**. If you draw the value added along the chain, the line looks like a smile. At the beginning (research, development, design) and at the end (brand, marketing, service) the value added is high. In the middle, in pure manufacturing, it tends to be low. That is why many companies keep research and their brand in their own hands.

In **vertical integration**, a company carries out several stages itself, for example a retailer with its own production plants. The opposite is **outsourcing**: tasks such as accounting, cleaning or production are given to specialised outside firms. If production is moved to a faraway country, this is called offshoring. With **nearshoring**, a nearer country is chosen, for example in Eastern Europe instead of Asia.

Today many products are made in **global value chains** across several countries. This can be cheap, but it makes the chain vulnerable. During the **Covid-19 pandemic**, factories were closed and ports blocked. As a result there was a shortage, for example, of semiconductors for cars and electronics and of certain medicines. Since then many companies have been thinking about how to make their supply chains more secure.

gewusst: A single smartphone contains parts from many different countries.
The total of all value added in a country in one year is an important part of gross domestic product (GDP).

teile.einleitung: Some children really want to know what a device looks like inside and why it works. This curiosity about technology is a real strength. In Switzerland there are many exciting technical jobs for it.
wichtigste: Curiosity about technology goes well with technical jobs.
Polymechanics make parts for machines and assemble machines.
Electronics technicians develop and test electronic circuits.
Spatial awareness and maths are helpful for technical jobs.
The apprenticeships as polymechanic EFZ and electronics technician EFZ last four years.
Technical jobs are open to girls and boys in exactly the same way.

abschnitte.text: People with a gift for technology like taking things apart and putting them back together. Such people are **curious**, good with their hands and patient when tinkering. They can often picture well how parts fit together. This is called **spatial awareness**. Enjoying maths and physics also helps in technical jobs.

The **polymechanic** makes individual parts out of metal or plastic. She works with lathes and milling machines, which are often controlled by a computer. Then she assembles the parts into machines, devices or tools and checks that everything is exactly right. Sometimes it is a matter of fractions of a millimetre. The apprenticeship as a polymechanic EFZ lasts four years.

The **electronics technician** works with electronic circuits like those inside mobile phones, cars or medical devices. She builds them, takes measurements and looks for faults. Other technical jobs include, for example, **automation technician**, design engineer, computer scientist or plant and equipment builder. Many of these jobs belong to the engineering, electrical and metal industries, which are very important in Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: Finding out whether it suits you
abschnitte.text: The best way to find out whether a technical job suits you is a **taster apprenticeship**. There you see a working day in the workshop close up. Technology courses, robotics at school or repairing bikes also show whether you enjoy technology. The careers advice service at the careers information centre, **BIZ** for short, gives tips. Technical jobs are just as suitable for girls as for boys.

gewusst: After a technical apprenticeship with a vocational Matura you can study, for example, mechanical or electrical engineering at a university of applied sciences.
Polymechanics often work so precisely that they use measuring instruments for thousandths of a millimetre.

teile.einleitung: Many things we use every day are not made in one place. A T-shirt or a smartphone often travels a long way around the world before it reaches our shops. This is called global production.
wichtigste: Raw materials, manufacturing and sales often take place in different countries.
After China, Bangladesh is one of the largest exporters of clothing.
In 2013 the Rana Plaza textile factory collapsed in Bangladesh, and more than 1100 people died.
Cotton needs a great deal of water to grow.
The Aral Sea has largely dried up because of the irrigation of cotton fields.
Much of the cobalt for batteries comes from the DR Congo.
Fast fashion means cheap fashion that changes quickly.

abschnitte.text: In global production, manufacturing is spread across many countries. This is called a **supply chain**. Raw materials are extracted in one place, processed in another and assembled in a third. Companies often choose the places according to cost. Labour-intensive work such as sewing is hard to automate and so moves to where **wages are low**.

China is the largest exporter of clothing, followed closely by **Bangladesh**. There the textile industry is the most important export sector. On 24 April 2013 the **Rana Plaza** factory building near Dhaka collapsed, and 1134 people died. After that, an agreement on fire and building safety was created. **Fast fashion** is also criticised: new, cheap collections arrive in the shops every few weeks.

**Cotton** is often grown with artificial irrigation in dry areas. A single T-shirt can require several thousand litres of water. A well-known example is the **Aral Sea** in Central Asia. Since the 1960s, water from its feeder rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, has been diverted to cotton fields. As a result, the lake lost most of its area.

A smartphone contains raw materials from many countries. According to the US Geological Survey, the **DR Congo** mined about three quarters of the world's **cobalt** in 2023, which is used in batteries. Small-scale mining and child labour there are criticised. China dominates the mining and processing of **rare earths**. Many devices are assembled by contract manufacturers such as **Foxconn** from Taiwan, which runs large factories in China.

gewusst: The Aral Sea was once one of the largest lakes on Earth.
Foxconn's official name is Hon Hai Precision, and among other things it assembles iPhones.

teile.einleitung: Animals from all over the world live in the zoo, from elephants to penguins. To keep them well, zookeepers look after them every day. They feed the animals, clean the enclosures and watch closely how the animals are doing.
wichtigste: Zookeepers feed the zoo animals and clean the enclosures.
They watch the animals closely and notice when one is ill.
They provide activities so that the animals do not get bored.
The apprenticeship is called animal keeper EFZ, specialism wild animals, and lasts three years.
The work takes place every day, including weekends and public holidays.
Basel Zoo is the oldest zoo in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The working day begins early in the morning. First the zookeepers check that all the animals are healthy. Then they **clean** the enclosures and stables and prepare the **food**. Each animal gets what it needs: hay, vegetables, fish or meat. They top up fresh water and check the facilities. They often also explain things about the animals to the visitors.

Zookeepers know their animals very well. They notice when an animal eats differently or moves differently. Then they inform the **zoo vet**. **Enrichment** is also important: food is hidden or put in boxes so that the animals have to search for it as they would in the wild. Some animals are trained so that they keep still of their own accord for an examination.

In Switzerland there is the three-year apprenticeship as an **animal keeper EFZ**. For work in a zoo you choose the specialism **wild animals**. There are also the specialisms of pets and laboratory animals. You need a love of animals, patience, courage and good powers of observation. The work is physically demanding and takes place in all weathers. Because animals have to be looked after every day, you also work at weekends.

**Basel Zoo**, called “Zolli” by many people, opened in 1874 and is the oldest zoo in Switzerland. **Zurich Zoo** opened in 1929. There are also animal parks such as Dählhölzli in Bern or the Wildnispark Zürich Langenberg. Many zoos take part in **species conservation** programmes so that rare animal species do not die out.

gewusst: An elephant eats a great deal of plant food every day, so feeding time in the elephant house is a big job.
Zurich Zoo has a large hall with a recreated rainforest from Madagascar, the Masoala Hall.

teile.einleitung: A shopping list is a small list of everything you want to buy in the shop. It helps you not to forget anything and not to buy anything you do not need.
wichtigste: You write everything you need on the shopping list.
Beforehand you look in the fridge and the store cupboard.
Your own shopping bag saves waste.
You find yoghurt and milk in the chiller cabinet.
Shopping is a good way to practise maths.

abschnitte.text: Before you write the **shopping list**, it is best to look in the **fridge** and the store cupboard. That way you can see what is still there and what is missing. Then you do not buy anything twice. You can also think about what you would like to cook in the next few days. Everything you need for it goes on the list.

With the list you go round the shop and cross off what is in the basket. In the shop, products have fixed places. **Yoghurt** and **milk** have to stay cool, so they are in the **chiller cabinet**. Bread is often near the entrance, and fruit and vegetables have their own section. If you write your list sorted by sections, you finish more quickly.

When you go shopping, it is best to take your own **shopping bag** or a basket. Then you do not need new bags. This saves **waste** and often a little money too. Heavy things such as bottles go at the bottom of the bag. Eggs and soft fruit go on top.

Shopping is a good way to practise **maths**. A loaf costs 3 francs and a carton of milk 2 francs. Together that makes **5 francs**. Three apples at 50 centimes each cost 150 centimes, which is **1 franc 50 centimes**. If you pay for something costing 4 francs with a 5-franc coin, you get **1 franc** change.

gewusst: One franc has 100 centimes.
If you go shopping hungry, you often buy more than is on the list.

teile.einleitung: Bio Suisse is the umbrella organisation of Swiss organic farmers. It awards the “Knospe” (bud) label, the best-known sign for organic food in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Bio Suisse label is called the “Knospe” (bud).
Knospe farms use no chemical-synthetic pesticides and no artificial fertiliser.
The whole farm must be organic, not just part of it.
Air transport is in principle forbidden for Knospe products.
Organic farming includes manure, grazing and crop rotation.

abschnitte.text: Bio Suisse was founded in 1981 and brings together many organic organisations. Its label is the **Knospe**, or bud, a green symbol with a stylised plant. If you see the Knospe on a product, you know that it was produced according to the **guidelines** of Bio Suisse. In many respects these rules are stricter than the legal organic ordinance. Independent bodies check the farms regularly.

On a Knospe farm, **chemical-synthetic pesticides** and **artificial fertiliser** are forbidden. Instead of artificial fertiliser, **manure** and compost go onto the fields. A varied **crop rotation** keeps the soil fertile, and pests spread less. The animals have plenty of space to roam and go out to **pasture**. Beneficial insects such as ladybirds help against aphids.

At Bio Suisse the **whole-farm principle** applies. A farm cannot farm just one field organically and carry on as before with the rest. It must convert **completely**. The conversion takes some time. Only after that may the products be sold with the Knospe.

Bio Suisse in principle forbids **air transport**, because it causes a great deal of **CO2**. Imported Knospe products such as bananas or coffee therefore usually come to Switzerland by ship, rail or lorry. If a product also grows in Switzerland, Swiss origin is preferred. There are versions of the Knospe for Swiss and for imported products.

gewusst: In Switzerland a large proportion of organic farms are run according to the rules of Bio Suisse.
Bio Suisse does not only set rules for growing, but also for processing, for example which additives are allowed.

teile.einleitung: We come across **advertising** everywhere: on posters, on television, on the internet and in the letterbox. It wants to catch our attention and get us to buy. If you know how advertising works, you can make better decisions for yourself.
wichtigste: Advertising wants to get people to buy a product.
The AIDA formula describes four stages: attention, interest, desire, action.
In product placement, a product is deliberately shown in films or videos.
Paid posts by influencers must be recognisable as advertising.
You can report unfair advertising to the Swiss Commission for Fairness in Advertising.
A “No advertising, please” sticker on the letterbox stops unaddressed advertising.

abschnitte.text: Advertising wants to catch **attention** and get people to buy a product or use a service. That is why it mainly shows the **advantages**. Every advert is aimed at a **target group**, for example teenagers, families or sports fans. Pictures, music and language are chosen precisely for this group.

A well-known formula in advertising is called **AIDA**. It describes four stages. First, advertising should catch **attention**. Then it should create **interest**. After that a **desire** to buy should arise. At the end comes the **action**, which is the purchase.

Not all advertising can be recognised at first glance. With **product placement**, a company pays for its product to appear visibly in a film, a series or a video. **Influencers** are also often paid for posts. Such posts must be clearly marked as **advertising** or an **advert**. Hidden advertising counts as **unfair**.

There is also advertising in the shop. Sweets are often placed right by the **checkout**, exactly at children's eye level. While waiting, customers have time and grab things on impulse. In German such products are called **Quengelware**, “whining goods”, because children often whine for them. If you know this, you can avoid an **impulse buy** more easily.

If you find an advert unfair or misleading, you can contact the **Swiss Commission for Fairness in Advertising**. It is the self-regulatory body of the advertising industry, and anyone can submit a complaint to it **free of charge**. If you want fewer leaflets, you stick a **“No advertising, please”** sticker (in German “Bitte keine Werbung”) on your letterbox. The distribution companies must respect it.

gewusst: The German word Quengelware comes from children whining (quengeln) for sweets at the checkout.
Anyone can submit a complaint to the Commission for Fairness in Advertising free of charge.

teile.einleitung: We use **electricity** every day: for lights, the fridge, the computer and the mobile phone. If you save electricity, you protect the environment and your family's wallet. Even small actions help.
wichtigste: When you leave an empty room, you switch off the light.
Switch devices off completely instead of leaving them on standby.
Only open the fridge door briefly.
Unplug chargers when the phone is full.
LED lamps use much less electricity than old light bulbs.

abschnitte.text: If a light is on in an empty room, it uses **electricity for nothing**. So the rule is: whoever goes out switches the **light off**. One click on the switch is enough. During the day, the **daylight** from the window is often enough. And **LED lamps** use much less electricity than old light bulbs.

Many devices such as televisions or games consoles are only on **standby** after you switch them off. You can often tell by a small light. Even then they still use electricity. With a **power strip with a switch** you can switch several devices off completely at once. You unplug chargers when the phone is full.

The **fridge** runs day and night. If you open the door for a long time, warm air gets in and it has to work harder. That is why you think beforehand about what you need and close the door again quickly. When cooking, a **lid** on the pan saves a lot of energy. Water also boils faster with it.

Electricity is produced in **power stations**. In Switzerland it comes mainly from **hydropower** and nuclear power, and more and more from the sun. Every power station needs space and raw materials or changes nature. Electricity that you do not need does not have to be produced. And it does not cost the family any money.

gewusst: In Switzerland hydropower supplies the largest share of electricity.
For the same amount of light, an LED lamp uses only a fraction of the electricity of a light bulb.

teile.einleitung: **Minerals** are substances from non-living nature that our body needs to live. It cannot make them itself, so we have to take them in with food and drink. The body needs some in larger amounts and others only in tiny traces.
wichtigste: Calcium is the most important building material for bones and teeth.
Iron is found in the red pigment of the blood and helps to transport oxygen.
The thyroid gland needs iodine, which is why Swiss table salt has been iodised since 1922.
Fluoride hardens tooth enamel and protects against tooth decay.
Table salt consists of sodium and chloride.
Magnesium is important for muscles and nerves.

abschnitte.text: Minerals are divided into two groups. The body needs **major minerals** such as calcium, magnesium, sodium or potassium in larger amounts. It needs **trace elements** such as iron, iodine or zinc only in very small amounts, but they are still vital. **Calcium** is the most important building material for **bones and teeth**. In Switzerland, dairy products are an important source of calcium.

**Iron** is built into **haemoglobin**, the red pigment of the blood. Haemoglobin carries oxygen from the lungs to the whole body. If you lack iron, you are often tired and pale. Iron is found, for example, in meat, pulses and wholegrain foods. The body needs **magnesium** for the work of **muscles and nerves**. There is a lot of it in nuts, wholegrain products and pulses.

The **thyroid gland** in the neck needs **iodine** to make hormones. Swiss soils contain little iodine. That is why in the past many people in many mountain valleys had a **goitre**, which is an enlarged thyroid gland. Since **1922**, iodine has been added to table salt in Switzerland. Since then goitre has become rare here. Iodised salt was one of the most successful health measures in the country.

The chemical name for table salt is **sodium chloride**; it consists of sodium and chloride. Sodium is important, but too much of it can raise **blood pressure**. The World Health Organization recommends at most about **5 grams of salt** a day, which is roughly a teaspoon. Many people in Switzerland eat a lot more. **Fluoride** is also often added to salt; it hardens tooth enamel and protects against **tooth decay**.

gewusst: Switzerland was one of the first countries to add iodine to table salt.
A lot of salt is hidden in bread, cheese, sausages and ready meals, not just in the salt shaker.

teile.einleitung: No single job can do everything alone. When a new house is built, many specialists work together. Each job takes on one task, and only together does a finished house come about.
wichtigste: A house needs many different jobs.
Bricklayers build the walls, carpenters the roof.
Electricians lay the cables for electricity.
At the end, painters give the walls colour.
The work has to happen in the right order.
Good teamwork needs agreements, punctuality and consideration.

abschnitte.text: Before building starts, an **architect** draws the plans. They show how big the rooms are and where the windows and doors will go. Later a **site manager** organises the building site. He or she makes sure that all the trades come at the right time. Without good planning, things would quickly get into a muddle on the building site.

First a digger digs out the foundations pit. Then the **bricklayers** pour the foundations and build the walls of brick or concrete. When the walls are finished, the **carpenters** come and build the wooden roof frame. After that **roofers** cover the roof with tiles so that the rain does not come in. In Switzerland people then often celebrate the **Aufrichte**, the topping-out.

Now the work inside begins. **Electricians** lay cables for lights and sockets. **Plumbers** fit the pipes for water, the shower and the toilet. Heating engineers make sure the rooms are warm. **Plasterers** plaster the walls, and tilers lay tiles in the bathroom and kitchen. Cabinetmakers fit doors, cupboards and kitchens.

At the end the **painters** paint the walls and give the house colour. Because so many trades are involved, the **order** is important: the painter can only start work once the electricians have laid their cables in the walls. That is why there are regular meetings on the building site. Good **teamwork** means being on time, agreeing on things and showing consideration for other people's work.

gewusst: On a large building site, specialists from more than ten different trades can be working at the same time.
Being able to work in a team is one of the qualities that training companies pay special attention to when choosing apprentices.

teile.einleitung: A program is a series of commands that tells a computer what to do. Every game and every app is a program. Programs are written by computer scientists.
wichtigste: A program is a list of commands for the computer.
Every game and every app is a program.
Programs are written in a programming language.
Computer scientists write and test programs.
Errors in programs are called bugs.
In Switzerland you can do an apprenticeship as an IT specialist EFZ.

abschnitte.text: A computer cannot think for itself. It needs exact **commands**, step by step. Such a series of commands is called a **program**. When you start a game, the computer carries out thousands of such commands in a short time. Mobile phones, washing machines and cars also have programs.

Programs are written in a **programming language**. Well-known languages are called, for example, **Python**, Java or JavaScript. For children there is **Scratch**, where you put commands together like building blocks. Every language has fixed rules, similar to grammar. A small mistake can mean that the program does not run.

No program is perfect at the first attempt. Errors in a program are called **bugs**, the English word for insects such as beetles. That is why computer scientists **test** their programs again and again. Finding and fixing errors is called **debugging**. Often several people work as a team on a large program.

In Switzerland you can do an apprenticeship as an **IT specialist EFZ**. One specialism is **application development**, where you learn to write programs. Logical thinking, patience and enjoying tinkering with problems are important. You can also study computer science at a university of applied sciences, a university or the ETH.

gewusst: In the 19th century Ada Lovelace wrote instructions for a calculating machine. That is why she is seen as the first programmer.
The name “bug” became famous when a real moth caused a fault in an early computer.

teile.einleitung: Saving energy is good for the environment and for your wallet. In the household there are many simple tricks for using less heating energy and electricity.
wichtigste: Every degree lower in room temperature saves about 6 per cent of heating energy.
In winter it is best to air rooms briefly and thoroughly with the windows wide open.
A lid on the pan keeps the heat in.
LED lamps use the least electricity for the same brightness.
Devices on standby keep using electricity.
On the energy label, A is the best class.

abschnitte.text: Heating uses a lot of energy in the household. As a **rule of thumb**, every degree lower in room temperature saves about **6 per cent** of heating energy. If you lower it from 22 to 20 degrees, you save about 12 per cent. If a family lowers it from 23 to 20 degrees, that is 3 times 6, which is about **18 per cent**. Bedrooms can easily be a little cooler.

Fresh air is important. In winter it is best to air rooms with **burst ventilation**: you open the windows wide for a few minutes. This exchanges the air without the walls and furniture cooling down. **Tilted windows**, on the other hand, let heat escape for hours. While airing, you turn the heating down.

A **lid** on the pan saves energy. Less heat and steam escape, the water boils faster, and you can turn the hob down sooner. The **fridge** gives off the heat from inside it at the back. If it stands next to the oven, it has to work longer. That is why you put it in a cool place with enough air around it.

**LED lamps** turn a large part of their energy into light. Light bulbs and halogen lamps mainly produce heat and use several times as much electricity. On **standby**, a device waits for a command, for example from the remote control, and keeps using electricity while it does so. A **power strip with a switch** disconnects the devices completely from the mains.

When buying appliances, the **energy label** helps. It goes from **A** (very efficient, green) to **G** (not very efficient, red). An appliance in class A uses the least energy for the same performance. It sometimes costs more, but saves electricity over the years. In Switzerland, the federal SwissEnergy programme provides information on such energy-saving tips.

gewusst: An old light bulb turns most of its electricity into heat rather than light.
In winter, warm socks and a jumper often let you turn the heating down by one degree.

teile.einleitung: When a dog is limping or a cat stops eating, the vet helps. She examines and treats sick animals and uses vaccinations to keep them healthy. The job requires a long course of study and a great love of animals.
wichtigste: The vet examines and treats sick and injured animals.
She vaccinates dogs, cats and other animals against diseases.
Vets work with pets, farm animals, horses or zoo animals.
In Switzerland you study veterinary medicine at the universities of Bern and Zurich.
There is an aptitude test for studying veterinary medicine.
Vets also check foods such as meat and milk.

abschnitte.text: The **vet** examines animals when they are ill or injured. Because animals cannot say where it hurts, she has to observe very carefully. She listens to the heart, takes the temperature and, if necessary, takes an X-ray. Then she gives medicines, dresses wounds or **operates**. She also advises the owners on how to feed and look after their animal properly.

Some vets mainly treat **small animals** such as dogs, cats, birds and rabbits. Others look after **farm animals** such as cows, goats and pigs and drive out to the farms to do so. There are also specialists for horses or for zoo animals. Every kind of animal has a different body, so a lot of knowledge is needed.

To become a vet, you study **veterinary medicine**. In Switzerland this is possible at the **Vetsuisse Faculty** of the universities of Bern and Zurich. Because there are more people interested than places, there is an **aptitude test**. The course lasts several years and combines theory with a lot of practice. As a rule you need a Matura to study.

Vets do not only protect animals. They also check whether **foods** such as meat and milk are safe. In the cantons there are **cantonal vets** for this. These specialists make sure that animal diseases do not spread and that the Animal Welfare Act is followed.

gewusst: Since 2006 the universities of Bern and Zurich have trained vets together in the Vetsuisse Faculty.
Vets have to know many kinds of animals, whereas doctors for humans only treat one single species.

teile.einleitung: There are many different cooking methods. Whether you steam, braise or deep-fry changes the taste, colour and nutrients of the food.
wichtigste: When steaming, food cooks over hot steam.
At sea level water boils at 100 °C, in the mountains a little lower.
Braising begins with searing and continues covered with a little liquid.
When blanching, you dip vegetables briefly in boiling water and then plunge them into cold water.
The Maillard reaction gives browning and roasted flavours when frying.
In a pressure cooker, water only boils at about 115 to 120 °C.

abschnitte.text: When **boiling**, food cooks in bubbling water. At sea level water boils at **100 °C**. In the mountains the air pressure is lower, so it boils a little earlier there. When **steaming**, the vegetables lie in a basket over boiling water. This way fewer vitamins and minerals are lost. When **poaching**, delicate foods such as eggs without their shells are cooked at about 65 to 75 °C, without the water bubbling.

When **blanching**, you dip vegetables only briefly into rapidly boiling water. Then you **plunge** them into iced water. This keeps them crisp and colourful, for example before you freeze them. When **stewing** (Dünsten), vegetables cook covered at about 100 °C in a little liquid, a little fat or in their own juice. This preserves taste and nutrients.

When **frying** or roasting, food cooks in hot fat in the pan or in the oven. During this the **Maillard reaction** takes place: sugars and the building blocks of protein react with each other at high heat. This creates the brown crust and the typical roasted taste. When **braising**, for example for a ragout, meat is first seared well. Then it cooks covered in a little liquid until tender, and a sauce forms.

When **deep-frying**, the food floats in hot fat at about 160 to 180 °C. A well-known example is **chips**. Because of the great heat, the outside of the food quickly becomes **crispy**. But deep-fried food absorbs fat and is therefore very high in energy. Hot fat is dangerous: if it catches fire, you must never pour water on it, but cover it with a lid.

A **pressure cooker** is closed tightly. As it heats up, the **pressure** in the pot rises. As a result, the water only boils at about 115 to 120 °C. The food therefore cooks much faster than in a normal saucepan. This saves time and energy. Before opening it, the pressure must always be let out completely.

gewusst: On high mountains water boils well below 100 °C, which is why boiling eggs takes longer there.
The Maillard reaction is named after the French scientist Louis Camille Maillard.

teile.einleitung: There is a date on almost every food packet. The **best-before date** tells you until when a product is sure to keep its full quality. After that it is often still good for a long time. If you know this, you throw away less food.
wichtigste: The best-before date reads “best before” and is not a date for throwing things away.
After it has passed, you check food by looking, smelling and tasting.
Dry stores such as pasta or rice often keep for months longer.
Salt and solid sugar do not need a best-before date.
Highly perishable foods such as mince carry a use-by date, which you must keep to.
With “first in, first out” you use older stores first.

abschnitte.text: There are two kinds of dates on packets. The **best-before date** is shown as “best before”. Until then the manufacturer guarantees the taste, appearance and quality. After that, in Switzerland, the product may even still be sold if it is in perfect condition. The **use-by date**, shown as “use by”, is different. It appears on highly perishable foods such as fresh fish or **mince**, and after it you should no longer eat them.

If the best-before date has passed, you do not have to throw a food away straight away. You **look at it**, **smell it** and **taste** a small piece. If there is no mould to be seen, it smells normal and tastes good, you can usually still eat it. Yoghurt, for example, is often still good days or weeks after the date. This way there is less **food waste**.

**Dry foods** such as pasta, rice, flour or sugar often keep for many months after the date if they are stored dry and well sealed. **Table salt** and solid sugar practically never go off. That is why they are exempt from the requirement to have a best-before date. Fresh fish and mince, on the other hand, go off very quickly.

A simple rule is called **“first in, first out”**. You put newly bought products at the back and older ones at the front. This way you use the older ones first, and fewer go out of date. Opened **dairy products** belong in the **fridge**, because the cold slows down the growth of bacteria. You should use them up within a few days.

gewusst: A large part of food waste comes from households, often because the dates are misunderstood.
Salt does not go off because bacteria cannot find any water in it to live on.

teile.einleitung: At a university, young adults study a subject in depth and learn to work scientifically. Switzerland has cantonal universities and two Federal Institutes of Technology. The oldest is the University of Basel.
wichtigste: The University of Basel is the oldest university in Switzerland, opened in 1460.
The University of Fribourg is officially bilingual, German and French.
The Università della Svizzera italiana (USI) in Ticino was founded in 1996.
Measured by number of students, the University of Zurich is the largest in Switzerland (as of 2024).
Since the Bologna Declaration of 1999 there have been bachelor's and master's degrees.
One ECTS credit corresponds to about 25 to 30 hours of work.
In German-speaking Switzerland there is an aptitude test for medicine.

abschnitte.text: In 1459 Pope Pius II issued the founding bull, and in 1460 the **University of Basel** was opened. It is the oldest university in Switzerland; all the others came much later. The **University of Zurich** was founded in 1833, the first university in Europe to be founded by a democratic state. With about 28,000 students it is the largest university in Switzerland (as of 2024). There are also **ETH Zurich** and the **EPFL** in Lausanne, which belong to the Confederation.

Switzerland has several national languages, and this also shows at its universities. The **University of Fribourg** lies on the language border and is officially bilingual. Many courses are offered in German and French, and you can even gain bilingual degrees. The **Università della Svizzera italiana**, USI for short, was founded in 1996 and has sites in Lugano and Mendrisio. It is the only university in Italian-speaking Switzerland.

In 1999 the education ministers of 29 European countries, including Switzerland, signed the **Bologna Declaration**. The aim was a common higher education area with comparable degrees. Since then you first study for a **bachelor's degree** and then a **master's degree**. The workload is measured in **ECTS credits**. One credit corresponds to about 25 to 30 hours of work, including lectures, self-study and exams. A full-time year has 60 credits, and a university master's degree covers 90 to 120 credits.

To study at a university you usually need a **gymnasial Matura** or an equivalent certificate. If you want to start in the autumn semester, you usually register by **30 April**. In human medicine there are more people interested than places. That is why there is a **numerus clausus**: in German-speaking Switzerland, the **aptitude test for medical studies** (EMS) decides on admission. It tests abilities such as understanding texts and spatial awareness. For medicine there is therefore an earlier registration deadline.

gewusst: A full-time year with 60 ECTS credits corresponds to about 1500 to 1800 hours of work.
Universities of applied sciences and universities of teacher education also offer bachelor's and master's degree courses.

teile.einleitung: A household budget is a plan for money. You write down how much money comes in and what it is spent on. This shows you whether the money is enough and how much you can save.
wichtigste: In a budget, income and spending are set against each other.
The net wage is what counts for the budget.
Fixed costs such as rent and health insurance come up regularly.
Provisions spread rare, large bills over all the months.
You divide yearly expenses by twelve.
An emergency reserve of about three months' wages protects against debt.
Households with a low income can receive help with health insurance premiums.

abschnitte.text: From the **gross wage**, the employer deducts contributions for the AVS, IV, EO, unemployment insurance and the pension fund. What arrives in the account is the **net wage**, and that is what you work with in the budget. If there is a **13th month's salary**, you spread it over all twelve months. An example: 13 times 4800 francs is 62,400 francs a year; divided by 12, that makes 5200 francs a month.

**Fixed costs** come up regularly and at the same amount, such as rent, health insurance premiums, insurance and subscriptions. They can hardly be changed in the short term. **Variable costs** such as food, clothes or free time are easier to influence. This is where it is easiest to save when money is tight.

Some bills only come once or twice a year, for example taxes or the dentist. For these you put an amount aside every month. This is called a **provision**. If someone expects 3600 francs of tax a year, they put aside 3600 divided by 12 each month, which is **300 francs**. This way there is no shortfall when the bill arrives.
