If you save a fixed share first, you reliably build up money. With a net wage of 6000 francs, 10 per cent is exactly **600 francs**. Budget advice services recommend an **emergency reserve** of about three months' wages for the unexpected. Because health insurance premiums are high, the cantons give households with a low income a **premium reduction**. The rules differ from canton to canton.

gewusst: Budget Advice Switzerland provides sample budgets that show how much households typically spend on individual items.
Even a simple notebook with all the spending for a month often shows, surprisingly, where the money goes.

teile.einleitung: A spanner is a tool used to tighten or loosen screws and nuts. Mechanics, bike mechanics and many other tradespeople use one every day. It comes in many shapes and sizes.
wichtigste: With a spanner you tighten or loosen screws and nuts.
Mechanics use it very often.
There are different kinds, for example open-ended spanners and ring spanners.
The size is called the spanner size and is given in millimetres.
An adjustable spanner can be set to different sizes.
With a torque wrench you tighten screws exactly the right amount.

abschnitte.text: Many screws and nuts have a **hexagon**, which means six corners. The spanner grips this head. The handle works like a **lever**: the longer it is, the less force you need to turn. Turning clockwise usually makes the screw **tighter**, turning anticlockwise **loosens** it.

The **open-ended spanner** has an open side and can be put on quickly. The **ring spanner** surrounds the head completely and slips less. The **adjustable spanner** can be set to different sizes with a small wheel. For screws with a six-sided hole in the head you need an **Allen key**. You know this from a lot of flat-pack furniture.

Each spanner only fits one particular size. This is called the **spanner size** and is given in **millimetres**, for example 10 or 13. The number is usually printed on the spanner. If the spanner does not fit exactly, it can slip and damage the corners of the nut. That is why workshops have whole **sets** with many sizes.

**Automotive mechatronics technicians**, bike mechanics or agricultural machinery mechanics use spanners every day. When changing a wheel on a car, the wheel bolts have to be tightened exactly right. For this there is the **torque wrench**. It shows or clicks when the right force has been reached. This way the screw sits securely without breaking.

gewusst: In German, many people also call the adjustable spanner an “Engländer” (Englishman).
Some screws have a left-hand thread. They are tightened in the opposite direction.

teile.einleitung: Healthy teeth are important for eating, speaking and laughing. The dentist checks the teeth, finds holes and fills them. With regular visits and good brushing, your teeth stay healthy for a long time.
wichtigste: The dentist examines the teeth and fills holes with a filling.
A hole in a tooth is caused by tooth decay (caries).
Children have 20 milk teeth, adults up to 32 permanent teeth.
In Switzerland there is school dental care in the schools.
Dental assistants help the dentist with the work.
Brushing your teeth twice a day protects against holes.

abschnitte.text: At the **dentist's**, your teeth are checked. With a small mirror and a fine probe the dentist looks closely at every tooth. Sometimes he also takes an **X-ray**. If a tooth has a hole, he drills away the decayed part and seals it with a **filling**. So that it does not hurt, there is an injection that numbs the tooth.

Lots of **bacteria** live in the mouth. When they get sugar, they produce acids. These acids attack the hard **tooth enamel**. Over time this creates a hole, which is called **tooth decay** or caries. That is why it is important to brush your teeth twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and not to eat sweet things too often.

In Switzerland there is **school dental care**. Children are examined regularly, and a school dental care instructor shows the class how to brush properly. Children have 20 **milk teeth**. From about the age of six the **permanent teeth** grow, and adults have up to 32. In Switzerland people usually pay for the dentist themselves; basic health insurance does not normally cover it.

To become a dentist, you study **dentistry** at a university. In Switzerland this is possible in Basel, Bern, Geneva and Zurich. **Dental assistants** EFZ also work in the practice. They prepare the instruments, help with treatment and take X-rays. **Dental hygienists** clean the teeth thoroughly and remove tartar.

gewusst: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the whole human body.
The last permanent teeth are called wisdom teeth; they often only grow in adulthood, or not at all.

teile.einleitung: In almost every classroom in Switzerland there is a large board at the front. In Swiss German it is called a Wandtafel. On it the teacher writes what the class is learning. Today, besides the chalkboard, there are also whiteboards and large screens.
wichtigste: The blackboard usually hangs at the front of the classroom.
You write on a classic blackboard with chalk.
You write on a whiteboard with special felt-tip pens.
Today many schools also have interactive boards or large screens.
Many blackboards can be folded open or slid up and down.
In Switzerland teachers are trained at universities of teacher education.

abschnitte.text: The **blackboard** is one of the most important aids in lessons. The teacher writes words or sums on it or draws sketches. This way the whole class can see at the same time what it is about. Pupils also come to the front to solve a task. In Switzerland people usually say “Wandtafel”, while in Germany they tend to say “Tafel”.

On a classic blackboard you write with **chalk**. Chalk is made of limestone or gypsum. With a wet **sponge** you wipe the board clean again. In the past, boards were made of **slate**, a dark rock. Today they are usually made of steel with a special coating. Many blackboards can be folded open or slid up and down so that there is more space to write.

Besides the chalkboard there is the **whiteboard**. It is white, and you write on it with special felt-tip pens that can be wiped off again. Many schools also have **interactive boards** or large screens. On them the teacher can show films, pictures and programs. You can write directly on the screen with a pen or your finger.

If you want to teach at the blackboard, you become a **teacher**. In Switzerland you study for this at a **university of teacher education**, PH for short. There you learn how children learn and how to plan good lessons. The course includes many placements in school classes. There are courses for kindergarten, primary school and lower secondary school.

gewusst: In the past, schoolchildren often had their own small slate, which they wrote on with a slate pencil.
Many people find the squeak of chalk on the board very unpleasant.

teile.einleitung: The qualification procedure, QV for short, is the final examination at the end of an apprenticeship. Those who pass receive a Federal VET Diploma or a Federal VET Certificate. In the past it was called the final apprenticeship examination, LAP for short.
wichtigste: The QV is the final examination at the end of the apprenticeship.
QV stands for Qualifikationsverfahren, qualification procedure.
It used to be called the final apprenticeship examination (LAP).
Practical work, professional knowledge and general education are examined.
The marks from school during the apprenticeship also count.
Those who pass receive an EFZ or an EBA.
Those who do not pass may repeat the QV.

abschnitte.text: The **qualification procedure** takes place at the end of the apprenticeship, usually in May and June. It shows whether you can do everything the job requires. What exactly is examined is set out in the **training ordinance** for each job. It is run by the cantons together with the professional associations.

The most important part is usually the **practical work**. You carry out typical tasks from the job, for example building a piece of furniture or serving a customer. Depending on the job, there is a set task or an individual practical project in your own company (IPA). Specialists known as **examiners** watch and assess the work.

Another part tests your **professional knowledge**, often in writing and orally. On top of that comes general education, with an in-depth project and a final examination. The marks from the semester reports also count towards the overall mark. So it is not only the examination day that counts, but the whole apprenticeship.

To pass, you need at least a 4 in the overall mark and in important parts. Those who pass receive the **Federal VET Diploma** (EFZ) or the Federal VET Certificate (EBA). With it you are officially a trained specialist. In many cantons there is a formal diploma ceremony for this.

abschnitte.titel: If it does not work out
abschnitte.text: If you do not pass the QV, you may repeat it, as a rule no more than twice. Usually you only have to redo the parts that were not good enough. To do this, the apprenticeship contract is often extended by a year. Good preparation with old exam papers and practice tasks helps to reduce **exam nerves**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short for Qualifikationsverfahren, the final examination of an apprenticeship.
Individual practical project, an examination project carried out in your own company.
A mark from the school reports during the apprenticeship.
A specialist who watches and assesses examinations.

gewusst: Every year tens of thousands of apprentices in Switzerland take the QV.
Many cantons honour the apprentices with the best final marks at a special ceremony.

teile.einleitung: The probationary period is the first part of a new employment or apprenticeship. Both sides can check whether they suit each other well. The rules are set out in the Swiss Code of Obligations, the OR.
wichtigste: Without any agreement, the first month of a permanent employment contract counts as the probationary period.
In writing it can be extended to a maximum of three months.
During the probationary period the notice period is seven days.
In the case of illness or accident the probationary period is extended accordingly.
In an apprenticeship the probationary period lasts one to three months; without an agreement it is three months.
With the approval of the cantonal authority it can, in exceptional cases, last up to six months.
Special protection against dismissal during illness only applies after the probationary period.

abschnitte.titel: What the probationary period is for
abschnitte.text: At the beginning, neither side knows exactly whether it will work out. During the **probationary period**, employer and employee get to know each other. The company sees how someone works. The new employee finds out whether she likes the job. If it does not suit, the employment can be ended quickly and easily.

The rules are in **Art. 335b OR**. For a permanent employment contract, the **first month** counts as the probationary period if nothing else has been agreed. It can be arranged differently by a written agreement, a standard employment contract (NAV) or a collective labour agreement (GAV). But it may not last longer than **three months**. If you are off work because of **illness** or an accident, the probationary period is extended by that time.

abschnitte.titel: Giving notice during the probationary period
abschnitte.text: During the probationary period you can give notice at any time with a period of **seven days**, unless something else has been agreed. The notice does not have to end at the end of a month. The special **protection against dismissal** during illness, known as dismissal at an inopportune time under Art. 336c OR, also only applies **after** the probationary period. So during the probationary period, notice may be given even if someone is ill.

abschnitte.titel: The probationary period in an apprenticeship
abschnitte.text: For apprenticeships, **Art. 344a OR** applies. The probationary period lasts at least **one** and at most **three months**. If the apprenticeship contract says nothing, three months apply. In exceptional cases it can be extended to **six months**. For this, the training company and the apprentice must agree, and the **cantonal authority** must give its approval. The probationary period is a good opportunity for apprentices to really get to know the job.

gewusst: With fixed-term employment contracts there is only a probationary period if one has been expressly agreed.
Apprentices may also give notice during the probationary period if the job really does not suit them.

teile.einleitung: A **tenancy agreement** sets out who may use a flat and what it costs. In Switzerland more than half of households rent their homes, so tenancy law is important for a great many people. The rules are in the Code of Obligations (OR) and above all protect tenants.
wichtigste: You can give notice on a flat with at least three months' notice, on a furnished room with two weeks.
The landlord must give notice using an officially approved form, otherwise the notice is void.
You can challenge a notice within 30 days at the conciliation authority.
The tenant fixes small defects, the landlord larger ones.
If you want to move out earlier, you can propose a reasonable replacement tenant.
Rent increases require an official form with reasons.

abschnitte.text: For flats, a notice period of **three months** to a locally customary date applies (Art. 266c OR). In the contract, longer periods may be agreed, but not shorter ones. For a **furnished room**, **two weeks** to the end of a one-month rental period is enough. If you want to move out early, you can propose a **reasonable replacement tenant** who can pay and wants to take over the contract (Art. 264 OR). Otherwise you have to keep paying rent until the next notice date.

If the landlord gives notice on a flat, he must use a **form approved by the canton** (Art. 266l OR). Without the form the notice is **void**, which means invalid. If the tenant thinks the notice is unfair, they can challenge it within **30 days** at the **conciliation authority**. These proceedings in tenancy matters are in principle free of charge. In the case of **rent arrears**, the landlord must first set a written deadline of at least 30 days and warn that notice will be given.

The landlord must hand over the flat in good condition and keep it that way. However, the tenant must fix **small defects** that can be dealt with by simple cleaning or a minor repair themselves and at their own cost (Art. 259 OR). These include, for example, a dripping tap or a blocked drain. Larger defects such as broken heating must be fixed by the landlord. It is best to report them to him in writing.

abschnitte.titel: Rent and the reference interest rate
abschnitte.text: If the landlord wants to raise the rent, he needs an **official form with reasons** (Art. 269d OR). It must arrive at least ten days before the start of the notice period. An important basis is the **mortgage reference interest rate** of the Federal Office for Housing. In September 2025 it fell to 1.25 per cent and was still at this level in September 2026. If the rate rises by 0.25 percentage points, the net rent may rise by at most **3 per cent**. If it falls, tenants can ask for a reduction.

gewusst: If the reference interest rate rose by a quarter of a percentage point, a rent of 2000 francs could rise to 2060 francs.
A notice or rent increase without the official form is void.
Going to the conciliation authority costs nothing in principle in tenancy matters.

teile.einleitung: Housework is everything that needs doing in the household: cooking, cleaning, washing, shopping and much more. On top of this comes caring for children and relatives. A large part of this work is done without pay.
wichtigste: Care work is work looking after others, such as childcare and caring for relatives.
Mental load is the invisible work of planning and remembering.
A chore rota (Ämtliplan) shares the tasks out clearly among everyone.
Under Art. 163 ZGB, married couples provide for the family together.
A cleaner in a private household must be registered with the AVS from the very first franc.
Household employees must be insured against accidents.
In Switzerland women do more housework and family work on average.

abschnitte.text: Cooking, washing, cleaning and shopping take a lot of time. On top of this comes **care work**, which means looking after others: caring for children or relatives. A large part of it is done **without pay**. The Federal Statistical Office measures this work regularly. For years the surveys have shown that women on average do more housework and family work, and men more paid work.

Behind every task there is also **thinking work**: remembering appointments, planning shopping, noticing that the washing powder is almost finished. This is called the **mental load**. You can hardly see this work, but it can be tiring. It is often shared unequally.

In many families and shared flats, a **chore rota** (in Swiss German an Ämtliplan) helps. It shows who does which task when, such as washing up, hoovering or taking out the rubbish. This makes the work visible and shares it fairly. For married couples, **Art. 163 ZGB** states that they provide for the family together. They agree on who contributes what: money, running the household or childcare.

If you employ a **cleaner**, you become an employer. For work in private households, contributions to the **AVS** and other social insurance schemes are in principle owed from the very first franc. There is an exception for young people up to 25 with a small annual wage. You must also insure the household help against accidents at work under the **Accident Insurance Act**, even if they only work a few hours.

gewusst: The word “Ämtli” is typical Swiss German and means a small, regular task or chore.
According to calculations by the Federal Statistical Office, unpaid work in Switzerland adds up to more hours than paid work.

teile.einleitung: Without roads we could hardly get to school, to work or on holiday. Road builders lay new roads, renew old ones and fill in potholes so that everyone can travel safely.
wichtigste: Road builders lay and repair roads, paths and squares.
A road consists of several layers; on top there is usually a surface of asphalt.
Asphalt is laid hot and compacted with heavy rollers.
The work almost always takes place outdoors, in sun, wind and cold.
In Switzerland the apprenticeship is called road and track builder EFZ (Verkehrswegbauer EFZ).
Safety on the building site is very important, so everyone wears bright high-visibility clothing.

abschnitte.text: Road builders build **roads**, pavements, cycle paths and squares. They dig out the ground, bring in gravel and compact it. Then they lay the **surface**, which people in everyday life often call “tar”. They also set kerbstones and make sure that rainwater can drain away well. When a road has holes or cracks, they patch these places.

A road is not simply a thin layer on the ground. Right at the bottom is a load-bearing layer of gravel called the **sub-base**. Above it come a **base course** and the **surface course**, on which the cars drive. Every layer must be well compacted. This way the road can carry heavy lorries and withstand many years of frost and heat.

Large machines work on a road building site. The **digger** digs out soil, the **road paver** spreads the hot asphalt evenly. Then the **roller** drives over it and presses the surface down firmly. Shovels, rakes and measuring instruments are also needed. With them the specialists check that the road has the right slope.

If you want to build roads in Switzerland, you do an apprenticeship as a **road and track builder EFZ**. There is a specialism in road building. You learn in the training company, at vocational school and in inter-company courses. Enjoying working outdoors, team spirit and good physical fitness are important. After the apprenticeship you can train further, for example as a foreman or site supervisor.

gewusst: Many road works are carried out in summer, because asphalt is hard to lay in cold and rain.
Asphalt is made with **bitumen**, a thick, black substance from crude oil, mixed with stones and sand.

teile.einleitung: If you rent a flat in Switzerland, you often have to pay a **rental deposit**. This is a sum of money that gives the landlord security in case damage or unpaid rent remains at the end. The Code of Obligations sets out exactly how high the deposit may be and where the money is kept.
wichtigste: For a flat, the deposit may be at most three months' rent.
Cash for the deposit goes into a blocked account at a bank in the tenant's name.
The interest on the deposit account belongs to the tenant.
The bank only pays out with the consent of both parties or on the basis of a legally binding decision.
If the landlord makes no claims one year after the tenancy ends, the tenant gets the money back.
For business premises there is no legal upper limit.

abschnitte.text: The deposit is a **security**. It protects the landlord in case the tenant leaves damage that goes beyond normal wear and tear when moving out. It also covers rent or service charges that have not been paid. If you look after the flat carefully and pay on time, you get all the money back. That is why a careful **handover report** is worthwhile when moving in and moving out.

The rules are in **Art. 257e OR**, that is in the Code of Obligations. When renting **residential premises**, the deposit may be at most **three months' rent**. With a monthly rent of 1500 francs, that is at most 4500 francs. For **business premises** such as shops or offices this limit does not apply; there both sides can agree the amount freely.

If the deposit is paid in cash, it must be paid into a **savings or deposit account** at a bank. This account is in the **tenant's name**. It is also called a **rental deposit account** or blocked account, because nobody can use it alone. Because the account belongs to the tenant, the **interest** is also theirs. The landlord may not simply put the money in his own pocket.

The bank may only release the deposit if **both parties agree** or if there is a **legally binding decision**, for example from debt collection or court proceedings. If the landlord has not legally asserted a claim within **one year** of the end of the tenancy, the tenant can ask the bank for the money back on their own. This way the landlord cannot hold on to the deposit without good reason.

Instead of paying money as a deposit, you can take out **rental deposit insurance**. Then you pay the insurer a **premium** every year, and the insurer acts as guarantor towards the landlord. This protects your savings, especially when you first leave home. The disadvantage: you never get the premiums back. If the insurer has to pay the landlord anything, it later claims the amount back from the tenant.

gewusst: For expensive flats, a deposit of three months' rent can come to several thousand francs.
The deposit account is in the tenant's name, even though the landlord also has a say over it.

teile.einleitung: Every product has an impact on the environment: when it is made, transported and used, and finally when it is disposed of. A **life cycle assessment** adds up these environmental impacts over the whole life of a product.
wichtigste: A life cycle assessment examines the environmental impact of a product over its whole life.
The life cycle begins with the extraction of raw materials.
Embodied (grey) energy is found in manufacturing, transport and disposal.
With a smartphone, most of the impact arises during manufacturing.
Repairing and upcycling extend the life of things.
The circular economy aims to keep materials in circulation for as long as possible.

abschnitte.text: A life cycle assessment looks at the whole **life cycle**. It starts with the **extraction of raw materials**, such as ore, crude oil or cotton. Then come manufacturing and transport. Then the product is used. Finally it is disposed of or recycled. For each stage, things such as energy, water and greenhouse gases are measured.

**Embodied energy**, also called grey energy, is the energy needed to make, transport and dispose of a product. You cannot see it, but it is contained in the object. With a **smartphone**, most of the environmental impact arises during **manufacturing**, not when charging it. So if you use your device for longer, you improve its life cycle assessment. A T-shirt also needs a lot: according to WWF, about 2700 litres of water are needed for the cotton.

**Planned obsolescence** is when a product is deliberately made so that it breaks early. Repairing helps against this. In a **repair café**, people meet to repair things together, from lamps to trousers. Volunteers with expert knowledge help. Such meetings also take place in many Swiss municipalities.

In **upcycling**, something old is made into something new of greater value, for example a bag from an old lorry tarpaulin. The **circular economy** goes even further. Its principle: materials should stay in the **cycle** for as long as possible. Products are designed so that they can be repaired, reused and finally recycled. This means fewer new raw materials are needed.

gewusst: The bags of the Zurich company Freitag have been sewn from old lorry tarpaulins since the 1990s.
Life cycle assessments are drawn up according to international standards so that results can be compared.

teile.einleitung: When a pet is ill or needs a vaccination, you go to the vet's surgery. Vets and their team work there to keep dogs, cats and other animals healthy.
wichtigste: At the vet's surgery, animals are examined, vaccinated and treated.
The vet leads the treatment.
Veterinary practice assistants help out in the team.
Cats and dogs are vaccinated regularly against dangerous diseases.
In Switzerland dogs must be marked with a microchip and registered.
Some vet's surgeries specialise in small animals, others in farm animals such as cows.

abschnitte.text: At the **vet's surgery**, animals are examined when they are ill or injured. The vet listens to the heart and lungs, for example, looks into the ears and mouth and feels the belly. There is often also an **X-ray machine** and a small laboratory for blood tests. Smaller operations are carried out right there at the surgery. The surgery usually has a waiting room where animals and their owners wait.

Like people, animals are also **vaccinated**. Vaccination protects cats and dogs from dangerous, infectious diseases. Many vaccinations have to be renewed after a while. The vet records them in a **vaccination certificate**. For trips abroad, a pet often needs a **pet passport** with certain vaccinations.

It is not only the vet who works at the surgery. **Veterinary practice assistants**, TPA for short, welcome the customers, hold animals during examinations and help with operations. They prepare instruments, do laboratory work and advise pet owners. The apprenticeship as a veterinary practice assistant EFZ lasts three years.

Many surgeries treat **small animals** such as dogs, cats, rabbits and guinea pigs. Others specialise in **farm animals** such as cows, pigs and horses. These vets often drive out to the farms, because a cow cannot simply be brought to the surgery. For emergencies there is also an **emergency service** at night and at weekends.

gewusst: A dog's microchip is about the size of a grain of rice and is placed under the skin.
In Switzerland vets are trained at the universities of Bern and Zurich.

teile.einleitung: In a block of flats many people live close together. The house rules set out how living together is organised, for example regarding noise, in the laundry room or in the stairwell. This means there are fewer arguments.
wichtigste: In most house rules, quiet time at night starts at 10 pm.
Many buildings have a quiet time at midday from about 12 to 1 pm.
The stairwell is an escape route and must be kept clear.
A laundry rota regulates the use of the laundry room.
Under Art. 257f OR, tenants must be careful and considerate.
Anyone who keeps causing disturbance despite a warning risks being given notice.
Small pets such as hamsters are usually allowed without permission.

abschnitte.text: Many house rules and municipal regulations set **quiet time at night** from 10 pm to 6 or 7 am. During this time there should be no disturbing noise, such as loud music. There is often also a **quiet time at midday** from about 12 to 1 pm. You should not do noisy work such as drilling or hammering then. On Sundays and public holidays stricter rules often apply.

The **stairwell** is an escape and rescue route. Under fire safety regulations it must be kept clear, so furniture or shoe racks do not belong there. Things that can burn could be dangerous in a fire. The shared **laundry room** is often regulated with a **laundry rota** or a booking list. This way every household can use the machines without arguments.

The basis is the **Code of Obligations**. Art. 257f OR requires tenants to use the flat **carefully** and to show **consideration** for other residents and neighbours. The house rules describe in more detail what this means. If a tenant continues to cause serious disturbance despite a written warning, the landlord can give notice of at least 30 days to the end of a month. Taking matters into your own hands, such as turning off the electricity, is not allowed.

**Small animals** such as hamsters, guinea pigs or pet birds in normal numbers count as normal use of the flat. As a rule you may keep them without permission. For **dogs and cats**, many tenancy agreements require the landlord's consent. That is why it is worth looking at the tenancy agreement before buying an animal.

gewusst: The laundry rota is so common in Swiss blocks of flats that it is often seen as typically Swiss.
The house rules are usually part of the tenancy agreement and are signed when you move in.

teile.einleitung: Working conditions are the circumstances under which people work: wages, working hours, safety and rights. They are very different around the world, and organisations and laws try to improve them.
wichtigste: The International Labour Organization ILO was founded in 1919 and has its headquarters in Geneva.
Its core labour standards include the ban on forced labour.
According to the ILO and UNICEF, about 160 million children were affected by child labour in 2020.
A living wage should cover a family's basic needs.
In Switzerland, collective labour agreements often set the wages, working hours and holidays of an industry.
Labels such as Fairtrade by Max Havelaar guarantee producers minimum prices.

abschnitte.text: The **International Labour Organization**, ILO for short, was founded in 1919. It is a specialised agency of the UN with its headquarters in **Geneva**. Governments, employers and trade unions work together in it. The ILO sets **core labour standards**: freedom of association, abolition of forced labour and child labour, a ban on discrimination and, since 2022, also safe and healthy working conditions.

According to an estimate by the ILO and UNICEF, about **160 million children** around the world were affected by **child labour** in 2020. Almost half of them were doing dangerous work. Many work in farming. Child labour often keeps children away from school. That is why it is an important topic in international cooperation.

A **living wage** should cover food, housing, health, education and a little in reserve. In many countries, legal minimum wages are below this. Many people work in the **informal sector**, for example as street traders or day labourers. They have no employment contract and no insurance. According to the ILO, this applies to about half to two thirds of people in work worldwide.

Many clothes are sewn in countries such as **Bangladesh**. In 2013 the **Rana Plaza** factory building collapsed there, and more than a thousand people died. After that, more than 200 fashion brands and trade unions signed the **Accord on Fire and Building Safety**. Independent inspections uncovered thousands of defects. Labels such as **Fairtrade** by Max Havelaar work for minimum prices and standards for food.

In Switzerland, trade unions and employers' associations often negotiate a **collective labour agreement**, GAV for short. For an industry it sets, for example, minimum wages, working hours and holidays. The responsibility of companies abroad is also a political issue. In November 2020 the **Responsible Business Initiative** received about 50.7 per cent Yes votes, but failed because it did not win a majority of the cantons. Supporters and opponents had very different opinions about it.

gewusst: The ILO is older than the UN: it was founded back in 1919, the UN only in 1945.
Max Havelaar is the name of a character in a novel who stands up for exploited people.

teile.einleitung: Not everyone starts the next step of their education straight after school, an apprenticeship or the Matura. Many first take a gap year. They learn a language, travel, work or do military or civilian service.
wichtigste: A gap year is a break between two stages of education.
In English it is called a gap year.
In the past, the Welschlandjahr in French-speaking Switzerland was very common for young people from German-speaking Switzerland.
Au pairs live with a host family, look after children and help in the household.
Basic military training (Rekrutenschule) usually lasts 18 weeks.
People who are not in work pay AVS contributions from 1 January after their 20th birthday.
The DELF is an official diploma for French.

abschnitte.text: A **gap year** is a period between two stages of education, for example between an apprenticeship or the Matura and university. In German it is called a Zwischenjahr, an in-between year. Many people use it for travel, internships, **voluntary work** or a language stay. If you are already at university, you can apply for a **leave semester**. You stay enrolled, but do not attend any classes.

In German-speaking Switzerland the **Welschlandjahr** used to be very popular. Many young people spent a year as a household helper or at a school in French-speaking Switzerland in order to learn French. Today there are programmes with language courses and internships for this. As an **au pair** you live with a host family, look after children and help in the household. In return you get board, lodging and pocket money, and you usually attend a language course. At the end you can take a diploma, for example the **DELF** for French, which is awarded by the French Ministry of Education.

Many young men do their **basic military training** (Rekrutenschule) in the Swiss Army during a gap year. It usually lasts 18 weeks. Anyone who cannot do military service for reasons of conscience does **civilian service**, for example in a hospital, a school or in nature conservation. Civilian service lasts **one and a half times** as long as the military training service not yet completed. The longer duration counts as proof of the conflict of conscience.

There are also obligations during a gap year. Anyone who is not in work pays AVS contributions from **1 January after their 20th birthday**. Missing years of contributions lead to a lower **AVS pension** later. That is why it is worth asking at the compensation office. Anyone who works and earns wages during the gap year pays the contributions through their employer.

gewusst: For English there is, for example, the TOEFL, for Spanish the DELE and for German the Goethe-Zertifikat.
A gap year can help you become clearer about your own interests before you start university.

teile.einleitung: **Proteins**, in German also called **Eiweisse**, are vital nutrients. They are the building materials for muscles, skin and hair and work as tools in the body. Proteins are found in animal and plant foods.
wichtigste: Proteins consist of long chains of amino acids.
The body cannot make essential amino acids itself; we have to eat them.
Pulses such as lentils and chickpeas are good plant sources of protein.
Adults need about 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day.
Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions in the body.
Gluten is a sticky protein in cereals.

abschnitte.text: Proteins are long chains of small building blocks, the **amino acids**. During digestion, the body breaks the proteins from food down into amino acids. From these it builds its own proteins. The body cannot make some amino acids itself. We have to take in these **essential amino acids** with our food.

Proteins are **building materials** for muscles, skin, hair and many parts of the cells. Some proteins work as **enzymes**. They speed up chemical reactions, for example during **digestion**, where they break food down into small pieces. Other proteins carry substances in the blood or help to fight off disease. Professional bodies recommend about **0.8 grams** of protein per kilogram of body weight per day for adults. For 60 kilos that is about 48 grams.

There is a lot of protein in meat, fish, eggs and dairy products. Plants also provide protein, especially **pulses** such as lentils, beans, peas and **chickpeas**. Plant proteins often do not contain all the amino acids in ideal amounts. But if you combine **pulses with cereals**, they complement each other well. Examples are lentils with rice or beans with maize.

When you fry an egg, the clear egg white turns **white and firm**. The heat changes the shape of the protein molecules; they **coagulate** or **denature**. Another well-known protein is **gluten**. This sticky protein is found in wheat, spelt, rye and barley and makes bread dough elastic. People with **coeliac disease** cannot tolerate gluten and must eat gluten-free food.

gewusst: The word protein comes from the Greek word for “first” or “most important”.
You cannot make a boiled egg runny again, because the protein has coagulated for good.

teile.einleitung: Cabinetmakers work with wood. They build furniture such as tables, wardrobes and beds, but also doors, windows and kitchens. In Switzerland cabinetmaker is a popular apprenticeship trade.
wichtigste: Cabinetmakers work mainly with wood.
They build furniture, doors, windows and kitchens.
They saw, plane, sand and glue wood.
Today they also work with computer-controlled machines.
You learn the job as a cabinetmaker EFZ.
In Germany people often say Tischler instead of Schreiner.

abschnitte.text: The cabinetmaker's most important material is **wood**. Every kind of wood is different: **oak** is hard and heavy, **spruce** is soft and pale. Cabinetmakers know which wood is suitable for what. Besides solid wood, they also use boards made of pressed wood. Sometimes glass, metal or plastic are added.

First the wood is cut to size with the **saw**. With the **plane** it becomes smooth and straight. Then the parts are **glued**, screwed or fitted together with wood joints. Finally everything is **sanded** and protected with varnish, oil or wax. This produces a beautiful, sturdy piece of furniture.

In a modern joinery workshop there are many **machines** as well as hand tools. Some are controlled by a **computer** and cut parts very precisely. Furniture is often **planned and drawn** on the computer first. Even so, skilful hands are needed, for example when assembling or during **installation** at the customer's home.

In Switzerland you learn the job as a **cabinetmaker EFZ**. There are different specialisms, for example for **furniture and interior fittings** or for windows and doors. The ability to picture things in three dimensions, carefulness and a love of craftsmanship are important. If you would like a shorter training course, you can become a joinery assistant EBA. Later you can train further, for example as a **master cabinetmaker**.

gewusst: Wood moves: it expands when damp and shrinks when dry. Cabinetmakers have to take this into account when building.
Wood joints such as the dovetail joint need neither nails nor screws.

teile.einleitung: As well as the actual rent, a flat has other costs, for example for heating and hot water. However, the tenant only has to pay these **service charges** if they are expressly agreed in the tenancy agreement. The Code of Obligations sets out how they are billed.
wichtigste: You only have to pay service charges if they are listed individually in the contract.
With payments on account, there is a statement every year with an additional payment or a refund.
With a flat rate, you pay a fixed amount with no additional claims.
Tenants may inspect the receipts for the statement.
The gross rent is the net rent plus the service charges.
Mortgage interest and large repairs are not part of the service charges.

abschnitte.text: Service charges are costs for services connected with the **use of the flat**. Typical ones are **heating and hot water**, as well as, for example, cleaning the stairwell, the caretaker or the lift. They do not include **mortgage interest** and large repairs, which are included in the net rent. Under **Art. 257a OR**, the tenant only has to pay service charges if they have been **specially agreed**. If nothing is in the contract, they count as included in the rent.

There are two ways of paying service charges. With **payments on account**, you pay an **advance** every month. Once a year the landlord works out the real costs. Then there is an **additional payment** or a **refund**. With a **flat rate**, you pay a fixed amount that should match the average values over three years. There is then no statement with an additional claim.

The **gross rent** is the total of the **net rent** and the service charges. If a flat costs 1650 francs net and there are 220 francs of service charges on top, the gross rent is **1870 francs**. An additional payment can also be calculated: if someone pays 180 francs a month on account, that is 12 times 180 in a year, which is 2160 francs. If the statement comes to 2400 francs, they have to pay an extra **240 francs**.

Under **Art. 257b OR**, the tenant may inspect the **original receipts** for the service charge statement. This way they can check whether the amounts are right. Many buildings have **heating bills based on consumption**. Here the amount of heat each flat uses is measured. Anyone who heats sparingly then also pays less. This creates an incentive to save energy.

gewusst: Heating costs usually make up the largest part of the service charges.
If the tenancy agreement says nothing about service charges, they are already included in the rent.

teile.einleitung: Liability insurance pays when you cause damage to another person. This can happen quickly, for example when a ball hits a window. In Switzerland it is compulsory for cars and voluntary for private individuals.
wichtigste: Personal liability insurance covers damage you cause to other people or their things.
Your own things are not insured.
Personal liability insurance is not required by law, but is highly recommended.
Liability insurance is compulsory for motor vehicles.
Personal liability insurance covers damage to a rented flat if tenant damage is included.
Under Art. 41 OR, anyone who causes damage unlawfully and through their own fault must pay for it.
With an excess, you pay part of the damage yourself.

abschnitte.text: **Personal liability insurance** covers damage that you cause to **third parties**, that is to other people or their things. It also defends you against unjustified claims. Your own things are not insured; for that there is household contents insurance. An example: if an expensive glass falls and breaks while you are visiting friends, personal liability insurance can pay.

The basis is the **Code of Obligations**. Under Art. 41 OR, someone must pay for damage if they caused it unlawfully and **through their own fault**, that is on purpose or through carelessness. This is called **fault-based liability**. For animal keepers, Art. 56 OR applies: they are liable for their animal even if it is not their fault, unless they prove that they took enough care. This is a mild form of **strict liability**.

Under federal law, personal liability insurance is **not compulsory**. However, many landlords ask for proof of it when a tenancy agreement is signed. For **motor vehicles**, the Road Traffic Act requires liability insurance. Without proof there are no number plates, and the car may not go on the road.

A rented flat belongs to the landlord, that is to a third party. If a tenant damages the washbasin, for example, personal liability insurance covers it if **tenant damage** is included. Many insurance policies have an **excess**: you pay a fixed amount of the damage yourself, for example 200 francs. A higher excess usually makes the premium cheaper.

gewusst: Children who live with their parents are often covered by the family policy.
Because liability insurance for cars is compulsory, the road traffic office checks the proof of insurance before it issues number plates.

teile.einleitung: Everyone is particularly good at something. These strengths help when looking for a job that suits you. If you like drawing and making things, for example, you will find many creative jobs.
wichtigste: Strengths are things you are good at and like doing.
There are, for example, creative, practical, technical and social strengths.
If you are good at drawing, you have a strength for design jobs.
Graphic designers design posters, books, logos and websites.
The apprenticeship as a graphic designer EFZ lasts four years.
Parents, teachers and friends help you discover your own strengths.

abschnitte.text: A **strength** is something you are good at and usually also enjoy doing. Some people are good at maths, others are good listeners, and others are skilful with their hands. There are **creative**, **practical**, **technical** and **social** strengths. Nobody is good at everything, and that is completely normal. The important thing is to know your own strengths.

If you like drawing, painting and making things, you have a **design** strength. Such people often have good ideas and an eye for colours and shapes. Jobs such as **graphic designer**, 3D polydesigner, gardener specialising in landscape gardening or florist suit them. Goldsmith, cabinetmaker or interactive media designer also combine design with craft or technology.

**Graphic designers** design posters, books, logos, packaging and websites. They think about how a message can be shown well with pictures and lettering. Today they mostly work on the computer, but sketches by hand are still part of it. The apprenticeship as a graphic designer EFZ lasts four years. It often requires a preliminary design course or an entrance exam.

You can find your strengths in different ways. You can ask yourself: what do I like doing in my free time? What do people praise me for? Parents, teachers and friends often see strengths that you do not notice yourself. At school and at the **careers advice service** there are tests and conversations about this. A **taster apprenticeship** then shows whether a job really suits your own strengths.

gewusst: Many famous company logos were created by graphic designers who use only a few shapes and colours.
Strengths can be trained: if you practise a lot, you get better and better at drawing, for example.

teile.einleitung: A covering letter is a short letter that you include with an application. In it you explain why you want to learn exactly this job and work in exactly this company. It should make the company curious to get to know you.
wichtigste: In the covering letter you explain why you want the apprenticeship place.
It is about one A4 page long.
If you know the name of the person in charge, you address them directly.
Concrete examples, for instance from your taster apprenticeship, are more convincing than general phrases.
Show that you have found out about the company.
At the end you ask for an interview and close with “Kind regards”.
Ask a second person to read the letter before you send it.

abschnitte.text: A CV shows what you have already done. The **covering letter** shows who you are and what drives you. You explain why the job interests you and what you like about the company. The company should want to invite you to an **interview**. That is why it is worth writing a separate letter for each application.

At the top go your address, the company's address, the place and date, and a **subject line**, for example “Application as a cabinetmaker EFZ”. Then comes the **greeting**, ideally with the person's name, such as “Dear Ms Muster”. In the main part you talk about your interest and your strengths. The whole letter fits on about **one A4 page**. Short and clear works better than long and complicated.

Sentences such as “I am motivated and a good team player” fit every company and therefore say little. A **concrete example** is better: what did you experience during your taster apprenticeship? What did you enjoy? Also mention what appeals to you about the **company**. You can find information on its website or during your taster days. This way you show real interest.

At the end you thank them for reading and write that you would be pleased to have an **interview**. Then comes the **closing formula**. In formal letters in Switzerland people usually write “Freundliche Grüsse”, which means “Kind regards”. Casual phrases such as “Bye” are not suitable. Finally comes your **signature**.

Typing mistakes look careless. A **second person** often finds mistakes that you overlook yourself. Parents, teachers or the **careers advice service** are happy to help. Also check that the company's name and address are correct. Only then do you send off the application.

gewusst: Many companies first read only a few lines. A good opening therefore often decides whether someone reads on.
Many training companies receive dozens of applications for one apprenticeship place. A personal letter helps you to stand out.

teile.einleitung: In the kitchen there are many utensils that help with cooking and baking. Each utensil has a particular job. If you know them and use them safely, cooking is easier and you do not hurt yourself.
wichtigste: You whip cream until stiff with the whisk.
You roll out dough with the rolling pin.
You peel potatoes and carrots with the peeler.
You drain pasta in the colander.
You grate cheese with the grater.
You turn pan handles inwards.
Metal does not belong in the microwave.

abschnitte.text: With the **whisk** you stir quickly. This gets air into the cream, and it becomes stiff. You can also beat eggs and sauces with it. The **rolling pin** is a wooden roller. With it you roll dough out thin and flat, for example for biscuits or a cake.

With the **peeler** you peel potatoes, carrots or apples. It only cuts off a thin layer, so a lot of the vegetable is left. The **grater** has sharp holes. If you rub cheese over it, you get fine pieces. You can also grate carrots or apples with it. Watch your fingers!

Pasta is cooked in plenty of water. Afterwards you drain it in the **colander**. The hot water runs through the holes and the pasta stays inside. It is best to put the colander in the sink. That way no hot water splashes onto your hands. You can also wash lettuce in the colander.

On the cooker you turn the **handle of a pan** inwards. A handle that sticks out can easily be knocked, and then the hot pan falls down. You only touch hot pans and baking trays with **oven gloves**. **Metal** does not belong in the **microwave**, because it can make sparks in there. That is dangerous.

gewusst: “Wallholz” (rolling pin) and “Schwingbesen” (whisk) are typical Swiss German words; in Germany people often say Nudelholz and Schneebesen.
The peeler with a blade set crosswise was invented in Switzerland and is often called the “Rex”.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland many people call the postman Pöstler and the postwoman Pöstlerin. They bring letters, newspapers and parcels to people's homes. They are out almost every day, in sunshine, rain and snow.
wichtigste: Pöstler is the Swiss name for the postman.
Postmen and postwomen deliver letters, newspapers and parcels.
They work for Swiss Post.
They often travel by electric scooter, by van or on foot.
The colour of the post in Switzerland is yellow.
You learn the job as a logistics specialist EFZ.

abschnitte.text: The day starts early. First, letters and parcels are sorted in the order of the **round**. Then the postman sets off and puts the post into the **letterboxes**. He hands over parcels and registered letters in person. If nobody is at home, he leaves a **collection notice**. Then you can collect the item later at the post office.

abschnitte.titel: Out and about by scooter and bike
abschnitte.text: Depending on the area, postmen and postwomen travel by **electric scooter**, by van or on foot. In town there are many letterboxes close together. In the countryside the distances are longer. Postmen and postwomen are outside in all weathers. That is why they need good clothing and a lot of stamina.

Most postmen and postwomen work for **Swiss Post**. It belongs to the **Confederation** and is easy to recognise by its **yellow colour**. The yellow **PostBuses**, which connect many villages with railway stations, also belong to the post. Besides letters and parcels, the post also offers banking services through PostFinance.

If you would like to become a postwoman, you can do an apprenticeship as a **logistics specialist EFZ** in the specialism **distribution**. You learn to sort items, plan rounds and serve customers in a friendly way. There is also a shorter training course with a Federal VET Certificate (EBA). Reliability, tidiness and enjoying contact with people are important.

gewusst: Postmen and postwomen often know almost all the names on the letterboxes in their neighbourhood.
Swiss Post even answers letters to the Christ Child or to Samichlaus (Santa Claus).

teile.einleitung: The **Swiss food pyramid** shows at a glance how to eat a balanced diet. At the bottom are foods you need a lot of, and at the top those you should only eat rarely. It is published by the Swiss Society for Nutrition together with the Confederation, and the recommendations were updated in 2024.
wichtigste: Every day 1 to 2 litres of unsweetened drinks, ideally tap water or tea.
Every day 5 portions of vegetables and fruit, 3 of vegetables and 2 of fruit.
Every day 3 portions of cereals or potatoes, half of them wholegrain.
Every day 2 to 3 portions of dairy products.
Meat at most 2 to 3 times a week, pulses at least once a week.
Sweet things, salty snacks and sugary drinks are at the top and belong on the plate only rarely.

abschnitte.text: Right at the bottom of the pyramid are **drinks**. About **1 to 2 litres** of unsweetened drinks a day are recommended. **Tap water** and unsweetened tea are best. In hot weather and when doing sport you need more. Sugary drinks do not count; they are right at the top of the pyramid.

Every day you should eat **5 portions** of vegetables and fruit, of which **3 portions of vegetables** and **2 portions of fruit**. A portion weighs about **120 grams**, which is roughly a handful. On top of this come **3 portions** of cereal products or **potatoes** every day. At least half of the cereal products should be **wholegrain**, because it provides more fibre.

Every day **2 to 3 portions** of milk or dairy products belong to the diet, ideally unsweetened. A portion is, for example, **2 decilitres of milk** or **30 grams of hard cheese**. As a source of protein you should vary between meat, fish, eggs, tofu and **pulses**. **Meat**, including poultry and sausages, should be limited to **2 to 3 times a week**. You should eat lentils, beans or chickpeas **at least once a week**.

At the **top** of the pyramid are **sweets**, **sugary drinks** and **salty snacks**. The body does not need them. You may enjoy them, but only in small amounts. The higher up a food is in the pyramid, the less of it you should eat. Getting enough exercise is also part of it.

gewusst: A portion of vegetables or fruit is about the size of a handful.
In Switzerland tap water is a cheap and healthy drink.

teile.einleitung: **Recycling** means using materials that have already been used again. New things are made from old bottles, cans or newspapers. Switzerland collects a great many materials separately.
wichtigste: The recycling symbol consists of three arrows in a circle.
New paper is made from waste paper.
You squash PET bottles flat and screw the lid back on.
Aluminium cans go into the aluminium collection.
You take old electrical appliances such as mobile phones back to the shop.
Even better than recycling is making less rubbish.

abschnitte.text: On many packages you can see **three arrows** running in a **circle**. This is the **recycling symbol**. It shows that a material can be used again. The circle means that the old thing becomes a new one, again and again. This means fewer new **raw materials** are needed.

**Waste paper** is soaked in water at the factory and made into new paper. This way fewer trees have to be felled. **Cardboard** is collected separately in the **cardboard collection**. You fold empty boxes flat first so that they take up less space. New cardboard is made from old cardboard.

You take **PET bottles** to the PET collection point, for example in the shop. First you squash them **flat** and screw the **lid** back on. Empty **drinks cans** made of aluminium belong in the **aluminium collection**. Aluminium can be melted down again and again. This needs much less energy than making new aluminium.

A broken **mobile phone** or an old charger does not belong in the rubbish. **Electrical appliances** contain valuable materials such as copper or gold. In Switzerland, **shops** that sell such appliances take old ones back free of charge. But best of all is when no rubbish is produced at all. Your own **water bottle** replaces lots of disposable bottles.

gewusst: Recycled aluminium needs only a tiny fraction of the energy that new aluminium requires.
An old mobile phone contains tiny amounts of gold.

teile.einleitung: Butchers process meat and turn it into steaks, roasts, mince and sausages. In Switzerland the job is now officially called meat specialist.
wichtigste: A butcher sells meat and sausages.
Butchers are now officially called meat specialists.
They cut up meat, make sausages and advise customers.
Hygiene and refrigeration are especially important with meat.
In Switzerland the apprenticeship as a meat specialist EFZ lasts three years.
The cervelat is seen as Switzerland's national sausage.

abschnitte.text: In the **butcher's shop**, the butcher works with meat from beef, pork, veal, lamb or poultry. She **cuts up** large pieces into steaks, roasts, escalopes or strips. From meat and spices she makes **sausages**, which she smokes or scalds. In the shop she **advises** customers, for example on which cut is suitable for a fondue chinoise or a Sunday roast.

Switzerland has many **meat specialities**. The **cervelat** is seen as the national sausage and is a must at every barbecue. Also well known are the St Gallen bratwurst, the Vaud saucisson and **Bündnerfleisch**, an air-dried beef from the Grisons. Many butcher's shops have their own recipes, which they pass down through the generations.

Meat goes off quickly if it is not handled properly. That is why **hygiene** is especially important in a butcher's shop. Work surfaces, knives and machines are cleaned thoroughly. The meat is stored in the **cold room**. The butcher wears an apron, a cap and, for some tasks, a metal **protective glove** so that she does not cut herself.

In Switzerland the apprenticeship is called **meat specialist EFZ** and lasts three years. You can choose between focuses, for example processing or refining and selling. The two-year basic training is called **meat assistant EBA**. Meat specialists work in butcher's shops, large plants or in the meat departments of shops.

gewusst: In Switzerland many millions of cervelats are eaten every year.
The German word “Metzger” for butcher is used mainly in Switzerland and southern Germany; in northern Germany people tend to say “Fleischer”.

teile.einleitung: Not everyone works full time every week. In part-time work you work fewer hours than in a full-time job. In Switzerland part-time work is very widespread, but it also has effects on wages, holidays and retirement provision.
wichtigste: The workload percentage shows what percentage of a full-time job you work.
Wages and working hours are calculated in proportion to the workload.
According to the Federal Statistical Office, anyone who works less than 90 per cent counts as part-time.
In Switzerland more than a third of people in work work part-time, and more than half of women.
In job sharing, two or more people share one job.
With several small jobs, pension fund cover often has gaps.
With on-call work, the time spent on standby must also be paid.

abschnitte.text: The **workload percentage** shows what percentage of a full-time job someone works. If full time is 42 hours a week, at 60 per cent you work 42 times 0.6, which is 25.2 hours. Wages are also **in proportion** to the workload: with a full-time wage of 6200 francs, at 80 per cent you earn 6200 times 0.8, which is 4960 francs. Holidays are also calculated proportionally. Anyone who works three days a week and has four weeks of holiday gets 4 times 3, which is 12 days of holiday.

The **Federal Statistical Office** counts people in work with an employment level of less than 90 per cent as part-time. According to its figures, more than a third of people in work in Switzerland work part-time. Among women it is more than half. This puts Switzerland among the countries with the **highest rate of part-time work** in Europe. Reasons include family, further education, hobbies or health reasons.

There are different forms of part-time work. In **job sharing**, two or more people share one job with joint tasks and responsibility. When two people share a management role, this is also called **top sharing**. In **on-call work**, the person waits to be called in. According to the case law of the Federal Supreme Court, this standby time must also be paid, although not necessarily at the full wage. The employer may not shift the risk of fluctuating work entirely onto the employees.

Anyone who works part-time earns less and therefore also pays less into their retirement provision. For the **AVS**, the first pillar, every wage counts. For the **pension fund**, the second pillar, there is an **entry threshold**: you are only insured from a certain annual wage. In addition, a **coordination deduction** is taken from the wage. Both apply per employer. That is why people with several small jobs are often only insured a little, or not at all, in the second pillar.

gewusst: Many people in Switzerland choose to work part-time to have more time for family, further education or hobbies.
With the third pillar you can save privately for old age as well, even with a part-time job.

teile.einleitung: A workshop is a room where things are made or repaired. Polymechanics usually work in a workshop with large machines that they use to work metal. Clear rules for tidiness and safety apply there.
wichtigste: In a workshop things are made or repaired.
Polymechanics usually work in a workshop with machines.
Lathes and milling machines work metal very precisely.
Today many machines are controlled by computer.
Safety goggles, ear protection and safety boots protect against accidents.
Large companies often have their own training workshop for apprentices.

abschnitte.text: A **workshop** is a workroom where something is made or repaired. There are workshops in many jobs: cabinetmakers have a wood workshop, car mechanics a car workshop, bike mechanics a bike workshop. In a **mechanical workshop** mainly metal is worked. Polymechanics, for example, work there.

There are large machines in the polymechanic's workshop. On the **lathe**, the workpiece turns and a tool removes material. This produces round parts such as axles or screws. With the **milling machine**, the tool turns and mills shapes out of a block of metal. Today many of these machines are controlled by computer. They are called **CNC machines**.

Anyone working in a workshop must protect themselves well. **Safety goggles** protect the eyes from metal shavings. **Ear protection** protects against noise, and **safety boots** protect the feet if something heavy falls down. Long hair is tied back so that it does not get caught in a machine. Tidiness is important so that you do not trip and can find every tool quickly.

Many larger companies have their own **training workshop**. There apprentices learn the basics in the first years of their apprenticeship before they work in production. They practise filing, drilling, turning and milling and learn to read technical drawings. In smaller companies you learn directly in the normal workshop. In addition there are **inter-company courses**, in which all apprentices practise the same basic techniques.

gewusst: With modern machines, metal parts can be made accurate to a thousandth of a millimetre.
When metal is worked, a cooling liquid is often used so that the tool and the workpiece do not get too hot.

teile.einleitung: Consumption means buying and using things, for example food, clothes or toys. Everything we buy has to be made and transported. If you consume wisely, you protect the environment.
wichtigste: Consumption means buying and using up.
Every new thing needs raw materials and energy.
Swapping is better than throwing away.
If something can be mended, you do not need to buy it new.
Second-hand and borrowing save money and protect the environment.
Before buying, you ask yourself: do I really need this?

abschnitte.text: Every day we consume something: food, electricity, water, clothes or toys. People who buy something are called **consumers**. Every new product needs **raw materials**, **energy** and **transport**. When it is broken or we no longer like it, it often becomes rubbish.

If an old toy is still good but you would like something new, you can **swap**. If you swap with a friend, each of you has something new to play with, and nothing is thrown away. **Flea markets** and **second-hand shops** are good places too. Many municipalities have **toy libraries** where you can borrow games.

abschnitte.titel: Mending and using things for longer
abschnitte.text: Things that are broken can often be **repaired**. A hole in a jumper can be sewn up, and a bike can be taken to be mended. In many places in Switzerland there are **repair cafés**, where volunteers help with repairs. The longer you use something, the less needs to be made new.

Before buying something, it helps to ask: **do I really need this?** Sometimes the wish has passed after a few days. If you do buy, you can look for good **quality**, because durable things last longer. **Quality labels** also show which products were made in a more environmentally friendly or fairer way.

gewusst: The first repair café opened in Amsterdam in 2009; today there are such meetings in many countries.
In a toy library you can borrow games just as you borrow books in a library.

teile.einleitung: Paramedics come in the ambulance when someone is seriously ill or injured. They give first aid and take the person safely to hospital. In Switzerland you call them on the emergency number 144.
wichtigste: Paramedics come in the ambulance.
They give first aid at the scene of an accident or at home.
They take injured and ill people to hospital.
The emergency number for the ambulance service is 144.
For rescues by helicopter there is Rega, on the number 1414.
You learn the job at a college of higher education.

abschnitte.text: When the emergency call comes, everything has to happen fast. The **paramedics** set off with blue lights. At the scene they first check how the person is. They check **breathing**, pulse and consciousness. Then they help, for example with oxygen, a bandage or medicines. After that they take the person to **hospital**.

In Switzerland you reach the ambulance service on **144**. At the control centre someone asks exactly: **where** did it happen, **what** is wrong and **how many** people are affected? Stay calm and do not hang up too early. The control centre often gives tips on the phone about what you can do until help arrives. For accidents in the mountains, **Rega** helps on the number **1414**.

An ambulance is like a small **hospital on wheels**. Inside there is a stretcher, oxygen, dressings and medicines. A **defibrillator** helps when the heart is not beating properly. With a monitor the paramedics watch the patient's readings. Everything is stored so that it is within easy reach even during the journey.

In Switzerland you become a **paramedic HF** at a **college of higher education**. The training usually lasts three years. Before that you usually need a completed apprenticeship or a Matura. Steady nerves, team spirit and enjoying helping others are important. Physical fitness is also needed, because patients often have to be carried.

gewusst: Rega was founded in 1952 and is supported by many patrons.
If you take a first aid course, you can already help a lot until the ambulance arrives.

teile.einleitung: Inter-company courses, üK for short, are courses outside the training company. There apprentices practise the basic skills of their job. Alongside the training company and the vocational school, they are the third place of learning in an apprenticeship.
wichtigste: üK stands for überbetriebliche Kurse, inter-company courses.
They take place outside the training company.
In the üK you practise the basic skills of the job.
They are the third place of learning alongside the company and vocational school.
They are organised by the professional associations.
Attendance is compulsory for apprentices.

abschnitte.text: **Inter-company courses** complement the training in the company and at school. In them, all apprentices in a job learn the same **basic skills**. This gives everyone the same chances, no matter which company they work in. The courses are required by the training ordinance for each job.

The courses are usually organised by the **professional associations**, also known as organisations of the working world (OdA). They often take place in their own training centres. There are workshops, machines and practice rooms there. The teaching is done by experienced skilled workers.

Depending on the job, you practise, for example, welding, bricklaying, cooking or caring for people using practice dummies. Commercial employees practise typical office work and procedures from their industry. Hairdressers practise cuts on **training heads**. What you learn in the üK, you then use in the company.

Depending on the job, an üK lasts a few days to several weeks per year of the apprenticeship. The days count as **working time**, so wages continue to be paid. In principle the training company pays the costs, supported by the canton and the professional association. Attendance is **compulsory** for apprentices.

Not every company can show all parts of a job itself. A small company may not have all the machines or tasks. The üK fill these gaps. You also get to know apprentices from other companies and can share experiences.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short for überbetriebliche Kurse, inter-company courses.
Organisation of the working world, for example a professional association.
A place where you learn during your apprenticeship.
A building with workshops where courses for apprentices take place.

gewusst: In some construction trades, apprentices spend several weeks in the üK in their first year before going onto the building site.
Many training centres for üK have their own practice building sites or practice kitchens.

teile.einleitung: Equality at work means that women and men should have the same opportunities and rights in their jobs. In Switzerland, important rules on this are set out in the Federal Constitution and in the Gender Equality Act.
wichtigste: Since 1981 the principle of “equal pay for work of equal value” has been in the Federal Constitution.
The Gender Equality Act has been in force since 1 July 1996.
It forbids discrimination on grounds of sex in recruitment, pay, promotion and dismissal.
Since 2020, companies with 100 or more employees must carry out an equal pay analysis.
On 14 June 1991 and 14 June 2019 there were large women's strikes.
Since 2021 there have been two weeks of paid paternity leave.

abschnitte.text: In 1981 the people and the cantons accepted the **equality article**. It calls for equal rights for women and men and equal pay for work of equal value. On 1 July 1996 the **Gender Equality Act** came into force. It forbids putting anyone at a disadvantage at work because of their sex. This applies to recruitment, pay, promotion and dismissal.

In Switzerland women earn less than men on average. Experts explain part of the difference by factors such as training, experience, position or industry. The rest is called the **unexplained pay gap** and can point to discrimination. Since a revision of the law in 2020, employers with 100 or more employees must carry out an **equal pay analysis** and have it checked.

**Horizontal segregation** is when women and men mostly work in different jobs, for example in nursing or in technical jobs. **Vertical segregation** concerns the levels of the hierarchy. The term **glass ceiling** describes invisible barriers: qualified women reach top positions less often, even though there is no official barrier.

On **14 June 1991**, ten years after the equality article, hundreds of thousands of women went on strike throughout Switzerland. On 14 June 2019 another large strike day followed. Combining work and family is also an issue. After a popular vote in September 2020, fathers have been entitled to two weeks of **paternity leave** since 1 January 2021, paid through the income compensation scheme.

gewusst: 14 June was chosen because the equality article was accepted on 14 June 1981.
In Switzerland women have only had the right to vote at federal level since 1971.

teile.einleitung: Schnuppern means trying out a job. You work in a company for a few days and see what the job is really like. If you want to know, for example, whether cook is the right job for you, you can try it out in a kitchen.
wichtigste: Schnuppern means trying out a job for a few days.
You work in a real company.
This way you see what the job is really like.
If you want to become a cook, you can for example try it out in a restaurant kitchen.
Trying out jobs is an important part of choosing a career in Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: An example: Nina in the kitchen
abschnitte.text: Nina likes cooking at home. She wonders whether **cook** is the right job for her. So she asks a restaurant whether she can **try it out** for a few days. In the kitchen she helps to prepare vegetables, watches the cooking and sees how hectic it gets at **lunchtime**. Afterwards she knows much better whether she likes the job.

abschnitte.titel: What you learn when trying out a job
abschnitte.text: When you try out a job, you see its **everyday reality**. You notice whether you prefer working indoors or outdoors, alone or in a **team**. You find out when the work starts and how tiring it is. You are often allowed to do small tasks yourself. This way you feel whether you enjoy the work.

In Switzerland many young people do an **apprenticeship** after compulsory school. So that they find the right job, they try out different companies at **lower secondary school**. The school and the **careers advice service** support them. If you try out several jobs, you can compare and decide better.

gewusst: Sometimes, while trying out jobs, you discover a job that you had never thought of before.

teile.einleitung: Fairtrade means “fair trade”. The label is meant to make sure that small farmers and workers in countries of the Global South are paid more fairly and have better working conditions.
wichtigste: Fairtrade aims for fair conditions for farmers and workers in the Global South.
In Switzerland, Fairtrade began under the name Max Havelaar.
The Max Havelaar Foundation was founded in 1992.
Farmers receive a minimum price plus a premium.
The farmers decide together how the premium is used.
Bananas are a particularly successful Fairtrade product in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Many products such as coffee, cocoa or bananas grow in tropical countries. The farmers there are often poor. When prices on the world market fall, they sometimes do not earn enough to live on. **Fairtrade** wants to change this. It sets rules for fairer pay, safe work and protecting the environment. **Child labour** is also forbidden under the Fairtrade rules.

In Switzerland the **Max Havelaar Foundation** was founded in 1992. It awards the **Fairtrade label**. The name comes from the main character of a **Dutch novel** from the 19th century. In it, Max Havelaar stands up against the exploitation of farmers in a colony. Today you can find the label in almost every Swiss supermarket.

Fairtrade guarantees a **minimum price**. It is meant to cover the costs of sustainable production, even when the market price is low. There is also a **premium**. The farmers decide together in their organisation what to use the money for. With it they fund, for example, **schools**, wells or better machines.

In Switzerland the **banana** is one of the best-selling Fairtrade products. Other well-known products are **coffee**, cocoa, chocolate, tea, sugar, rice and flowers such as roses. Apples, cherries or plums, on the other hand, also grow in Switzerland and usually do not carry a Fairtrade label. Fairtrade products often cost a little more. Whether and how much fair trade achieves is also discussed critically.

gewusst: The Fairtrade mark shows a figure raising one arm, on a blue and green background.
In some regions whole school buildings have been paid for out of the premium.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland bread is part of almost every breakfast and evening meal. Before a loaf is on the table, it takes the farmer, the miller and the baker.
wichtigste: Bread is made from flour, and flour from grains of cereal.
The combine harvester harvests the grain in the field.
In the mill the grains are ground into flour.
Yeast makes the dough rise.
The baker bakes the bread in the oven.
The Zopf is Switzerland's typical Sunday bread.

abschnitte.text: Bread begins in the field. The farmer sows **cereals** such as wheat, spelt or rye. The plants grow and form ears with lots of grains. In summer, when the field is golden yellow, the **combine harvester** comes. It cuts the cereal and separates the **grains** from the **straw**. The straw is used, for example, in the cowshed.

The grains go to the **mill**. There they are crushed finely between **rollers** or stones. This produces **flour**. The **miller** makes sure that the flour is nice and fine. For white flour the husk of the grain is removed. With **wholemeal flour** the whole grain stays in.

The **baker** mixes flour, water, salt and **yeast**. Then he kneads everything into a dough. Yeast is made of tiny fungi. They make small **gas bubbles**, and the dough becomes big and airy.
