Then the baker shapes the loaves and bakes them in the hot **oven**. Some breads are also made with **sourdough**.

In Switzerland there are many kinds of bread, for example Ruchbrot, Bürli or Ticino bread. A special bread is the **Zopf**. Its dough contains milk and butter. It is plaited from two or more strands of dough, like a plait of hair. In many families it is eaten on **Sundays** for breakfast, often with butter and jam.

gewusst: The holes in bread come from the gas bubbles that the yeast makes.
Bread is one of the oldest foods: people were already baking flatbreads thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: Social security deductions are amounts taken from the gross wage before the wage is paid out. They finance insurance schemes such as the AVS, unemployment insurance and the pension fund. What is left is the net wage.
wichtigste: Social security deductions are taken from the gross wage; what is left is the net wage.
For AVS, IV and EO, employees pay 5.3 per cent (as of 2026).
For unemployment insurance it is 1.1 per cent up to the maximum wage.
From an annual wage of 22,680 francs you are insured in the pension fund (as of 2026).
The pension fund is the second pillar of retirement provision.
The employer pays the premium for accidents at work.
You pay AVS contributions from 1 January after your 17th birthday.

abschnitte.text: The **gross wage** is the wage written in the contract. **Social security deductions** are taken from it. What arrives in your account is the **net wage**. The deductions are calculated as percentages. For example: 5.3 per cent of 5000 francs is 5000 times 0.053, which is **265 francs**. On the **payslip** you can see each deduction separately.

The **AVS** is old-age and survivors' insurance, the **IV** is disability insurance. The **EO** replaces part of your wages, for example during military or civilian service. Together they cost 10.6 per cent of wages. Employers and employees each pay half, so **5.3 per cent** each (as of 2026). People in work pay from **1 January after their 17th birthday**, including apprentices.

**Unemployment insurance** (ALV) helps when someone loses their job. The contribution is 2.2 per cent of wages up to an annual wage of 148,200 francs (as of 2026). Here too, employers and employees share the contribution. So employees pay **1.1 per cent**. This pays, for example, the daily allowances for jobseekers.

Swiss retirement provision rests on **three pillars**. The first is the state **AVS/IV**. The second is **occupational pension provision**, which is the pension fund under the BVG. The third is private saving. Membership of the pension fund is compulsory from an annual wage of **22,680 francs** with one employer (as of 2026). What is insured is the **coordinated wage**, which is the wage minus a coordination deduction of 26,460 francs.

All employees are insured against **accidents at work**. This premium is paid by the **employer** alone. Anyone who works at least **8 hours a week** for one employer is also insured against **non-occupational accidents**, that is in their free time. This premium may be deducted from wages. Anyone who works less needs accident cover through their health insurance.

gewusst: Apprentices already pay AVS contributions at 17, even though their pension only comes decades later.
The AVS has existed since 1948. It is one of the most important social welfare schemes in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Swiss watches are famous all over the world. Inside every mechanical watch there are many tiny parts that have to fit together exactly. Watchmakers build, repair and look after these little works of art.
wichtigste: Switzerland is known worldwide for its watches.
Watchmakers build and repair watches with fine tools.
Important places of the watch industry are in the Jura Arc, for example La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle.
Geneva and Biel are also important watch towns.
The watchmaking craft of Switzerland and France is part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.
The job requires patience, steady hands and good eyesight.

abschnitte.text: **Watchmakers** assemble watches from many small parts. They clean, oil and repair movements. For this they use tweezers, tiny screwdrivers and a **loupe**, which they clamp to their eye. Some parts are smaller than a grain of rice. A mechanical movement can consist of more than a hundred individual parts.

A **mechanical watch** does not need a battery. A wound-up spring provides the power. The power is passed on through small gear wheels. The **balance wheel**, a fine little wheel, swings back and forth and makes sure that the hands move evenly. In automatic watches, the spring winds itself up through the movement of the arm.

Many watches are made in the **Jura Arc**, between Geneva and Basel. In the past, farming families made watch parts at home in winter. The towns of **La Chaux-de-Fonds** and **Le Locle** were planned entirely for the watch industry and have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009. The Vallée de Joux, Geneva and Biel are also important. Since 2020 the watchmaking craft of Switzerland and France has been UNESCO **intangible cultural heritage**.

In the 1970s cheap **quartz watches** from Asia came onto the market. Many Swiss companies got into difficulties, and thousands of people lost their jobs. This is called the **quartz crisis**. In the 1980s, the inexpensive plastic **Swatch** from Biel was one of the things that helped to make the watch industry strong again. Today watches are one of Switzerland's most important exports.

gewusst: The watch towns of La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle have long, straight streets so that plenty of light falls into the workshops.
With regular care, a good mechanical watch can run for many decades.

teile.einleitung: **Cleaning products** help to remove dirt, grease and limescale. Depending on the dirt, you need an acidic or an alkaline product. Because some cleaning products can be dangerous, you must use them properly and store them safely.
wichtigste: Acidic products such as vinegar or citric acid help against limescale.
Alkaline products such as washing soda or soft soap help against grease.
You must never mix chlorine cleaners with acidic cleaners.
In cases of poisoning, Tox Info Suisse helps on the number 145.
Cleaning products always stay in their original bottle.
A pH value of 7 is neutral.

abschnitte.text: The **pH scale** goes from 0 to 14. Values below 7 are **acidic**, values above 7 are **alkaline**, and exactly **7** is **neutral**. Against **limescale** in the bathroom, acidic products such as **vinegar** or citric acid help, because limescale dissolves in acid. Against **grease** in the kitchen, alkaline products such as **washing soda** or soft soap help. They dissolve grease and protein well.

You must never mix **chlorine cleaners** with **acidic** cleaners, for example with a descaler. This can produce poisonous **chlorine gas**. It strongly irritates the airways and can be dangerous. It is safest always to use only one product at a time. When cleaning, you should air the room well.

Dangerous cleaning products carry **hazard pictograms**. These symbols, which are the same all over the world (GHS), are **red-bordered diamonds** with a black symbol. You never pour cleaning products into empty **drinks bottles**. Children in particular could otherwise mistake them for something drinkable. Cleaning products stay in their **original bottle** and are kept out of reach of small children.

If someone has swallowed a cleaning product or got it in their eyes, you call **145**. This number belongs to **Tox Info Suisse**, the advice centre for poisoning. Experts there help round the clock. In a life-threatening emergency you dial **144**, the ambulance service. 117 is the police and 118 the fire brigade.

More cleaning product does not clean better. Too much of it pollutes **rivers and lakes** and costs money for nothing. The instructions on the packet help you to **use the right amount**. Often warm water and a microfibre cloth are enough. This way you clean more cheaply and in a more environmentally friendly way.

gewusst: Tox Info Suisse can be reached day and night on the short number 145.
Vinegar helps against limescale because the acid dissolves the limescale chemically.

teile.einleitung: Opticians help people to see better. They measure how well the eyes can see, advise on choosing glasses and make them to fit. In Switzerland optician is an apprenticeship trade with a Federal VET Diploma.
wichtigste: You get new glasses from the optician.
Opticians measure your eyesight with an eye test.
They grind lenses to shape and fit them into the frame.
The glasses are adjusted to fit your nose and ears exactly.
The job is called optician EFZ.
For eye diseases, the eye doctor (ophthalmologist) is responsible.

abschnitte.text: If you do not see well, you go to the **optician**. There your **eyesight** is measured first. Then together you choose a frame that fits well and that you like. The optician orders the right **lenses**, grinds them to the shape of the frame and fits them in. Finally the glasses are adjusted so that they sit comfortably and do not slip.

In an **eye test** you read letters or symbols that get smaller and smaller. With different lenses the optician checks which ones let you see most sharply. If things far away look blurred, you are **short-sighted**. If you have trouble close up, you are **long-sighted**. The lenses correct these problems.

In Switzerland you learn the job in an apprenticeship as an **optician EFZ**. You work in the shop and attend vocational school. Skilful hands, enjoying dealing with people and an interest in technology are important. After the apprenticeship you can train further, for example as an **optometrist**, who examines the eyes even more closely and fits contact lenses.

The optician and the eye doctor are two different jobs. The **eye doctor** is a doctor and treats diseases of the eyes. The **optician** looks after glasses and visual aids. If an optician notices something unusual, he sends the person to the doctor. In this way the two work together.

gewusst: Glasses have existed since the Middle Ages. The first ones were reading glasses without arms.
Sunglasses can also have ground lenses with a prescription.

teile.einleitung: The pipe wrench is a large, strong wrench for gripping pipes. Plumbers need it to tighten or loosen pipes and nuts. Its toothed jaws also hold round parts firmly.
wichtigste: With a pipe wrench you tighten or loosen pipes and nuts.
It is used mainly by plumbers.
Its jaws have teeth so that it does not slip on round pipes.
The opening can be adjusted to different sizes.
The harder you press, the more strongly the wrench grips.

abschnitte.text: A pipe wrench has a long **handle** and two **jaws**. The jaws have small **teeth**. With an adjusting screw or a joint you can make the opening bigger or smaller. This means the wrench fits thin and thick pipes. The long handle works like a **lever**: you need less force to turn something.

You put the jaws round the **pipe** or the **nut** and squeeze the handle. The teeth bite in, and you can turn. If you turn in one direction, the part gets tighter. In the other direction you loosen it. You often need **two wrenches**: one holds, the other turns.

**Plumbers** lay water pipes and fit washbasins, toilets and showers. They have to connect a lot of pipes. The pipe wrench is one of their most important tools for this. Because the teeth can leave marks, for attractive chrome-plated parts they prefer to use another tool or put a cloth in between.

gewusst: The pipe wrench grips all the more firmly the harder you pull on the handle. That makes it so practical for smooth pipes.

teile.einleitung: To make goods or offer services, certain resources are needed. These are called **factors of production**. Economics traditionally distinguishes labour, land and capital, today often with knowledge added.
wichtigste: The classic factors of production are labour, land and capital.
In economics, capital mainly means machines, tools and buildings.
Each factor brings an income: wages, interest or rent from land.
Human capital covers people's knowledge and skills.
In Switzerland land is particularly scarce and expensive.
More of the same factor eventually brings less and less extra output.

abschnitte.text: Classical economists such as **Adam Smith** and **David Ricardo** named three foundations of all production: **labour**, **land** and **capital**. Labour is the activity of people. Land includes ground and raw materials. In economics, **capital** mainly means **real capital**: machines, tools and buildings that have themselves been made and serve further production. Money on its own does not produce anything yet.

Each factor of production brings its owner a **factor income**. For labour you receive **wages**. Capital brings **interest**. For the use of land you pay a **land rent**, for example as a **lease** or rent. A farmer who leases land therefore pays the owner a land rent.

Today **knowledge** is also seen as an important factor. **Human capital** means the education, experience and skills of the workforce. Investment in training increases it. This is especially important for Switzerland, which has few raw materials. In business economics, **Erich Gutenberg** distinguished the basic factors of labour, equipment and materials from the **managerial factor**, that is leadership, planning and organisation.

A large part of Switzerland consists of **mountains**, lakes and other unproductive areas. Land for settlements and farming is therefore **scarce**. This leads to high **land prices**, especially in cities and on the Central Plateau. That is why spatial planning tries to use land economically.

Factors of production can partly replace each other. If wages rise, it often pays to replace labour with machines. This is called the **substitution of labour by capital**. If you increase only one single factor, for example the fertiliser on the same field, output rises less and less strongly beyond a certain point. This **law of diminishing returns** goes back to **Turgot** and to agriculture.

gewusst: In Switzerland a large part of the country's area is mountains and therefore hardly usable as building land.
For a country with few raw materials, like Switzerland, well-trained staff are one of the most important factors of production.

teile.einleitung: A flat tyre, a squeaking brake or a chain that has come off: that is when the bike mechanic helps. In Switzerland many people ride bikes, so specialists are needed to sell, mend and service bikes.
wichtigste: Bike mechanics mend tyres, brakes and chains.
Officially the job is called bicycle mechanic EFZ.
They also repair e-bikes with a motor and battery.
They advise customers when they buy a bike.
A well-serviced bike is safer in traffic.
With a little practice you can mend a flat tyre yourself.

abschnitte.text: **Bike mechanics** work in a bike shop with a workshop. They mend flat **tyres**, adjust **brakes** and gears and change worn chains. They also assemble new bikes and adjust them to the size of the rider. In the shop they advise customers on which bike suits them. Officially the job is called **bicycle mechanic EFZ**.

In Switzerland many **e-bikes** are sold. These bikes have an electric motor and a **battery**. That is why bike mechanics today also need to understand something about electronics. With a computer they read faults from the motor. In this way the job combines craft with modern technology.

With a little practice you can mend a **flat tyre** yourself. First you take the wheel out and lever the tyre off the rim with tyre levers. Then you look for the hole in the **inner tube**, for example in a bowl of water, where air bubbles rise. The hole is sealed with a **patch**. It is important to also check inside the tyre for splinters of glass or thorns.

A well-serviced bike is much safer in traffic. Brakes, lights and tyres should be checked regularly. If you want to learn the job, you need technical understanding, skilful hands and enjoyment of contact with people. The apprenticeship as a bicycle mechanic EFZ lasts three years. If you like riding a bike yourself, you already have a good starting point.

gewusst: The Swiss word “Velo” comes from the French “vélocipède”, which means “fast foot”.
Switzerland has a large network of signposted cycle routes, looked after by “SwitzerlandMobility” (SchweizMobil).

teile.einleitung: Tailors sew clothes and alter them. In Switzerland the apprenticeship trade is now called clothing designer EFZ. With needle, thread and sewing machine they make trousers, skirts, jackets and much more.
wichtigste: A tailor sews clothes.
Officially the job is called clothing designer EFZ.
She also alters clothes, for example when a pair of trousers is too long.
First she takes measurements, then she makes a pattern.
Her most important tool is the sewing machine.
The job requires patience and precise work.

abschnitte.text: A made-to-measure garment begins with the **tape measure**. The tailor measures, for example, the length of the arms, the waist and the width of the shoulders. With these measurements she draws a **pattern**. This is a paper template that shows what the pieces of fabric must look like. This way the garment will later fit exactly.

The pattern is laid on the **fabric**. Then the tailor cuts out the pieces with large **fabric scissors**. She holds the pieces together with **pins** and tries them on. After that she sews everything with the **sewing machine**. She sometimes does fine work, such as buttons or a hem, by hand.

Often a garment you have bought does not fit quite right. Then the tailor helps: she **shortens** trousers that are too long, takes in a skirt or replaces a broken zip. An **alterations workshop** mainly does this kind of work. Mending is also good for the environment, because you can wear clothes for longer.

In Switzerland you do an apprenticeship as a **clothing designer EFZ**. The apprenticeship lasts three years. You learn about fabrics, how to make patterns and how to sew neatly. A love of fashion, patience and skilful hands are important. Later you can train further, for example in **fashion design** or costume design for the theatre.

gewusst: For theatre and film, tailors sew whole costumes, for example for knights or princesses.
In the past, tailors often had their own workshop in the village, where people had all their clothes made.

teile.einleitung: A place setting is everything one person needs at the table to eat: plate, cutlery, glass and napkin. If you lay the table properly, everyone finds what they need straight away, and the meal is relaxed.
wichtigste: The plate goes in the middle in front of the chair.
The fork lies to the left of the plate.
The knife lies on the right, with the blade facing the plate.
The soup spoon lies to the right of the knife.
The glass stands at the top right above the knife.
The dessert cutlery lies across the top of the plate.
The napkin lies next to or on the plate.

abschnitte.text: The plate goes exactly in front of the seat, about two finger widths from the edge of the table. The **fork** lies on the left, the **knife** on the right. Most people hold the knife in their right hand, which is why it lies on that side. The **blade** of the knife always faces the plate, so that nobody cuts themselves. If there is soup, you put the **spoon** to the right of the knife.

The **drinking glass** stands to the top right of the plate, roughly above the tip of the knife. This way you can reach it easily with your right hand without reaching across the plate. If you need several glasses, you put them side by side in a row. The glass should be clean and free of fingerprints.

The **dessert cutlery** lies across the top of the plate. You only need it at the end of the meal. A dessert spoon usually lies with its handle to the right, a dessert fork with its handle to the left. This way you can later easily pull the cutlery towards the right hand.

You use the **napkin** to wipe your mouth while eating. It lies to the left of the fork or folded on the plate. After the meal you help to **clear the table**: plates, cutlery and glasses go into the sink or the dishwasher. If everyone helps, the table is clean again in no time.

gewusst: At a formal meal with several courses, the cutlery is laid from the outside in, in the order in which you need it.
If you put your knife and fork side by side at an angle on the plate, in many places this shows that you have finished eating.

teile.einleitung: Carpenters are specialists in large structures made of wood. They build roof frames, wooden houses and sometimes even bridges. Wood is an old building material, but also a very modern one.
wichtigste: Carpenters build large wooden structures such as roof frames and wooden houses.
The roof frame is the wooden framework that holds up a roof.
Today many wooden parts are cut in the workshop with computer-controlled machines.
When the roof frame is finished, people in Switzerland celebrate the Aufrichte (topping-out).
The apprenticeship is called carpenter EFZ.
Wood grows back and stores carbon.

abschnitte.text: **Carpenters** build large structures out of wood. The best known is the **roof frame**, the framework of beams that holds up a roof. But they also build whole **wooden houses**, stairs, balconies, halls and bridges. They also restore old wooden buildings, for example farmhouses or church towers. In Switzerland a woman in this job is called a **Zimmerin**.

abschnitte.titel: From the workshop to the building site
abschnitte.text: First the wooden parts are prepared in the **workshop**. In the past every beam was marked out and cut by hand. This is called **framing** (Abbund). Today computers and large machines help, sawing and milling the wood precisely. Then a lorry brings the parts to the building site. There the carpenters put them together with a crane, often within a few days.

When the roof frame is up, people in Switzerland celebrate the **Aufrichte**, the topping-out ceremony. Often a small decorated fir tree is placed on the highest point of the roof. The client invites the tradespeople to a meal and thanks them for their work. This custom is very old and is also known in other countries; in Germany, for example, it is called **Richtfest**.

Wood is light, strong and easy to work. It also **grows back**. While a tree grows, it takes carbon dioxide from the air and stores the carbon in the wood. Switzerland has a lot of forest, so people like to build with Swiss wood. If you want to become a **carpenter EFZ**, you need a love of craftsmanship, a head for heights and good spatial awareness.

gewusst: The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne is one of the oldest surviving covered wooden bridges in Europe.
After their apprenticeship, some carpenters go “on the Walz” and travel from place to place for years as journeymen.

teile.einleitung: When **sorting rubbish**, you sort waste by material. In Switzerland this is also often called **separating waste** or **separate collection**. This way a lot can be recycled, and fewer new raw materials are needed.
wichtigste: Peelings such as carrot peel belong in the green waste.
You take empty jars to the glass collection, sorted into clear, green and brown.
Old newspapers belong in the waste paper.
Leftover rubbish goes into the rubbish bag and is burned.
Green waste is turned into compost or biogas.
Sorted rubbish can be recycled.

abschnitte.text: **Peelings and scraps** such as carrot peel, apple cores or lettuce leaves are **green waste**. Grass cuttings and leaves from the garden also belong to it. Many municipalities have a **green waste bin** for it. Green waste is made into **compost**, which is good, nutrient-rich soil for the garden. In large plants it is also turned into **biogas**, which can be used to produce electricity and heat.

You take empty jars and bottles to the **glass collection**. At the bottle bank there are holes for **clear, green and brown** glass. This way new glass of the right colour can be made from it. Old newspapers and exercise books go into the **waste paper**. New paper is made from it. In many municipalities cardboard is collected separately.

Whatever cannot be recycled is **leftover rubbish**. It goes into the **rubbish bag**. In many municipalities you have to pay a **charge** for these bags. That is why it is worth sorting well. The leftover rubbish is burned in a **waste incineration plant**. The heat is used to make electricity and heat houses.

Sorted rubbish can be **recycled**. Then fewer new **raw materials** such as wood, sand or crude oil are needed. This often also saves a lot of energy. But it is best if not so much rubbish is produced in the first place. Your own water bottle or a shopping bag help with this.

gewusst: In many Swiss municipalities you pay a charge for every rubbish bag.
The heat from burning rubbish is used to produce electricity and district heating.

teile.einleitung: A **seasonal calendar** shows when each fruit and vegetable is ripe here. Every fruit and every vegetable has its own time of year. If you shop by the season, you get fresh things from nearby.
wichtigste: In Switzerland strawberries are available in early summer.
Cherries ripen in June and July.
Plums are ripe in late summer.
Apples and pumpkins are harvested in autumn.
Asparagus is a spring vegetable.
Bananas do not grow in Switzerland and come from far away.

abschnitte.text: In spring it gets warmer and the first plants grow. **Asparagus** grows from April to June. In the woods you find **wild garlic**. From May the first **strawberries** ripen, but most of them in June. In winter no strawberries grow outdoors.

In **June and July** the **cherries** ripen in Switzerland. Then you can pick them straight from the tree. In summer there are also lots of berries, tomatoes and cucumbers. In **August and September** the **plums** are ripe. Then people like to bake a delicious **plum tart** (Zwetschgenwähe).

Autumn is the big harvest time. Most **apples** and pears are picked now. They are stored somewhere cool so that you can eat them until well into winter. The **pumpkin** is also harvested in autumn. People make **pumpkin soup** from it or carve it for Halloween.

In winter little grows outdoors. Then people eat **stored vegetables** such as carrots, cabbage or beetroot and also **Brussels sprouts**. In many places there are **chestnut stalls**. **Marroni** are sweet chestnuts. They are roasted and eaten hot, a real winter treat.

Fruit and vegetables in season grow nearby. They do not have to be **transported** far and often taste better because they are harvested ripe. Some fruits do not grow here at all. **Bananas** need a warm climate and come from far away by **ship**. Apples, pears and plums, on the other hand, grow here.

gewusst: Marroni are the fruit of the sweet chestnut tree, which grows especially in Ticino.
Well-stored Swiss apples are available almost all year round.

teile.einleitung: After a good application, the training company often invites you to an interview. There both sides want to get to know each other. With good preparation you can make a strong impression.
wichtigste: Arriving on time and well prepared shows respect and interest.
You find out about the company and the job beforehand.
A common question is: why do you want to learn this job?
If you do not understand a question, you politely ask.
Your mobile phone is switched off or on silent and in your bag.
Your clothes are clean and suit the job.
Asking your own questions at the end shows real interest.

abschnitte.text: Before the interview you find out about the **company** and the **job**: what does the firm make, and what tasks will you have in the apprenticeship? You think about answers to typical questions. A very common one is: “Why do you want to learn this job?” A convincing answer with examples, for instance from your taster apprenticeship, is important. It is best to practise the interview in a **role play** with your parents, a teacher or friends. That takes away the nerves.

**Punctuality** is very important, so you plan your journey with some time to spare. Your **clothes** are clean and tidy and suit the job. In a workshop they are different from in a bank, but always neat. At the start you greet the interviewer with **eye contact** and a friendly hello and introduce yourself by name. Your mobile phone is switched off or on silent and is in your bag.

You listen carefully and answer honestly. If you do not understand a question, you may **politely ask**. This shows that you want to be precise. A wrong answer to a question you misunderstood makes a worse impression. You sit up straight, look at the person and speak clearly. It is normal to be a little nervous, and training companies know that.

At the end the company often asks: “Do you have any questions?” Then it is good to ask your own **questions**, for example about how things work or about the tasks during the apprenticeship. This shows real interest in the company. It is best to prepare two or three questions at home. Finally you thank them for the interview and say goodbye in a friendly way.

gewusst: Some training companies invite you to an extra taster day after the interview, to get to know each other even better.
In the interview, many training companies pay close attention to motivation and reliability, not just to school marks.

teile.einleitung: CH is the abbreviation for Confoederatio Helvetica. That is Latin and means Swiss Confederation. You can see the abbreviation on cars, in internet addresses and in many other places.
wichtigste: CH stands for Confoederatio Helvetica.
The name is Latin and means Swiss Confederation.
Latin is neutral because it does not favour any of the four national languages.
Helvetica recalls the Helvetii, a Celtic tribe.
Coins and stamps often say “Helvetia”.
Swiss internet addresses end in .ch.

abschnitte.text: **Confoederatio** is Latin for alliance or confederation. **Helvetica** means Helvetian, in other words Swiss. Together this gives **Swiss Confederation**, the official name of Switzerland. The abbreviation **CH** is made up of the first letters of the two words. This gives an abbreviation that is the same in every part of the country.

Switzerland has four national languages: **German**, **French**, **Italian** and **Romansh**. The country has a different name in each of them, for example Schweiz, Suisse, Svizzera or Svizra. An abbreviation from one of these languages would favour that language. **Latin** belongs to nobody in particular and is therefore neutral. That is why it is used for coins, stamps and the country code.

The name Helvetica goes back to the **Helvetii**. They were a **Celtic tribe** who lived more than 2000 years ago in the area of present-day Switzerland. The Romans wrote about them, for example Julius Caesar. Later **Helvetia** became the name of a female figure who represents Switzerland. You can see her on some franc coins.

We come across the abbreviation CH often. It appears as the **country identification sign** on cars that travel abroad. Swiss internet addresses end in **.ch**. Postcodes are also sometimes written with CH in front. And the typeface **Helvetica**, one of the best-known typefaces in the world, was developed in Switzerland and named after the country.

gewusst: Although Switzerland is called a “Confederation”, it has been a federal state since 1848.
The world-famous typeface Helvetica was created in Switzerland in the 1950s.

teile.einleitung: Dietary fibre is made up of parts of plants that our body cannot digest, or only barely. Even so, fibre is very important for healthy digestion and for the bacteria in our gut.
wichtigste: Dietary fibre is made up of indigestible parts of plants.
Adults should eat about 30 grams of fibre a day.
Fibre is only found in plant foods, not in cheese or meat.
If you eat a lot of fibre, you should drink enough water.
Gut bacteria partly feed on fibre.
Pectin is soluble, cellulose is insoluble.

abschnitte.text: **Dietary fibre** is found in plants, for example in the cell walls. Our body cannot break it down in the small intestine. That is why people used to think it was useless “ballast” (in German it is called Ballaststoffe). Today we know that it is very valuable. It fills you up, stimulates **digestion** and keeps the gut healthy. A distinction is made between **soluble** and **insoluble** fibre.

**Pectin** is a soluble fibre. It is found in apples, quinces and citrus fruits. Pectin binds water and makes **jam** set. **Cellulose**, on the other hand, is insoluble. The cell walls of plants are made mainly of it. Humans cannot digest it, but it stimulates the activity of the gut.

Dietary fibre is only found in **plant** foods. There is a lot of it in **wholemeal bread**, oat flakes, pulses such as lentils and beans, and in vegetables, fruit and nuts. **Cheese**, meat, eggs and butter contain no fibre. Professional bodies recommend that adults eat at least about **30 grams** a day. Many people eat much less.

Countless useful **bacteria** live in the **large intestine**. Together they are called the **gut flora**. Many types of fibre are broken down there by these bacteria. So they are food for a healthy gut flora. This can also produce gases. That is why it is best to get your body used to more fibre slowly.

Fibre **binds water** and swells up in the gut. This makes the contents of the gut softer so they can be moved along better. But without enough liquid it can lead to **constipation**. If you eat a lot of fibre, you should therefore drink enough **water** or unsweetened tea throughout the day.

gewusst: An apple with its skin contains more fibre than a peeled one, because a lot of it sits just under the skin.
Cows can digest cellulose because special microorganisms live in their stomach.

teile.einleitung: A country's economy is often divided into **sectors**. Each sector groups together similar activities: extracting raw materials, making goods or providing services.
wichtigste: The primary sector extracts raw materials, for example in farming.
The secondary sector turns raw materials into goods, for example in industry and crafts.
The tertiary sector covers services such as retail, banks or insurance.
In Switzerland about three quarters of employees work in the tertiary sector (as of 2024).
Jean Fourastié described the shift of work from the first to the third sector.
Gross value added is the value of production minus the inputs.

abschnitte.text: The **primary sector** includes farming, forestry and fishing, and often mining too. Here **raw materials** are taken directly from nature. A dairy farmer in the Emmental is a typical example. In the past a large part of the population worked in this sector. Today it is only a small share in Switzerland.

The **secondary sector** turns raw materials into products. It includes **industry**, **crafts**, energy supply and construction. A joinery workshop that makes tables out of wood belongs to it, as does a watch factory or a chemical plant. Switzerland still has a strong industry today, for example in pharmaceuticals and engineering.

In the **tertiary sector**, no goods are made; **services** are provided instead. Examples are retail, transport, tourism, schools, hospitals, banks and insurance advice. In Switzerland about three quarters of employees work in this sector (as of 2024). Some experts separate out a **quaternary sector**: it covers information and knowledge services such as computing, research and consulting.

The French economist **Jean Fourastié** shaped the **three-sector hypothesis**. It states that, as a country develops, employment shifts from the primary sector via the secondary sector to the tertiary sector. One reason is increased **labour productivity**: thanks to machines, a few farmers today produce as much food as many did in the past. The workers who are freed up find jobs in industry and services.

How much a sector contributes to the economy is shown by **gross value added**. It is calculated like this: value of production minus **inputs**, that is minus what was bought from other businesses. This way nothing is counted twice. The Federal Statistical Office publishes such figures for Switzerland regularly.

gewusst: A farm can belong to several sectors, for example if it makes cheese or offers farm holidays.
Fourastié's well-known book of 1949 is called “The Great Hope of the Twentieth Century” in English.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland it is not only politicians who make decisions: the voters themselves also decide on many issues. This is called direct democracy. Hardly any other country in the world lets its people vote as often as Switzerland.
wichtigste: In direct democracy, the people themselves vote on laws and changes to the constitution.
Switzerland is organised on three levels: Confederation, cantons and municipalities.
At federal level there are four regular voting dates each year.
Changes to the constitution need the double majority, that is a majority of the people and of the cantons.
Women have only been allowed to vote and stand for election at federal level since 1971.
Since 1991 the voting age at federal level has been 18.
In Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden people vote in the open air at the Landsgemeinde.

abschnitte.text: In a **democracy**, power comes from the people. In many countries the people only elect a parliament every few years, which then decides everything else. In Switzerland the voters can also decide on individual issues themselves. That is why it is called **direct democracy**. There are still elected parliaments, so the mixture is also called semi-direct democracy.

With a **popular initiative**, citizens can demand a change to the Federal Constitution. This requires 100,000 valid signatures, which must be collected within 18 months. With the **optional referendum**, the people can bring a new law passed by parliament to a vote if 50,000 people sign within 100 days. Changes to the constitution always go to the people; this is called a mandatory referendum.

For changes to the constitution it is not enough for just a majority of voters to say yes. A majority of the cantons is also needed, the so-called **majority of the cantons**. Together this is called the **double majority**. This means that small cantons such as Uri also have an important say. It has happened that a proposal had more yes votes but still failed because it did not win a majority of the cantons.

At federal level, Swiss citizens aged 18 and over may vote; this has applied since 1991. Women only received **women’s suffrage** at federal level in 1971, much later than in most European countries. The canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton to introduce it, and only in 1990 after a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court. In 2007 the canton of Glarus became the first canton to allow a **voting age of 16** for cantonal and municipal matters.

The **Landsgemeinde** is the oldest form of democracy in Switzerland. The voters of a canton gather in a large square in the open air. They vote by raising their hand or their voting card. Today the Landsgemeinde only exists in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden. It takes place every spring and attracts many spectators.

Before every vote, the voters receive a booklet with information by post. You can vote at a polling station or very conveniently **by post**, which is what most people do today. Votes are also held regularly in the cantons and municipalities, for example on new school buildings or taxes. Turnout is often around 40 to 50 per cent.

begriffe.erklaerung: A proposal from the people to change the constitution, for which signatures are collected.
The right of the people to vote on a law or a change to the constitution.
The majority of the cantons in a vote.
An open-air assembly of all the voters of a canton.

gewusst: Swiss voters often vote on ten or more proposals a year at federal level.
At the Landsgemeinde in Appenzell Innerrhoden, some men traditionally carry a sword as their voting card.
The popular initiative at federal level has existed since 1891.

teile.einleitung: Food hygiene means handling food cleanly and carefully. This prevents germs from multiplying or being passed on to other foods. Chilling properly, cooking thoroughly and working cleanly are the most important rules.
wichtigste: The fridge should be at most about 5 °C.
Frozen products are stored at minus 18 °C or colder.
Raw eggs and raw poultry can contain salmonella.
Raw meat and salad belong on separate boards.
After the use-by date you no longer eat a food.
You throw mouldy bread away completely.
Pasteurising makes milk safer by heating it briefly.

abschnitte.text: At no more than about **5 °C**, most bacteria multiply only very slowly. That is why the fridge should not be warmer. A fridge thermometer helps you check. **Frozen products** are stored at **minus 18 °C** or colder. At this temperature microorganisms cannot multiply, but they are not all killed.

**Salmonella** are bacteria that are often found in raw eggs and raw poultry. They can cause stomach and bowel illnesses. Cooking food **thoroughly** kills them. For raw meat and for salad you use **different chopping boards**. Otherwise germs from the meat can get onto foods that will not be heated any more. This is called **cross-contamination**.

**“Use by”** is the use-by date. It appears on highly perishable foods such as mince. After this date you should no longer eat them. **“Best before”** is the best-before date. It is the manufacturer's **guarantee of quality**. Many foods are still fine to eat after it.

If **mould** appears on one spot of a loaf, you throw the whole loaf away. The threads of the mould grow invisibly through the airy bread, and many moulds produce **toxins**. Milk is often **pasteurised**: it is heated briefly to about 72 to 75 °C. This kills germs. The process is named after the scientist **Louis Pasteur**.

gewusst: Louis Pasteur originally developed the process in the 19th century to make wine and beer keep longer.
A damp kitchen sponge can also contain lots of bacteria, so you should change it often.

teile.einleitung: Cabinetmakers and carpenters both work with wood, but their work is very different. The carpenter builds large wooden structures such as roofs and wooden houses. The cabinetmaker builds furniture, doors and kitchens.
wichtigste: Cabinetmakers and carpenters both work with wood.
The carpenter builds large wooden structures such as roof frames and wooden houses.
The cabinetmaker builds furniture, doors, windows and kitchens.
The carpenter often works outdoors on the building site.
The cabinetmaker usually works in the workshop.
In Switzerland you can learn both jobs with an EFZ apprenticeship.

abschnitte.text: Carpenters build with **large wooden beams**. They put up **roof frames**, which are the framework of a roof, and whole **wooden houses**. Wooden bridges, stairs or building fronts are also part of the job. Many parts are prepared in the workshop hall and then put together on the **building site**. Carpenters often work at great heights.

Cabinetmakers work with **smaller, finer pieces of wood**. They build **furniture** such as tables, wardrobes and beds. **Doors**, windows and kitchens are also made in the joinery workshop. They usually work in the **workshop** and then install their work at the customer's home. Often every millimetre counts.

You can remember it like this: **big timber** belongs to the carpenter, **furniture** belongs to the cabinetmaker. The carpenter builds the **framework** of a house, the cabinetmaker fits it out inside. Carpenters must not be afraid of heights and should enjoy working outdoors. Cabinetmakers need great care for fine details. With a new wooden house, both often work together.

In Switzerland there is the apprenticeship as a **carpenter EFZ** and as a **cabinetmaker EFZ**. Both jobs need practical skills and spatial thinking. Today both also plan on the **computer**, and machines cut the wood precisely. If you are not sure, you can try out both jobs in a **taster apprenticeship**.

gewusst: After their apprenticeship, some carpenters go “on the Walz”: they travel from place to place in a black traditional outfit and work for different master craftsmen.
Wood is a renewable building material. In Switzerland more and more houses are being built of wood.

teile.einleitung: Division of labour means that not everyone does everything themselves, but that people specialise in particular tasks. This applies in the household, in the factory and in the whole economy.
wichtigste: In 1776 Adam Smith used the example of pins to show how the division of labour increases production.
In 1817 David Ricardo used comparative advantage to explain why trade is worthwhile.
Frederick W. Taylor broke work down into the smallest, precisely measured steps.
One disadvantage of assembly-line work is monotony and one-sided strain.
Job rotation is meant to bring variety.
An economy based on the division of labour needs exchange, mostly through money and markets.

abschnitte.text: In 1776 the Scottish economist **Adam Smith** wrote the book “The Wealth of Nations”. In it he describes a **pin factory**. Ten workers, each specialising in one step, make many thousands of pins a day. A single person doing everything alone, on the other hand, manages hardly twenty. In this way Smith showed the advantages of the **division of labour**.

Countries also divide up work. In 1817, using the example of wine and cloth in England and Portugal, **David Ricardo** showed that if each country specialises in what it does **relatively** best, both gain through trade. This is called the theory of **comparative advantage**. It applies even if one country could produce everything more cheaply.

Around 1900, **Frederick W. Taylor** studied work processes with a stopwatch. He strictly separated planning from carrying out the work. This is called **scientific management** or **Taylorism**. Later the **assembly line** was introduced in factories. Later still, **Toyota** developed **just-in-time production**: parts arrive exactly when they are needed, and stocks stay small.

The division of labour makes production faster and cheaper. But people who always do the same movement often suffer from **monotony** and one-sided physical strain. The philosopher **Karl Marx** spoke of **alienation** from work. That is why, in **job rotation**, employees switch between different tasks according to a plan. This brings variety and broader knowledge.

In the **economic division of labour**, people specialise in jobs and companies in industries. If you specialise, you do not make everything yourself and have to **exchange**. **Money** makes this exchange much easier. Work is also divided up in the **household**: one person cooks, another washes up or does the shopping. Families and flatmates agree among themselves how to share the housework.

gewusst: Without the division of labour, every person would have to make their own food, clothes and house.
A single mobile phone contains parts made in many different countries.

teile.einleitung: Fats are one of the main nutrients, along with carbohydrates and protein. The body needs them for energy, to absorb some vitamins and as a building material. But the type and the amount matter.
wichtigste: The body can only absorb vitamins A, D, E and K well together with fat.
Vegetable oils are usually liquid at room temperature, butter is solid.
Rapeseed oil and fish such as salmon provide a lot of omega-3 fatty acids.
Cholesterol is only found in animal foods.
One gram of fat provides about twice as much energy as one gram of carbohydrates.
Trans fats are harmful and are limited in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Fat provides the body with a lot of **energy**. It is also a building material for the cells. The body also needs fat to absorb vitamins **A, D, E and K**. These vitamins are **fat-soluble**. That is why a little oil with a carrot salad makes sense. One gram of fat provides about twice as much energy as one gram of carbohydrates or protein. That is why too much fat quickly leads to an energy surplus.

**Vegetable oils** contain a lot of **unsaturated fatty acids**. That is why they are liquid at room temperature. Animal fats such as **butter** have more **saturated fatty acids** and are solid. The Swiss dietary recommendations (as of 2024) advise 2 tablespoons of vegetable oil a day, at least 1 tablespoon of which should be **rapeseed oil**. Rapeseed oil has a favourable ratio of omega-3 to omega-6 fatty acids.

**Omega-3 fatty acids** are especially valuable. Oily sea fish such as **salmon**, herring and mackerel contain a lot of them. Lean freshwater fish such as perch or zander contain much less. Only humans and animals make **cholesterol**. It is found, for example, in egg yolk, butter and meat, but not in vegetable oils.

Oil and water do not normally mix. But in an **emulsion**, tiny droplets of fat and water are finely spread through each other. One example is **mayonnaise**. There the **lecithin** from the egg yolk holds the oil and water together. Milk is also an emulsion in which small droplets of fat float.

**Trans fatty acids** are formed mainly when vegetable oils are partly **hardened** and when they are heated very strongly. They increase the risk of **heart and circulatory diseases**. That is why their content in food is limited by law in Switzerland. It is therefore best to eat deep-fried food and highly processed snacks only now and then.

gewusst: Milk is a natural emulsion of fat and water.
A tablespoon of oil provides almost as much energy as a whole slice of bread and butter.

teile.einleitung: Consumer credit is borrowed money that private individuals use to buy something, for example a car or furniture. The money has to be paid back with interest. In Switzerland the Consumer Credit Act (KKG) protects people against over-indebtedness.
wichtigste: Consumer credit must be paid back with interest.
Since 2026, cash loans may cost at most 10 per cent interest.
For overdraft credit, such as on credit cards, the limit is 12 per cent.
You can cancel a consumer credit agreement within 14 days.
The lender must check the borrower's creditworthiness.
The IKO collects data on existing consumer loans.
A private car lease also counts as consumer credit.

abschnitte.text: With **consumer credit**, a bank or credit company lends a private individual money for spending. This includes **cash loans**, **overdraft credit** on an account or credit card and **leasing agreements** for consumer goods such as a car. You pay **interest** on the borrowed money. That is why consumer credit makes every purchase more expensive.

In the ordinance on the Consumer Credit Act, the Federal Council sets a **maximum interest rate**. Since 1 January 2026 it has been **10 per cent** for cash loans; in 2025 it was still 11 per cent. For overdraft credit there is a limit of 12 per cent. An example: with a loan of 5000 francs at 10 per cent annual interest, that is 500 francs interest a year without repayment. If you repay in instalments, the interest is somewhat lower.

Before a cash loan, the lender must carry out a **creditworthiness check**. It must be possible to repay the loan within **36 months** without using the part of the income that cannot be seized (Art. 28 KKG). Lenders must report consumer loans to the **Consumer Credit Information Office (IKO)**. This way they can see whether someone already has loans or leasing agreements.

Under Art. 16 KKG, you can cancel a consumer credit agreement in writing within **14 days**. In this way the law protects against hasty decisions. Since 2016, the Unfair Competition Act has banned **aggressive advertising** for consumer credit. The industry has drawn up its own self-regulation, which, for example, rules out advertising aimed at young people.

gewusst: Legally, a lease is a form of consumer credit, even though the car is not bought but rented.
Budget advice services recommend saving first and buying afterwards wherever possible, instead of taking out a loan.

teile.einleitung: Choosing a career is one of the first big decisions in life. In Switzerland most young people choose an apprenticeship after compulsory school, in which they work in a company and also attend vocational school. This chapter explains how to find a job that suits you and how an apprenticeship works.
wichtigste: Most young people in Switzerland do an apprenticeship after school.
In an apprenticeship you work in the training company and also attend vocational school.
A taster apprenticeship lasts a few days and helps you get to know a job.
EFZ stands for Federal VET Diploma (Eidgenössisches Fähigkeitszeugnis).
An EBA apprenticeship lasts two years and leads to the Federal VET Certificate.
The vocational Matura makes it possible to study at a university of applied sciences without an entrance exam.
Information about jobs and apprenticeship places is available on berufsberatung.ch and from the cantonal careers advice service.

abschnitte.titel: Finding a job that suits you
abschnitte.text: It starts with the question of what you like doing and what you are good at. If you really like working with animals, for example, you could become an **animal keeper**. The canton's careers advice service helps with tests, conversations and information. On berufsberatung.ch you can find descriptions of almost all jobs and vacant apprenticeship places.

In a **taster apprenticeship** you spend a few days in a company and experience the job at first hand. Many people try out several jobs before they decide. Careers fairs and information events also help with the choice. Choosing a career usually begins in the 7th or 8th school year.

An apprenticeship takes place in three places of learning: in the **training company**, at vocational school and in inter-company courses. You spend the most time in the company, where you really work alongside others. The rights and duties are set out in the apprenticeship contract, which the canton approves. Apprentices receive wages and at least five weeks of holiday until their 20th birthday.

A three- or four-year apprenticeship ends with the **EFZ**, the Federal VET Diploma. A two-year apprenticeship leads to the **EBA**, the Federal VET Certificate. After an EBA apprenticeship you can often still do the EFZ in the same job. At the end of every apprenticeship comes the qualification procedure, the final examination.

With the **vocational Matura** you can study at a university of applied sciences without an entrance exam. With the Passerelle, the way to universities and the ETH is even open. Without a Matura you can attend a college of higher education or take a professional examination. The Swiss education system is flexible, and no qualification is a dead end.

begriffe.erklaerung: Training in a company with lessons at vocational school.
A few days in a company to get to know a job.
Federal VET Diploma after a three- or four-year apprenticeship.
Federal VET Certificate after a two-year apprenticeship.
An office that helps with choosing a job and training.

gewusst: In Switzerland you can choose between about 250 different apprenticeship trades.
Many training companies give out their apprenticeship places a year before the apprenticeship starts in August.

teile.einleitung: Economies are constantly changing. Some industries shrink, others grow, and people move into new jobs. This long-term transformation is called **structural change**. Switzerland has experienced it, for example, in the watch and textile industries.
wichtigste: Structural change is the long-term shift between industries and sectors.
Tertiarisation means the rise of the service sector.
Deindustrialisation means fewer industrial jobs.
The quartz crisis hit the Swiss watch industry hard in the 1970s and early 1980s.
Eastern Switzerland once lived from embroidery.
Further training and retraining prepare people for structural change.

abschnitte.text: The economy is divided into three **sectors**. The first sector is farming, the second is industry and the third is **services**. In the past most people worked in farming, then in factories. Today the great majority in Switzerland work in the service sector. This development is called **tertiarisation**. When industrial jobs disappear, this is called **deindustrialisation**.

In the 19th century the **embroidery and textile industry** shaped eastern Switzerland. Around 1900, **St Gallen** was a world centre of embroidery, and its embroidery went to many countries. After the First World War and because of a change in fashion, the industry collapsed sharply. Many people lost their jobs. Today there are only a few, but specialised, textile companies there.

In the **1970s and early 1980s** the Swiss **watch industry** fell into a deep crisis. Cheap **quartz watches** from Japan and Hong Kong pushed out the mechanical Swiss watches. The number of people employed in the industry fell by more than half. The industry had to reinvent itself. Today Switzerland is very successful again, especially with high-quality watches.

A well-known example from Germany is the **Ruhr** area. For a long time the region lived from **coal and steel**. Little by little, pits and blast furnaces were closed, and in **2018** coal mining ended there. Today services, universities and culture shape the region. Some old industrial sites have become museums.

Structural change can lead to **structural unemployment**. This arises when jobs in shrinking industries disappear and the people affected do not fit the new jobs. **Further training**, **retraining** and good vocational education help. In Switzerland, **unemployment insurance** supports such labour market measures.

gewusst: Around 1900, St Gallen embroidery was one of Switzerland's most important exports.
Former pits in the Ruhr are now museums and event venues.

teile.einleitung: If you are choosing a job, you should know well what you can do and what interests you. Strengths and interests are like a compass: they show which work could be enjoyable and go well.
wichtigste: A job that interests you is more likely to be enjoyable and motivating.
A distinction is made between professional skills, social skills and personal skills.
Social skills are the ability to get on well with other people.
Personal skills include reliability, punctuality and persistence.
In a self-assessment you judge your own abilities yourself.
Feedback from others adds to your own picture.
Some jobs have special requirements, for example a head for heights on the roof.

abschnitte.text: **Interests** show what you like to spend your time on: people, animals, technology, numbers or design. If you are interested in the tasks of a job, you stay more motivated and learn more easily. That is why getting to know your own interests is a **first step** in choosing a career. A helpful question is: what do I like doing, even when I do not have to?

Strengths are often divided into groups. **Professional skills** are abilities such as maths, languages or practical skills, for example handling tools skilfully. **Social skills** concern how you deal with others, such as teamwork, politeness and helpfulness. **Personal skills** concern how you deal with yourself, for example punctuality, reliability and determination. Training companies pay close attention to these qualities in applications.

abschnitte.titel: Self-image and how others see you
abschnitte.text: In a **self-assessment** you think for yourself about what you are good at and like doing. People often judge themselves too strictly or too kindly. That is why it is worth asking your parents, teachers or friends for honest feedback. This is called an **assessment by others**. If you compare the two, you get a good picture of your own strengths.

Every job has its own **requirements**. If you have a lot of contact with customers in retail, you should be friendly and open, because that builds trust. Roofers work at great heights and so must have a **head for heights**. The workshop needs skill, the office needs accuracy. If your own strengths match the requirements of a job, that is a good starting point.

In Switzerland the **careers advice service** supports young people in choosing a career, for example at the BIZ careers information centre. There are conversations, tests and information about many jobs. At school, choosing a career is usually covered at lower secondary level. Finally, a **taster apprenticeship** shows whether your strengths and interests really fit everyday life in a job.

gewusst: In Switzerland you can choose from about 250 jobs with basic vocational training.
Interests can change over time, so it is good to check them again and again.

teile.einleitung: **Sustainable economics** means producing and consuming in such a way that future generations can also live well. The environment, the economy and society should all be kept in view at the same time. The topic concerns states, companies and every single household.
wichtigste: The Brundtland Report of 1987 shaped the best-known definition of sustainability.
The three-pillar model links ecology, economy and society.
The UN's 2030 Agenda contains 17 goals for sustainable development.
ESG criteria assess environmental, social and governance factors.
Greenwashing is looking green without acting green.
Since 2008 Switzerland has charged a CO2 levy on fossil fuels.

abschnitte.text: In 1987 the report **“Our Common Future”** was published by a UN commission led by **Gro Harlem Brundtland**. It describes sustainable development as development that meets the needs of the present without taking away the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. This definition is still often used today. The **three-pillar model** adds that something is only sustainable if it takes **ecology**, **economy** and **society** into account at the same time.

In 2015 the member states of the UN adopted the **2030 Agenda**. It contains **17 Sustainable Development Goals**, SDGs for short. They include, for example, less poverty, good education, climate protection and decent work. Switzerland has also committed itself to these goals. In companies, the three pillars are also called the **triple bottom line**.

Many banks and pension funds pay attention to **ESG criteria** in their investments. ESG stands for environmental, social and governance, which means the environment, social matters and good corporate management. Not every company that calls itself green really is. If a company presents itself as more environmentally friendly than it is, with advertising or vague labels, this is called **greenwashing**.

Since **2008** Switzerland has charged a **CO2 levy** on fossil fuels such as heating oil and natural gas. It makes them more expensive and is meant to encourage saving. A large part of the money is given back to the population through **health insurance premiums**. But efficiency alone is not always enough. If you drive more kilometres with a more economical car, consumption falls less than expected. This is called the **rebound effect**.

Every year the **Global Footprint Network** calculates **Earth Overshoot Day**. From this day on, humanity has used more resources than the Earth can renew in a whole year. For years this day has fallen in the summer. This shows that worldwide much more is being used than grows back.

gewusst: The idea of sustainability originally comes from forestry: you should not fell more wood than grows back.
A large part of the CO2 levy flows back to the population through health insurance premiums.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland schoolchildren go for regular dental check-ups, often with the school dentist. There, small holes in the teeth are discovered early. Then filling them is easier and hurts less.
wichtigste: Schoolchildren go for regular dental check-ups.
This way holes in the teeth are discovered early.
A hole in a tooth is called tooth decay (caries).
School dental care is organised by the municipalities.
In many classes a specialist shows how to brush your teeth properly.
Brushing your teeth twice a day and eating few sweet things protect your teeth.

abschnitte.text: A hole in a tooth is called **tooth decay**, or caries. It happens when bacteria turn sugar into acid, which attacks the tooth. At first a hole is tiny and does not hurt. That is why you often do not notice it yourself. At the **check-up** the dentist spots small holes early. Then **filling** them is easier and quicker.

In Switzerland the **municipalities** look after **school dental care**. Schoolchildren are regularly called in for a check-up, usually once a year. Some municipalities have their own **school dentist**, others work with dental practices. The rules for this are set by the **cantons**. This way every child gets a dental check-up.

In many classes a **school dental care instructor** visits regularly. She shows how to **brush your teeth properly** and why sugar is harmful. Sometimes you colour your teeth with a tablet. Then you can see exactly where there is still **plaque**. This way children learn early to look after their teeth well.

It is best to brush your teeth **twice a day** with a toothpaste containing **fluoride**. Fluoride makes tooth enamel harder. You should not eat **sweets** and sugary drinks constantly throughout the day. Water is the best drink for your teeth. If you live like this and go for regular check-ups, you have a good chance of healthy teeth.

gewusst: Tooth enamel is the hardest material in the human body.
Milk teeth fall out, but the permanent teeth have to last a whole lifetime.

teile.einleitung: Consumer protection means protecting people from disadvantages when they shop. In Switzerland, laws cover things such as guarantees, prices and the right of withdrawal. Organisations and the media also help by providing information on consumer issues.
wichtigste: A purchase contract can also be made verbally.
New products have a legal guarantee of 2 years.
The guarantee can be excluded by contract.
For online purchases there is no general legal right of return.
Doorstep sales over 100 francs can be cancelled within 14 days.
Displayed prices include VAT.
The Consumer Protection Foundation stands up for consumers in German-speaking Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: When you buy something, you make a **purchase contract**. The seller must hand over the goods, and the buyer must pay the price. A purchase contract does not need a signature. It can also be made **verbally**, for example at the baker's. The receipt proves when and where you bought a product.

In Switzerland **new products** have a legal guarantee of **2 years**. For second-hand products it may be shortened to 1 year. However, a seller can exclude the guarantee in the contract or in the **general terms and conditions**, or replace it with one of their own. If you want to use the guarantee, you usually need the **receipt**. Without proof, a complaint is often difficult.

For **online purchases** in Switzerland there is no general legal right of withdrawal. Many shops voluntarily offer returns, and this is written in their **general terms and conditions**. It is different for **doorstep sales** and contracts made by phone: if the value is over 100 francs, you can cancel within **14 days**. Prices in shops must include **VAT**; the Price Disclosure Ordinance requires this.

The **Consumer Protection Foundation** (SKS) was founded in 1964 and is based in Bern. In French-speaking Switzerland there is the **FRC**, and in Ticino the **ACSI**. They give advice when there are problems and campaign politically for consumers. On television, SRF's **“Kassensturz”** tests products and reports on consumer traps.

gewusst: “Kassensturz” is one of the oldest programmes on Swiss television and has been running since the 1970s.
Even when you buy a bread roll at a kiosk, legally speaking you are making a contract.

teile.einleitung: Every day, every household produces rubbish. In Switzerland a lot is collected separately and recycled, and for the remaining household waste you pay through the bag charge.
wichtigste: In most municipalities you pay a bag charge when you buy official rubbish bags.
The bag charge follows the polluter pays principle: people who produce more rubbish pay more.
Since 2000, combustible waste may no longer be put in landfill.
Household waste is burned in waste incineration plants, which supply electricity and heat.
According to the FOEN, about 660 kg of municipal waste per person was produced in 2024.
Old medicines go back to the pharmacy, electrical appliances back to the shop.

abschnitte.text: In most Swiss municipalities you may only put household waste out on the street in **official bags** or with a **charge sticker**. The price of the bag includes the charge for disposal. Behind this is the **polluter pays principle**: whoever causes the costs should bear them. If you avoid and sort your rubbish, you need fewer bags and save money.

Since 2000, combustible waste in Switzerland may no longer be stored in **landfill sites**. It goes to a **waste incineration plant**, KVA for short. The heat of the fire is used: it generates **electricity** and **district heating**, which heats houses. Filters clean the exhaust gases. The ash that is left over is treated further.

According to the FOEN, about **664 kg** of municipal waste per person was produced in Switzerland and Liechtenstein in 2024. A little more than half was collected separately and **recycled**. Paper, cardboard, glass, aluminium, green waste and PET have their own collection points. The return rate for PET drinks bottles in 2024 was over 84 per cent. Old PET is made into new bottles again.

Making new **aluminium** from the ore **bauxite** takes a great deal of electricity. When old aluminium is melted down, most of this energy is saved. That is why it is particularly worthwhile collecting aluminium cans, foil and tubes. Glass can also be melted down again and again.

Some things belong neither in the rubbish nor down the drain. You take **medicines** back to the pharmacy or chemist's, otherwise active ingredients get into rivers and lakes. **Electrical appliances** such as old mobile phones contain valuable metals and pollutants. Shops take them back free of charge, because an **advance recycling fee** was paid when they were bought. Batteries, paints and chemicals also need to be disposed of separately.

gewusst: In some Swiss cities, the heat from waste incineration plants heats whole neighbourhoods.
Collected green waste is turned into compost and, in some plants, also into biogas.

teile.einleitung: Every house has a **toilet**, in Switzerland often called the **WC**. When you flush, everything is washed into the sewers. But so that the pipes do not get blocked, not everything may go in.
wichtigste: Only toilet paper belongs in the toilet.
Wet wipes do not dissolve in water and block the pipes.
Rubbish such as wet wipes or cotton buds belongs in the bin.
The water flows through the sewers to the sewage treatment plant.
After using the toilet you wash your hands with soap.

abschnitte.text: Only **toilet paper** belongs in the toilet. Toilet paper is made so that it **dissolves** quickly in water. **Wet wipes**, on the other hand, do not dissolve. They block the pipes and the pumps. That is why wet wipes, cotton buds and other rubbish belong in the **bin**. Food scraps and oil have no business in the toilet either.

When you press the **flush**, the water flows through pipes into the **sewers**. This is a large network of pipes under the streets. At the end the waste water reaches a **sewage treatment plant**. There it is cleaned before it flows back into a river or lake. Things that do not belong in the toilet make a lot of work for the treatment plant.

After using the toilet you always wash your **hands** with **soap**. This removes germs that can make you ill. You rub your hands well, including between the fingers, and rinse them with water. Then you dry them well.
Many toilets have **two flush buttons**: a small one and a large one. With the small button you use less water. So you only flush as much as you need. It is best to close the **lid** before flushing.

gewusst: Wet wipes are one of the most common causes of blocked sewage pumps.
Waste water from the toilet is cleaned at the sewage treatment plant before it flows into rivers and lakes.

teile.einleitung: A sewing machine joins pieces of fabric with thread, much faster than you can sew by hand. It is the most important tool of clothing designers. It is also often used at home, for mending or for making your own clothes.
wichtigste: With a sewing machine you sew fabric much faster than by hand.
It works with two threads: an upper thread and a lower thread.
The needle has its eye down at the tip.
Sewing machines were invented in the 19th century.
Clothing designers need one every day.
The Swiss company Bernina has been making sewing machines for a long time.

abschnitte.text: A sewing machine needs two threads. The **upper thread** comes from a reel of thread at the top and runs through the needle. The **lower thread** is wound onto a small **bobbin** under the fabric. With every stitch the needle goes through the fabric and the two threads loop around each other. This creates a strong seam, the **lockstitch**.

On a normal hand-sewing needle the eye is at the top. On a sewing machine needle the **eye is at the bottom**, close to the tip. Only this way can the needle carry the thread down through the fabric. A foot, the **presser foot**, presses the fabric flat at the same time. A small feed dog pushes the fabric along stitch by stitch.

For a long time all clothes were sewn by hand. In the **19th century**, inventors in several countries developed the first usable sewing machines. At first they were driven by hand or with a **foot pedal**. Today most have an electric motor. In Switzerland, the company **Bernina** from Steckborn in the canton of Thurgau is well known for its sewing machines.

**Clothing designers** EFZ sew clothes to measure or alter them. They work with different machines, for example with an **overlocker**, which neatly finishes the edges of fabric. For the job you need patience, precise work and a love of fabrics. Upholsterers and bag makers also work with sewing machines.

gewusst: Modern sewing machines can even embroider letters and pictures.
A sewing machine manages hundreds of stitches a minute; by hand it is only a few.

teile.einleitung: In a Swiss apprenticeship you learn in three places: in the training company, at vocational school and in the inter-company courses, üK for short. In these courses apprentices practise the most important basic techniques of their job.
wichtigste: Basic vocational training has three places of learning: training company, vocational school and inter-company courses.
Attending the üK is compulsory for apprentices if the training ordinance provides for them.
The training company pays the costs; they may not be passed on to the apprentices.
The üK are usually organised by the organisations of the working world (OdA).
In the üK apprentices practise tasks that rarely come up in their own company.
The cantonal office can grant an exemption in certain cases.

abschnitte.text: Basic vocational training in Switzerland has **three places of learning**. In the **training company** you work and learn the practice. At **vocational school** you learn the theory and general education. The **inter-company courses** connect the two: here school knowledge is linked with targeted practical exercises. Together this is also called the **learning triangle**.

Not every company can show all the **basic techniques** of a job. A small company may specialise in only a few tasks. So in the üK apprentices practise tasks that rarely come up in their own company. This way all apprentices in a job learn the same **basics**. The courses usually last a few days or weeks and take place in special course centres.

As a rule the **professional associations** are responsible for the üK, that is, the **organisations of the working world**, OdA for short. The OdA include professional associations, industry associations and social partners. They also help decide the content of the apprenticeship. According to the Vocational Training Ordinance, the **training company** pays the costs of the courses. The course costs may not be passed on to the apprentices.

Attending the üK is **compulsory** for apprentices if the training ordinance for the job provides for such courses. So you cannot simply stay away. There is one exception, though: at the request of the training company, the **cantonal office** can exempt apprentices. This is possible if the content is already taught in a company training centre or a **training workshop**.

gewusst: The üK days count as working time, and apprentices receive their normal apprentice wages for them.
In some jobs, work in the üK is also assessed and counts towards the final mark.

teile.einleitung: Pilots fly aeroplanes or helicopters. They are responsible for making sure that passengers or cargo reach their destination safely. The job requires long training, a lot of knowledge and steady nerves.
wichtigste: A pilot flies an aeroplane or a helicopter.
In the cockpit of an airliner there are usually two people: the captain and the co-pilot.
Before every flight they check the weather, the route and the aircraft.
They are in constant radio contact with air traffic control.
You do not become a pilot through an apprenticeship, but at a flying school.
In the simulator, pilots also practise difficult situations.

abschnitte.text: The **cockpit** is the pilot's workplace. On large passenger aircraft there are usually two people there: the **captain** and the **co-pilot**. They share the work and check each other. During the flight an **autopilot** helps, but take-off and landing need full attention. Many instruments show the altitude, speed and direction.

Before every flight the pilots look at the **weather** and plan the route. They calculate how much **fuel** is needed. On a walk round the aircraft they check that everything is in order. In the cockpit they go through **checklists** point by point. This way nothing is forgotten.

Pilots do not simply fly wherever they like. **Air traffic control** on the ground tells them which altitude and direction to take. In Switzerland the company **Skyguide** is responsible for this. The radio is usually in **English**, so that people from all countries understand each other. That is why good English is very important for pilots.

abschnitte.titel: The path to becoming a pilot
abschnitte.text: Pilot is not an apprenticeship trade. You usually need a **Matura** or a completed apprenticeship. Then come **aptitude tests** and training at a **flying school**, with theory, simulator and real flights. In Switzerland young people can test whether flying suits them with the Air Force's **SPHAIR** programme. Even after their training, pilots practise regularly in the simulator.

gewusst: The captain and the co-pilot often do not eat the same meal, so that they could not both fall ill at the same time.
In the simulator you can practise thunderstorms, fog and technical faults without anyone being in danger.
