teile.einleitung: In a taster apprenticeship you work for a few days in a company and get to know a job close up. This way you find out whether it really suits you. In Switzerland taster days are a firm part of choosing a career.
wichtigste: In a taster apprenticeship you check whether a job suits you.
Usually you ask a company yourself.
A taster apprenticeship usually lasts a few days up to about a week.
Be on time, ask questions and show interest.
Many companies give you an assessment form afterwards.
A taster report helps you to compare jobs.
Even a disappointing taster apprenticeship helps you move forward.

abschnitte.text: From books or videos you do not yet know what a job really feels like. In a **taster apprenticeship** you experience **everyday working life** close up. You see what tasks are done, what the team is like and how long a working day lasts. This way you find out whether the activities and surroundings suit you. This helps you with **choosing a career**.

You usually organise a taster apprenticeship **yourself**. You phone a company, write an **email** or use online platforms with taster offers. Some companies want a short application. The **careers advice service** and your teacher help you with this. A taster apprenticeship usually lasts between one and five days.

On the first day, **punctuality** is especially important. Dress suitably for the job and greet people in a friendly way. Ask **questions** when something interests you and help wherever you can. If you show interest, you leave a good impression. Sometimes a good taster apprenticeship even leads to an **apprenticeship place** later.

Many companies fill in an **assessment form** after the taster apprenticeship. You can later add good assessments to your **application**. Also write a short **taster report** yourself: what did you like and what not? This helps you to compare your impressions. The report is also useful in conversations with your parents and the careers advice service.

It is worth trying out **different jobs**. This way you can compare better and decide with more confidence. You often discover new interests along the way. And if you did not like a taster apprenticeship at all, that is valuable too. Think about **what exactly** did not suit you. This way you can search more precisely.

gewusst: Many apprentices first got to know their training company as a taster company.
For some jobs there are taster days when several young people visit a company at the same time.

teile.einleitung: We need electricity every day: for lights, the fridge, mobile phones and trains. But electricity is also dangerous. That is why only trained specialists work on electrical wiring, cables and sockets.
wichtigste: An electric shock can seriously injure people.
In Switzerland the electricity from the socket has a voltage of 230 volts.
Only trained specialists may build and repair electrical installations.
Electricians lay cables and fit sockets and lights.
A large part of Switzerland's electricity comes from hydropower.
Children should never play with sockets, bare cables or power lines.

abschnitte.text: Electricity flows through cables, but also through the human body. An **electric shock** can cause burns and make the heart beat irregularly. That is why cables are insulated with plastic. In houses, a **residual current device**, RCD for short, protects against dangerous accidents. It switches off the electricity in a flash if something is wrong. Even so, the rule is: keep your hands off damaged cables and devices.

In Switzerland the electricity from the socket is **230 volts**. Swiss sockets and plugs have their own shape, which you hardly find abroad. All the cables in a house come together in the **fuse box**. Fuses switch off when too much current flows. This prevents cables from getting too hot and starting a fire.

Many specialists work with electricity. **Electricians** EFZ lay cables in houses and connect lights, sockets and appliances. **Network electricians** build and maintain the large power lines outdoors. There is also the apprenticeship as an electrical fitter EFZ. In all these jobs you learn strict safety rules, for example: switch off the electricity before working and check that there is no voltage left.

A large part of the electricity in Switzerland is generated with **hydropower**. This includes reservoirs in the Alps and river power stations. Electricity is also produced in nuclear power stations, with **solar panels** on roofs and with wind turbines. Through a large network of power lines, the electricity reaches every flat. Specialists make sure that this network works safely and reliably.

gewusst: The unit of electrical voltage, the volt, is named after the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta.
Birds can sit calmly on a power line, because the electricity cannot flow through them to the ground.

teile.einleitung: Automation means that machines, robots or computer programs do work that people used to do. It has already changed the world of work greatly several times and continues to do so.
wichtigste: Around 1804 the Jacquard loom was controlled with punched cards.
In England the Luddites destroyed textile machines from around 1811 to 1816.
In the Uster fire of 1832, home weavers set fire to a mechanical weaving mill.
In 1913 Henry Ford introduced the assembly line for building the Model T.
The term Industry 4.0 stands for networked factories.
Routine tasks with clear rules are especially easy to automate.

abschnitte.text: Around 1804 **Joseph-Marie Jacquard** built a loom whose patterns were controlled with **punched cards**. The principle later inspired early calculating machines. That is why he is seen as a forerunner of programming. During the **Industrial Revolution**, machines took over more and more of the work in textile production. Many craftspeople feared for their income.

In England, between about 1811 and 1816, workers destroyed textile machines. They were called **Luddites**, after a legendary figure called Ned Ludd. In Switzerland the best-known example is the **Uster fire** on 22 November 1832. Home weavers and smallholders set fire to a mechanical weaving mill in Uster in the canton of Zurich. Such events are called **machine breaking**.

In 1913 **Henry Ford** switched the assembly of the **Model T** at his factory in Highland Park to assembly-line work. The time needed to assemble a car fell from more than twelve hours to about one and a half. As a result, cars became much cheaper. Today **industrial robots** work in many factories. According to the International Federation of Robotics, **South Korea** had the highest robot density in the world in 2023.

The term **Industry 4.0** became known in Germany in 2011. It describes factories in which machines and products are networked via the internet. It is seen as the fourth industrial revolution, after the steam engine, the assembly line and the computer. Today programs with **artificial intelligence** can also take over tasks, such as translating texts.

abschnitte.titel: What does this mean for jobs?
abschnitte.text: When technology replaces human work, this is called **technological unemployment**. In 2013 **Frey and Osborne** from Oxford estimated that about 47 per cent of jobs in the USA could be at risk from computers. The figure was widely quoted and also criticised. **Routine tasks** with clear rules are especially easy to automate. Social and creative work is harder to replace, and new jobs often appear as well.

gewusst: The word “robot” comes from a Czech play of 1920 and is based on a word for work.
Punched cards were still used to feed computers until well into the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: Police officers keep things safe and orderly. They help at accidents, direct traffic and make sure that everyone keeps to the law. In Switzerland you can reach the police on the emergency number 117.
wichtigste: The police keep things safe and orderly.
They help at accidents and direct traffic.
The police emergency number is 117.
In Switzerland there are cantonal police, city police and municipal police.
For the Confederation there is the Federal Office of Police, fedpol.
You become a police officer at a police school.

abschnitte.text: The police are there for **public safety**. They come to **accidents**, secure the scene and help the people involved. They check **traffic** and make sure that the rules are kept. In the case of thefts or other crimes, they look for evidence and find out what happened. Often they also simply help people who need advice.

In Switzerland the police are mainly a matter for the **cantons**. Every canton has a **cantonal police force**. Larger cities also have a **city police force**, and some municipalities have a municipal police force. At federal level there is the **Federal Office of Police** (fedpol). It works, for example, with police authorities in other countries.

If you need help from the police, you dial **117**. It is important to stay calm and say clearly **who** is calling, **where** it happened and **what** is going on. The number is meant for real emergencies. For other questions you can also go to a police station. There police officers are happy to help.

Police officer is not an apprenticeship trade. First you need a completed **apprenticeship** or a Matura. After that you attend a **police school** and finish with the federal certificate as a police officer. You learn about the law, self-defence, first aid and how to deal with people properly. Fairness, steady nerves and enjoying teamwork are important.

gewusst: The police also use dogs, for example to search for missing people.
In some Swiss cities the police also go about on bicycles or on horseback.

teile.einleitung: Plumbers make sure that water flows in houses. They lay pipes and fit washbasins, toilets and showers. If the tap drips or a pipe is broken, you call them for help.
wichtigste: If the pipe drips, you call the plumber.
Plumbers lay water pipes.
They fit washbasins, toilets, showers and baths.
They also make sure that waste water drains away properly.
In Switzerland you learn the job as a plumber EFZ (Sanitärinstallateurin or Sanitärinstallateur EFZ).
The job is part of building services engineering.

abschnitte.text: For water to come out of the tap, many **pipes** are needed. Plumbers lay them in walls and floors. They connect pipes made of metal or plastic and check that everything is **watertight**. They make sure that there is **cold and hot water**. For this they also connect boilers or water heaters.

In the bathroom, plumbers fit **washbasins**, **toilets**, showers and baths. In the kitchen they connect sinks and dishwashers. The **waste water** is just as important: it must drain away cleanly into the sewers. This needs pipes with the right slope.

If a tap **drips** or a drain is **blocked**, the plumber comes. He looks for the fault and repairs it, for example with a new washer. His tools include the **pipe wrench**, spanners and measuring instruments. Good work also helps to **save water**, because a dripping tap wastes a lot of water.

In Switzerland you do an apprenticeship as a **plumber EFZ**. You work on building sites and in the workshop and attend vocational school. Practical skills, the ability to picture things in three dimensions and a liking for technology are important. Later you can train further, for example as a **building services planner** or as a site supervisor.

gewusst: A dripping tap can waste thousands of litres of water a year.
The word “sanitary” comes from the Latin word for health. Clean water protects against disease.

teile.einleitung: The fridge keeps food cold and fresh. In the cold, bacteria multiply only slowly, so food goes off less quickly. If you put things in properly, you can enjoy your food for longer.
wichtigste: The fridge should be at most about 5 degrees.
Vegetables and lettuce belong in the vegetable drawer at the bottom.
Ice cream goes in the freezer at about minus 18 degrees.
You close the door again quickly so that the cold stays inside.
Milk belongs in the fridge, bananas do not.
You do not eat mouldy food.

abschnitte.text: The **fridge** should be at most about **5 degrees Celsius**. Then food stays fresh, because bacteria multiply only slowly in the cold. In the **freezer** it is much colder, about **minus 18 degrees**. There, for example, **ice cream** stays frozen. A small thermometer shows whether the temperature is right.

Right at the bottom is the **vegetable drawer**. Vegetables and lettuce stay nice and fresh there. **Milk**, yoghurt and cheese also belong in the fridge, because opened milk goes off quickly in the warm. Pasta, rice and sugar, on the other hand, are kept dry in the cupboard. **Bananas** do not like the cold and quickly turn brown in the fridge. They are kept at room temperature.

If the **door** stays open for a long time, warm air flows in. The fridge then has to work harder and uses more **electricity**. That is why you close the door again quickly. You let hot food cool down first before putting it in.

Sometimes **mould** forms on food. These are tiny fungi that you can see as green, white or blue fluff. Mould can make you ill. You do not eat mouldy food. Every now and then you should **clean** the fridge and check what needs to be eaten soon.

gewusst: It is usually colder at the back of the fridge than in the door.
In the past people cooled food with ice that was cut from lakes in winter and stored in ice cellars.

teile.einleitung: Polymechanics make metal parts for machines. They drill, mill and turn, often on machines controlled by a computer. The job is very much in demand in Swiss industry.
wichtigste: Polymechanics make metal parts for machines.
They drill, mill and turn workpieces.
Many machines are controlled by computers; they are called CNC machines.
They work very precisely, often to a hundredth of a millimetre.
The apprenticeship as a polymechanic EFZ lasts four years.
The parts are used to make machines, tools or devices.

abschnitte.text: Polymechanics make **individual metal parts**, for example gear wheels, axles or housings. To do this, they first read a **technical drawing**, which shows exactly what the part should look like. Then they work the metal. Finally they check with measuring instruments that everything is right. Machines are assembled from many such parts.

**Drilling** makes holes. In **milling**, a tool turns and removes metal from a workpiece that is held still. In **turning** it is the other way round: the workpiece turns and a tool peels off shavings. This produces round parts such as shafts or bolts. Often the work has to be accurate to a hundredth of a millimetre.

Many machines in the workshop are **CNC machines**. CNC means that a computer controls the machine. The polymechanic writes or checks the **program**, sets up the machine and monitors the work. This way you can make many identical parts very precisely. That is why the job also needs a liking for computers and maths.

The apprenticeship as a **polymechanic EFZ** lasts **four years**. You work in the training company and attend vocational school and inter-company courses. Good apprentices can do the **vocational Matura** at the same time. If you would like a shorter training course, you can become a mechanical assistant EBA. After the apprenticeship there is a lot of further training, for example to become a technician or an engineer.

gewusst: The name comes from the Greek word “poly”, which means “many”: polymechanics can do many things.
In the Swiss engineering and watch industries, polymechanic is one of the most common technical apprenticeship trades.

teile.einleitung: The food pyramid shows in a simple way how to eat healthily. At the bottom are foods you need a lot of, and at the top those you should eat only a little of. Switzerland has its own pyramid.
wichtigste: The pyramid shows what you should eat a lot of and what only a little of.
Right at the bottom are unsweetened drinks such as water.
5 portions of vegetables and fruit a day are recommended.
One portion of fruit is about a handful.
Bread, rice, pasta and potatoes: 3 portions a day.
Oils and fats are near the top; you need only a little of them.
Sweet and salty things are right at the top.

abschnitte.text: The **food pyramid** has several levels. The bottom level is the widest; you need the most of this. The higher up a level is, the less of it you should eat. The top is the smallest level. This way you can see at a glance how to eat a **balanced** diet. In Switzerland the pyramid is published by the Swiss Society for Nutrition and the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office.

Right at the bottom are **unsweetened drinks** such as water or unsweetened tea. You drink enough of these every day. Above them come **vegetables and fruit**. **5 portions** a day are recommended, that is 3 portions of vegetables and 2 portions of fruit. A portion is about a **handful**, for example one apple.

The next level includes **cereals and potatoes**: bread, rice, pasta and potatoes give you energy for a long time. **3 portions** a day are recommended, and wholegrain keeps you full especially long. Above them are **dairy products** such as yoghurt, cheese and quark, as well as meat, fish, eggs and tofu.

Near the top are **oils and fats** such as butter or rapeseed oil. You need only a little of these, but good oils and nuts are important. Right at the top are **sweet and salty things**: sweets, crisps and sugary drinks. They are not forbidden, but are only meant for now and then and in small amounts.

gewusst: The food pyramid does not forbid anything; it only shows in what amounts something is good.
Pulses such as lentils and chickpeas also provide a lot of protein.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss federal administration is divided into seven departments. Each department looks after particular tasks, and each is headed by a member of the Federal Council.
wichtigste: There are seven departments, as many as there are federal councillors.
Each member of the Federal Council heads one department.
The FDFA, for example, is responsible for foreign policy.
Many federal offices work within the departments.
After elections, the Federal Council shares out the departments among its members.
In addition there is the Federal Chancellery as a staff office.

abschnitte.text: A **department** is a large part of the administration, similar to a ministry in other countries. It looks after a particular area, such as health, transport or finance. Each department is divided into several **federal offices**. Experts work there who prepare laws and put them into practice. Each department is headed by a federal councillor.

The **FDFA** looks after relations with other countries. The **FDHA**, the Department of Home Affairs, is responsible among other things for health, culture and the AVS. The **FDJP** deals with justice and police, the **DDPS** with defence, civil protection and sport. The **FDF** manages the finances, the **EAER** the economy, education and research. Finally, the **DETEC** is there for the environment, transport, energy and communications.

After every general election, or when a new member is elected, the **Federal Council** shares out the departments among its members. Usually the existing members keep their department. Sometimes someone moves to another department. The tasks of the departments can also change over time when areas are reassigned.

It is not only the Confederation that has departments. Many **cantons** also divide up their administration in this way. Depending on the canton, they are called departments or **directorates**. There is, for example, an education department that is responsible for schools. They are headed by the members of the **cantonal government**.

gewusst: The Federal Chancellery does not belong to any department and is headed by the Federal Chancellor.
The abbreviations of the departments come from their long names: in German, EDA (FDFA in English) stands for the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, for example.

teile.einleitung: People live in very different ways: renting, in their own flat, in a cooperative or in new forms of living together. In Switzerland the majority rent their homes.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the majority of households live in a rented flat.
In 2021 the home ownership rate was about 36 per cent.
In a housing cooperative, members buy share certificates and pay a cost rent.
With condominium ownership, you own a flat and a share of the whole building.
For a home of your own, banks usually require at least 20 per cent equity.
In September 2025 the people voted to abolish the imputed rental value.

abschnitte.text: Most people in Switzerland **rent** their homes. The **home ownership rate**, that is the share of households living in their own home, was about 36 per cent in 2021. That is low compared with other countries in Europe. How many flats are free is shown by the **vacancy rate**. On 1 June 2025, according to the Federal Statistical Office, it was about 1.0 per cent, and much lower in many cities.

A **housing cooperative** belongs to its members. Anyone who moves in buys **share certificates** and so becomes a co-owner of the cooperative. They pay a **cost rent**: it covers the costs of the building, but no profit is made. That is why cooperative flats are often cheaper. There are especially many cooperatives in Zurich.

With **condominium ownership**, a flat belongs to you, plus a share of the whole building with its roof, stairwell and garden. If you buy a home of your own, you need **equity**: banks usually require at least 20 per cent of the purchase price, and the rest is a **mortgage**. Until now, owners have had to pay tax on an **imputed rental value** as income. In September 2025 the voters approved a change of system that abolishes this tax.

A **cluster flat** combines small private flats, each with its own bathroom and sometimes a small kitchen, with large **shared rooms**. This way you have both privacy and company. In a **shared flat**, several people share one flat. For older people there is **assisted living**: you live in your own flat and can use support and emergency services when needed.

gewusst: Part of the equity for a home of your own may come from the pension fund.
The Federal Statistical Office counts the empty flats every year on 1 June.

teile.einleitung: After a meal, plates, glasses and pans are dirty. When you wash up, you make them clean again, either by hand or with the dishwasher.
wichtigste: By hand, you wash dishes with warm water and washing-up liquid.
Warm water and washing-up liquid loosen grease and food remains.
You start with the cleanest dishes, for example glasses.
Then you rinse the dishes and leave them to dry.
A dishwasher does the job automatically.

abschnitte.text: First you scrape the bigger food remains into the bin or the compost. Then you fill the sink with **warm water** and add a little **washing-up liquid**. With a sponge or a brush you rub the dishes clean. The washing-up liquid helps to loosen the **grease** from the dishes. Then you rinse the dishes briefly with clean water.

It is worth starting with the **cleanest dishes**. First come the **glasses**, then the cutlery and plates. At the very end you wash the greasy **pans**. This way the water stays clean for longer. If the water gets too dirty, you let it out and use fresh water. You do not put sharp knives into the sink, so that you do not cut yourself.

You put the clean dishes on a **draining rack**. There the water can drain off. You can also dry them with a clean **tea towel**. When everything is dry, you put it away in the cupboard. Washing up goes faster when several people help: one washes, one dries.

Many households have a **dishwasher**. You put the dishes in, add detergent and start a programme. The machine sprays hot water onto the dishes and then dries them. It is best to switch it on only when it is **full**. This way you save water and electricity.

gewusst: Grease hardly dissolves in cold water, but it does in warm water with washing-up liquid.
A full dishwasher often uses less water than washing up by hand under running water.

teile.einleitung: Nurses look after people who are ill, injured or old. They work in hospital, in a care home or in home care, known as Spitex. Without them no hospital could function.
wichtigste: Nurses look after people who are ill.
They take temperatures and blood pressure and give medicines.
They help patients in everyday life, for example with washing or eating.
They work closely with doctors.
In Switzerland you learn the job at a college of higher education or a university of applied sciences.
In hospital, work also goes on at night and at weekends.

abschnitte.text: Nurses are with the **patients** all day. They take their **temperature**, pulse and blood pressure. They give **medicines** as instructed by the doctor, change dressings and watch how the patients are doing. They help with washing, dressing and eating. And they listen when someone is frightened or sad.

In hospital many professions work together: doctors, nurses, **healthcare assistants**, physiotherapists and many more. Nurses are often the first to notice when a patient is getting worse. That is why good **communication** is very important. At every change of shift, what has happened is discussed in detail.

Many start with an apprenticeship as a **healthcare assistant EFZ**. After that you can become a nurse at a **college of higher education** (HF). Another path leads via the Matura to a **university of applied sciences** with a bachelor's degree in nursing. Empathy, a sense of responsibility and steady nerves are important.

People who are ill also need help at night. That is why nurses work in **shifts**: early shift, late shift and night shift. There is also someone there at weekends and on public holidays. In 2021 the Swiss voters accepted the **nursing initiative**. It aims to improve training and working conditions in nursing.

gewusst: Florence Nightingale is seen as the founder of modern nursing. Her birthday on 12 May is now International Nurses Day.
In the past people said “Krankenschwester” (sister), but today the job is called nurse (Pflegefachfrau or Pflegefachmann).

teile.einleitung: Batteries are found in torches, remote controls and many toys. They store energy and release it as electricity. Empty batteries do not belong in the rubbish, but in the battery collection.
wichtigste: A battery stores energy and releases it as electric current.
You take empty batteries to the collection box in the shop.
Batteries contain substances that harm nature.
A rechargeable battery can be charged again.
Button batteries must be kept out of the hands of small children.

abschnitte.text: Inside a **battery** there are different substances that react with each other. This produces **electric current**. Every battery has a **positive terminal** and a **negative terminal**. If you put it into the device the right way round, the current flows and the device works. When the substances are used up, the battery is flat. An early battery was invented by the Italian **Alessandro Volta** around the year 1800.

You only use a normal battery once. A **rechargeable battery** is a battery that you can **charge** again. Rechargeable batteries are found, for example, in mobile phones, tablets and bikes with motors. They can be charged many hundreds of times. This saves money and waste. For toys there are also rechargeable batteries in the shape of normal batteries.

Batteries contain **metals** and other substances that can harm nature. That is why they never belong in the rubbish or out in nature. In Switzerland many shops have a **collection box**. Anyone who sells batteries must take empty ones back. When you buy them you already pay a small fee for **recycling**. Valuable metals are recovered from old batteries.

Small round **button batteries** are dangerous for babies and toddlers. If they are swallowed, they can cause serious injuries. That is why you keep them safely shut away. Damaged **lithium batteries** can also get hot and even catch fire. You should never cut them open or throw them into a fire.

gewusst: The unit “volt”, used to measure electrical voltage, is named after Alessandro Volta.
Metals such as zinc, iron and manganese are recycled from collected batteries.

teile.einleitung: Epiphany, also called Three Kings’ Day, on 6 January recalls the three wise men from the East. In Switzerland people eat a Three Kings’ cake on this day. Whoever finds the hidden king may wear the crown.
wichtigste: Epiphany is on 6 January.
It recalls the wise men who, according to the Bible, visited the baby Jesus.
In tradition they are called Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar.
A small king figure is hidden in the Three Kings’ cake.
Whoever finds the king is king or queen for a day.
In some places star singers go from house to house.

abschnitte.text: According to the **Bible**, star-gazers from the East followed a bright star to Bethlehem. There they found the **baby Jesus** and gave him gold, frankincense and myrrh. In tradition they became **three kings** called **Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar**. The Church celebrates this day as **Epiphany**, the feast of the appearance of the Lord. For many people the Christmas season ends on 6 January.

The **Three Kings’ cake** is made of several round balls of dough which together form a kind of crown. The dough is a sweet yeast dough, often with raisins and pearl sugar. A small plastic **king figure** is hidden in one of the balls. Whoever finds it puts on the **paper crown**. The king or queen is often allowed to decide what happens that day.

As early as the Middle Ages there were cakes with something hidden inside, for example a bean. After that the custom was almost forgotten in Switzerland. In the 1950s the bread researcher **Max Währen** made it popular again. Since then bakeries and shops have sold a great many Three Kings’ cakes every year. In France there is a similar cake, the **Galette des Rois**.

In many Catholic parishes, children go from house to house as **star singers**. They are dressed as kings and carry a star. They sing songs and collect money for children in poor countries. Above the front door they often write **C+M+B** and the year in chalk. This stands for a Latin blessing: “May Christ bless this house”.

gewusst: The Bible gives neither the number nor the names of the wise men; these were added later in tradition.
In some cantons, 6 January is a public holiday, for example in Ticino.

teile.einleitung: Protective clothing protects people during dangerous work. A forestry worker using a chainsaw, for example, wears a helmet, ear protection and cut-resistant trousers. In many jobs protective clothing is compulsory.
wichtigste: Protective clothing protects you during dangerous work.
A forestry worker wears a helmet, ear protection and cut-resistant trousers.
Cut-resistant trousers can stop a running chainsaw.
Safety boots, gloves and safety goggles are also part of it.
It is also called personal protective equipment.
In Switzerland, Suva works for safety at work.

abschnitte.titel: The forestry worker in the forest
abschnitte.text: **Forestry workers** look after the forest and fell trees. To do this they work with the **chainsaw**. The saw is loud and dangerous, and branches or trees can fall down. That is why they wear a **helmet** with a face guard, **ear protection** and special **cut-resistant trousers**. On top of that come sturdy boots and gloves.

Inside **cut-resistant trousers** there are long, very strong fibres. If the running chain of the chainsaw touches the trousers, these fibres are pulled out. They wind round the drive wheel and **block** the chain within a very short time. This prevents a serious injury to the leg. After such an incident the trousers must be replaced.

There is protective clothing in other jobs too. On the **building site**, workers wear helmets and **safety boots** with steel toecaps. Anyone working by the road wears a bright **high-visibility vest**. In the laboratory, coats and **safety goggles** provide protection. Firefighters have clothing that can withstand heat. This is called **personal protective equipment**, PPE for short.

In Switzerland, employers must make sure that their employees can work safely. They provide the necessary **protective equipment**. The employees must also **wear** it. **Suva**, the largest accident insurer in Switzerland, informs and advises on safety at work. Apprentices in particular are trained well, because they still have little experience.

gewusst: Ear protection is important because too much noise can permanently damage your hearing.
A helmet for cycling or skiing is also a kind of protective equipment.

teile.einleitung: A budget is a plan for your own money. You write down how much money comes in and what you spend it on. This way you keep track and do not get into debt.
wichtigste: A budget compares income and spending.
The most important rule: do not spend more than you take in.
With a youth allowance, young people manage a fixed amount for their own spending.
If you do not pay a bill, you get a reminder, often with fees.
In Switzerland you come of age at 18.
Saving regularly helps you to fulfil bigger wishes.

abschnitte.text: **Income** includes, for example, pocket money, wages or presents. **Spending** includes everything you need money for. There are **fixed costs** that are the same every month, such as a mobile phone contract or a bus pass. Other spending changes, for example on free time or snacks. An example: Mia has 120 francs a month, pays 30 francs for her phone and 25 francs for her bus pass. That leaves her **65 francs** for other things.

If you regularly put something aside, you can afford bigger things later. Lea gets 50 francs pocket money and saves 15 francs every month. After a year she has 15 times 12, which is **180 francs**. Tim would like a bike for 600 francs. He saves 40 francs a month and so needs **15 months**. A **savings goal** helps you to keep going.

With a **youth allowance** (Jugendlohn), young people receive a fixed amount every month. With it they pay for spending agreed with their parents themselves, for example clothes, phone or free time. If you spend too much, you have to wait until the next month. This way you learn early how to handle money and set **priorities**.

If you do not pay a bill on time, you get a **reminder**. There are often extra fees. If you still do not pay, **debt collection proceedings** can be started against you. Later this can, for example, make it harder to find a flat. In Switzerland you **come of age at 18**. Before that, larger contracts such as a mobile phone contract need your parents' consent.

gewusst: At budget advice services in Switzerland you can get help setting up a budget free of charge or cheaply.
Small daily expenses, such as a drink on the go, often add up to a surprisingly large amount over a year.

teile.einleitung: **Drinking water** is clean water that you can drink without worrying. In Switzerland it comes fresh out of the tap. Water is the best thirst-quencher, and our body needs it every day.
wichtigste: Water is the best thirst-quencher because it has no sugar.
In Switzerland you can drink the tap water.
About 80 per cent of drinking water comes from groundwater and springs.
In hot weather and when doing sport you need to drink more.
More than half of the body is made of water.
A water bottle can be refilled again and again.

abschnitte.text: About **80 per cent** of Swiss drinking water comes from **groundwater** and **springs**. Groundwater collects in the ground when rain and snow seep away. The soil filters the water as it does so. The rest of the drinking water comes mainly from **lakes**. Switzerland has a lot of water, which is why it is also called the **water tower of Europe**.

**Tap water** in Switzerland is **checked** regularly. You can drink it without worrying. It is much cheaper than bottled water and creates no rubbish. When you are out and about, it is best to take a **water bottle** with you. You can refill it again and again, for example at a fountain with drinking water.

**Water** has no sugar and quenches thirst best. **Sugary drinks** such as lemonade, on the other hand, contain a lot of sugar. This harms your **teeth** and does not really fill you up. That is why you only drink them rarely. Unsweetened tea is also a good thirst-quencher.

**More than half** of the body is made of water. Every day we lose water, for example when breathing and sweating. That is why you have to drink every day. **Thirst** is the body's signal that it needs water. When it is **hot** or when you do **sport**, you sweat more and need to drink more.

gewusst: Many fountains in Swiss towns supply clean drinking water.
Large rivers such as the Rhine and the Rhone have their source in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Quality labels, also just called labels, are symbols on products. They show that a product meets certain rules, for example on the environment, animal welfare or fair work. This helps you choose better when shopping.
wichtigste: A quality label shows that a product keeps to certain rules.
Usually independent bodies check whether the rules are met.
FSC appears on wood and paper from responsible forestry.
IP-Suisse has a ladybird as its symbol.
The Bio Suisse Knospe (bud) marks organic products.
Not every symbol on a package is a strict label.

abschnitte.text: You cannot see on a package how a product was made. A **quality label** helps with this. It stands for fixed rules, for example less spraying, more space for animals or fair wages. With good labels, **independent inspection bodies** check whether the rules are kept. But there are also symbols that companies invent themselves and that say little.

**FSC** stands for Forest Stewardship Council. The label marks wood and paper from forests that are managed responsibly. No more wood is felled than grows back, and the rights of the people in the forest are respected. You can find the FSC symbol on furniture, exercise books, cardboard boxes and toilet paper.

**IP-Suisse** is an association of farmers who produce in a way that is close to nature and animal-friendly. Its symbol is a **ladybird**. The **Knospe** (bud) of Bio Suisse stands for organic products made according to strict organic guidelines. There are also labels for fair trade, for example **Fairtrade Max Havelaar**.

For fish there is the **MSC** label for sustainably caught wild fish and the **ASC** label for fish from responsible farming. For electrical appliances, the **energy label** shows how much electricity an appliance uses. If you want to know more about a label, you can look up on the internet which rules lie behind it.

gewusst: The ladybird is seen as a beneficial insect because it eats aphids, so it suits farming that is close to nature.
There are so many labels in Switzerland that consumer organisations publish their own guides to them.

teile.einleitung: Cheese is made from milk. Switzerland is famous for its many kinds of cheese, for example Emmental, Gruyère or Appenzeller. It takes a lot of work and patience before a cheese is ready.
wichtigste: Cheese is made from milk.
The job is called cheesemaker.
In cheesemaking, the milk separates into curds and whey.
Cheese ripens in the cool cheese cellar.
The holes in Emmental are made by gas bubbles.
On the alpine pastures, alpine cheese is made in summer.

abschnitte.text: The job is called **cheesemaker**. In Switzerland the apprenticeship is now called dairy technologist. In the **cheese dairy**, the cheesemaker turns milk into cheese. This needs a lot of knowledge and experience, because the temperature and the timing have to be exactly right. A village cheese dairy often processes the milk from the farms in the area.

First the milk is warmed in a large **cheese vat** (Kessi). Then **rennet** and bacterial cultures are added. The milk thickens. It is cut into small grains, the **curds**. As this happens, a yellowish liquid separates off, the **whey**. The curds are pressed into moulds, and this makes a wheel of cheese.

Then the wheels go into a salt bath and then into the cool **cheese cellar**. There they **ripen**, often for months. The wheels are cared for, rubbed with salt water and **turned** regularly. As Emmental ripens, bacteria produce a **gas**. The gas bubbles make the typical **holes**.

In summer many cows are up on the **alpine pastures**. Fresh grass with lots of herbs grows there. In the **alpine hut** the milk is made straight into **alpine cheese**, often still over a wood fire. In autumn the cows come back down to the valley, and the cheese is shared out or sold.

gewusst: A wheel of Emmental can weigh about 100 kilograms.
It takes about 12 litres of milk to make one kilogram of hard cheese.

teile.einleitung: Some people like helping others, listen well and stay calm even in difficult moments. This is a valuable strength. There are many jobs for them in healthcare and social care.
wichtigste: Patience and enjoying helping are important strengths for nursing.
Nurses look after people who are ill, injured or old.
In Switzerland the path often begins with the apprenticeship as a healthcare assistant EFZ.
You become a nurse at a college of higher education or a university of applied sciences.
Social care workers also work with people, for example with children or people with disabilities.
Nursing staff are urgently needed in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: People who like helping quickly notice when someone is not feeling well. Such people are often **patient**, **sensitive** and reliable. They can listen well and comfort others. These qualities are also called **social skills**. They are important in many jobs, but especially where people are cared for or looked after.

Nurses work in hospital, in old people's and care homes or for **Spitex**, which cares for people at home. They help with washing and eating, give out medicines and measure things such as blood pressure and temperature. They watch closely how the patients are doing and consult with doctors. Because people need help round the clock, the work also takes place in the evening, at night and at weekends.

A common way in is the three-year apprenticeship as a **healthcare assistant EFZ**, FaGe for short. After that you can train as a nurse at a **college of higher education** (HF) or a **university of applied sciences** (FH). There is also the two-year basic training as a health and social care assistant EBA. A **taster apprenticeship** helps you find out whether the job really suits you.

It is not only in nursing that people who like helping are needed. **Social care workers** support children in the Kita, older people or people with disabilities in their everyday lives. Paramedics help in emergencies. Teachers, physiotherapists and social workers also support other people. The careers advice service shows which of these jobs suits your own strengths best.

gewusst: The apprenticeship as a healthcare assistant is one of the most frequently chosen apprenticeships in Switzerland.
Men also work in nursing: in German the job title is then Pflegefachmann.

teile.einleitung: Knives are very useful in the kitchen, but they are also sharp. If you know a few simple rules, you can work with them safely and hurt neither yourself nor others.
wichtigste: You carry a knife with the point facing down.
You walk slowly while doing so.
When cutting, the blade points away from your body.
You cut on a chopping board.
You never put a knife into a full bowl of washing-up water.

abschnitte.text: When you carry a knife through the kitchen, the **point faces down**. It is best to hold it close to your body. This way you cannot accidentally hurt anyone, even if someone suddenly gets in the way. You **walk slowly** and never run with a knife. If you pass a knife to someone, it is best to put it down on the table rather than handing it over directly.

You always cut on a **chopping board** that lies flat and does not slip. You curl the fingers of the hand holding the vegetable slightly inwards. This position is called the **claw grip**. This way your fingertips do not get under the blade. A **sharp knife** is safer than a blunt one, because you have to press less and it slips less.

You never put a knife into a full bowl of washing-up water where you cannot see it. You wash it separately and dry it with the blade pointing away from your body. Then you **put it away** in a knife block or in a drawer with a guard. Small children should only cut with adults and with suitable children's knives.

gewusst: The Swiss army knife is world-famous and has been made in Switzerland since the 19th century.

teile.einleitung: Our body constantly needs energy: for breathing, for the heartbeat, for thinking and for every movement. It gets this energy from food. How much you need is called your energy needs.
wichtigste: The basal metabolic rate is the energy the body needs when completely at rest.
Exercise clearly increases energy needs.
Children and teenagers need more energy per kilogram because they are growing.
The official unit for energy is the joule; one kilocalorie is about 4.2 kilojoules.
1 g of fat provides 9 kcal, 1 g of carbohydrates or protein 4 kcal each.
If you eat more than you use for a long time, you put on weight.

abschnitte.text: Even when we are lying completely still, our body is working. The heart beats, we breathe, and the body keeps itself **warm**. The energy for this is called the **basal metabolic rate**. When exercise is added, the body needs extra energy. This is the **activity energy expenditure**. An hour of **cycling** increases the need a lot, whereas reading or watching television hardly does.

Children and teenagers have higher energy needs per kilogram of body weight than adults. When **growing**, the body builds new bones, muscles and other tissues. For this it needs extra energy and enough **nutrients**. That is why a balanced diet is especially important at this age.

The official unit for energy is the **joule**, named after the scientist James Prescott Joule. On food, energy is given in **kilojoules** (kJ) and in **kilocalories** (kcal). One kilocalorie equals 4.184 kilojoules, so about 4.2 kJ. 1 g of **fat** provides 9 kcal, 1 g of carbohydrates or protein 4 kcal each. A muesli with 50 g of carbohydrates, 10 g of fat and 10 g of protein therefore provides 200 plus 90 plus 40, which is **330 kcal**.

**Energy density** tells you how much energy there is in a certain amount of a food, for example per 100 grams. **Vegetables** have a low energy density because they contain a lot of water. **Nuts** and chocolate have a high energy density because they contain a lot of fat. So you can eat a lot of vegetables, while a handful of nuts is enough.

The **energy balance** compares how much energy you eat and how much you use. If you regularly eat more than you need, the balance is **positive**. The body stores the extra energy mainly as **fat**, and you put on weight. If you use more than you eat, you lose weight. Exercise and balanced eating help you to stay in balance.

gewusst: The brain uses a large part of the energy of the basal metabolic rate, even though it makes up only about two per cent of body weight.
Being cold also increases energy needs, because the body then has to produce more heat.

teile.einleitung: Your first flat of your own is a big step. As well as the excitement, there is a lot to organise: the application, the tenancy agreement, moving in, registering and a budget for the housing costs.
wichtigste: Landlords often ask for an extract from the debt collection register.
When you move in, a handover report records the condition of the flat.
You report defects discovered later quickly and in writing.
In most municipalities you register with the residents' registration office within 14 days.
The kitchen and bathroom do not count in the number of rooms.
Housing costs should take up at most about a third of your net income.

abschnitte.text: For a rented flat you usually have to apply. Many landlords ask for an **extract from the debt collection register**. It shows whether debt collection proceedings have been started against someone. For landlords this is a sign of whether someone pays their bills reliably. In Switzerland the **number of rooms** only counts living rooms and bedrooms. The kitchen, bathroom, toilet and hallway do not count. A half room is often a dining area or a kitchen-diner.

Budget advice services recommend that **rent and service charges** should not take up more than about a quarter to a **third of your net income**. Otherwise there is too little money left for other things. The landlord often asks for a **rental deposit**. It may be at most three months' rent and is paid into a blocked account. On top of this comes the **radio and television licence fee**: in 2026 it is 335 francs per household and is collected by the collection agency Serafe.

When you move in, the tenant and the landlord draw up a **handover report** together. It records damage and defects that already existed. This way you do not have to pay for damage done by the previous tenant when you move out. If you discover further **defects** shortly after moving in, you report them to the landlord quickly and **in writing**. Many tenancy agreements set a short deadline for this.

After the move you register with the **residents' registration office** of the new municipality. In most cantons this must be done within **14 days**. The exact rules are set by the cantons and municipalities. **Household contents insurance** and **personal liability insurance** are also sensible. The second pays if you accidentally damage something that belongs to someone else.

gewusst: In Switzerland the majority of households rent their homes; in hardly any other country in Europe is the proportion so high.
For 2027 the Federal Council has decided to reduce the radio and television licence fee to 312 francs.

teile.einleitung: **Vitamins** are vital substances that the body needs only in small amounts. It cannot make most of them itself, so they have to come from food. A distinction is made between water-soluble and fat-soluble vitamins.
wichtigste: A lack of vitamin C causes scurvy.
With sunlight, the skin makes vitamin D.
Vitamin A is important for seeing in dim light.
Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods.
Vitamin K is needed for blood clotting.
Cooking briefly with little water protects the vitamins.

abschnitte.text: On long **sea voyages** in the past there was no fresh fruit or vegetables. Many sailors got **scurvy**, with bleeding gums and wounds that healed badly. The reason was a lack of **vitamin C**. Today we know that there is a lot of vitamin C in fruit and vegetables. **Red peppers** even contain more than oranges, often over 100 milligrams per 100 grams.

Vitamins **A, D, E and K** are **fat-soluble**. The eye needs **vitamin A** for the visual pigment in the retina. If there is not enough, **night blindness** can develop. Carrots contain a lot of **beta-carotene**, a precursor that the body turns into vitamin A. The skin can make **vitamin D** itself with the help of **sunlight**; it is important for strong bones. **Vitamin K** helps with **blood clotting** and is found mainly in green leafy vegetables.

The water-soluble vitamins include vitamin C and the **B vitamins**. **Folic acid** (vitamin B9) is important for **cell division** and **making blood**. Its name comes from the Latin word for leaf, because it is found in **leafy vegetables**. **Vitamin B12** is made by bacteria and gets into food mainly through meat, fish, eggs and dairy products. That is why people who eat a **vegan** diet should take it as a supplement.

Vitamin C and many B vitamins dissolve in **cooking water** and are **sensitive to heat**. If you boil vegetables for a long time in a lot of water, they are lost. **Cooking briefly** with little water is better, for example steaming. Raw vegetables and fruit also provide lots of vitamins. A varied diet usually covers your needs well.

gewusst: Red peppers contain more vitamin C than oranges.
Vitamin D is also called the “sunshine vitamin”, because the skin makes it with sunlight.

teile.einleitung: Carbohydrates are an important part of our food. They give the body energy. Carbohydrates include various kinds of sugar, starch and dietary fibre.
wichtigste: Carbohydrates are the body's most important source of energy.
Glucose is also called grape sugar and is carried in the blood.
Milk sugar is called lactose, fruit sugar is called fructose.
Household sugar is sucrose.
Potatoes, rice and cereals contain a lot of starch.
The body stores carbohydrates as glycogen in the liver and muscles.
Wholegrain fills you up for longer thanks to its fibre.

abschnitte.text: The simplest carbohydrates are **simple sugars**. The most important is **glucose**, also called grape sugar. It is carried in the blood. **Fructose**, or fruit sugar, is found in fruit and honey and tastes sweeter than household sugar. **Lactose** is milk sugar. People with lactose intolerance find it hard to digest.

Ordinary household sugar is called **sucrose**. It is a **double sugar** made of glucose and fructose. It is obtained from sugar cane or from **sugar beet**. In Switzerland it comes mainly from sugar beet, which is processed, for example, in Aarberg and Frauenfeld.

Plants store energy as **starch**, a **complex sugar** made of many glucose units. Potatoes, rice, maize and cereals are therefore important sources of starch. Humans also store carbohydrates: extra glucose is turned into **glycogen** and stored in the liver and muscles. When it is needed, it is broken down into glucose again.

The digestion of starch begins in the **mouth**. Saliva contains **amylase**, which splits starch into smaller sugar units. That is why bread tastes slightly sweet if you chew it for a long time. **Wholegrain products** contain lots of **fibre** from the outer layers of the grain. This makes blood sugar rise more slowly, and you stay full for longer.

The **brain** normally gets its energy almost entirely from glucose. It uses about a fifth of the energy the body needs at rest. That is why it is important to eat regularly. Carbohydrates from wholegrain, potatoes, pulses, vegetables and fruit are especially good.

gewusst: The brain makes up only about two per cent of body weight, but needs about a fifth of the energy used at rest.
Dietary fibre is one of the carbohydrates, but provides hardly any energy, because the small intestine cannot break it down.

teile.einleitung: Almost every item of clothing has a small label sewn into it. On it are **care label symbols**. These symbols tell you how the item may be washed, dried, ironed and cleaned so that it stays nice for a long time.
wichtigste: The washing tub stands for washing, the number inside for the highest temperature.
A hand in the washing tub means hand wash.
The triangle stands for bleaching; crossed out, it means do not bleach.
The circle in a square stands for the tumble dryer.
The iron shows with dots how hot you may iron.
An empty circle applies to professional textile cleaning.

abschnitte.text: The first symbol is a **washing tub**. The **number** inside gives the highest washing temperature in degrees Celsius. With 30 you may wash at no more than 30 degrees; colder is allowed. A **bar** under the tub calls for a **gentle wash**. **Two bars** mean an especially gentle wash, for example for wool. A **hand** in the tub means: hand wash only.

The **triangle** stands for bleaching. If it is **crossed out**, you may not use bleach or washing powder containing bleach. A **circle in a square** is the symbol for the **tumble dryer**. If it is crossed out, the item must not go in the tumble dryer. Then you hang it up to dry.

An **iron** on the label shows whether and how hot you may iron. The **dots** inside give the temperature. **One dot** stands for low heat, for example for synthetic fibres. **Three dots** allow the hottest setting. You often find them on **cotton** and **linen**. A crossed-out iron means: do not iron.

An **empty circle** stands for **professional textile care**, for example at a dry cleaner's. **Letters** in the circle show the specialist which cleaning method is allowed. If the circle is crossed out, the item must not be dry-cleaned. If you follow the symbols, you stop clothes from shrinking or losing their colour.

gewusst: The care symbols are the same internationally, so you can understand them without knowing the language.
Many clothes get just as clean at 30 degrees, and it uses less energy.

teile.einleitung: Household contents insurance protects your own belongings, such as furniture, clothes, electronics and other movable things. It pays if these things are damaged or lost through fire, water or theft.
wichtigste: Household contents include all movable things in the flat.
The insurance covers fire, natural hazards, water and theft.
Usually the replacement value is paid.
If the sum insured is too low, this is called underinsurance.
Simple theft away from home usually needs extra cover.
In many cantons the building is insured with a cantonal building insurer.
In cases of gross negligence, the insurer can reduce the payment.

abschnitte.text: **Household contents** include all movable things, such as furniture, clothes, books, crockery and electronics. The insurance pays for damage caused by **fire**, **natural hazards** such as floods or storms, by **water** and in the case of **burglary**. Most insurers pay the **replacement value**, which is the amount needed to buy equivalent new things.

The **sum insured** should match the replacement value of all your household contents. If it is too low, there is **underinsurance**. Then the insurer reduces its payment in the same proportion. An example: household contents worth 60,000 francs are only insured for 40,000 francs, so for two thirds. With water damage of 9000 francs, the insurer then pays only **6000 francs**.

A burglary in the flat is included in the basic cover. **Simple theft away from home**, such as a locked bike at the station, usually has to be insured in addition. Anyone who acts with **gross negligence**, for example by leaving a burning candle unattended, risks the insurer reducing its payment. Some policies waive this in return for an extra premium.

The **building** itself is not part of the household contents. In 19 cantons, buildings must be insured with a **cantonal building insurer**. This insurance is paid for by the owner. Tenants only insure their own household contents. This makes it clear who is responsible for what.

gewusst: Household contents insurance is compulsory in the cantons of Nidwalden, Fribourg and Vaud.
It is worth photographing valuable items and keeping receipts so that you can prove their value if there is damage.
